*Tarkatāṇḍava* — Chapter Two —
Homage to Lakṣmī-Hayagrīva, who is the essence of Śrīmad-Dhanvantari, Bhīma, Madhva, Ānanda-Tīrtha, Rāghavendra, Kṛṣṇācārya, and Vedavyāsa.
Oṃ.
Now follows the examination of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

Regarding this which is said: "If the Veda were not of human origin, it would lack validity because it would be devoid of the defining characteristics of a valid word, such as being the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*)," [we reply as follows].
*Nyāyadīpākhyā* (The Lamp of Reasoning): A Commentary.
Now follows the investigation of expectancy (ākāṅkṣā).
I bow to that Supreme Bliss, the breast of the abode of Indirā, in whom reside the expectancy, semantic competency, and other [criteria] of the entire Veda.
Now, an objection is raised: it was improper to establish the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas in the first chapter;
for if that were the case, they would fail to qualify as authoritative words (*pramāṇa-śabda*) due to the absence of the defining characteristics of verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*).
And thus [the verse] says: "by those [words] devoid of a beginning..."

Having restated the objection—that since it was said "it was told with reverence," devotion (*śakti*) and intent (*tātparya*) are not applicable to Hari—he refutes it with the words "And that which... (*yacceti*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādipadena*), there is the inclusion of [the properties of] being preceded by a trustworthy person (*āptapūrvakaśabdatva*), being produced by a knowledge of the sentence-meaning that corresponds to reality (*yathārthavākyārthajñānajanyatva*), and being a sentence (*vākyatva*), and so forth.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Second Chapter, p. 2) 1. Endowed with infinite auspicious qualities—U. 2. [End of page 2] *----------------------- ----------------- -----------*
That is not so; for it has been stated in the *Paddhati* that the definition of scripture (*āgama*) consists in being a word free from defects or being a sentence free from defects.
Here, the first definition—“a word that is faultless and traditional” (āgama)—follows the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since the inclusion of the qualification “faultless” is necessary for the purpose of excluding defects such as being purposeless, there is no need to mention the term “sentence” (*vākya*), as it would otherwise result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to things that are non-expressive or lack syntactic connection.
The meaning is: "of that which is the definition of a word that has become a means of valid cognition."
Validity.
The meaning is "the state of being a producer of light.
The intention is that previously [it was stated] that its self-nature is established at a distance.
"In the manual" (paddhatau).
"Explanation" (*nirdeśa*) means "word" (*śabda*) or "scriptural tradition" (*āgama*), or alternatively, it means "statement" (*vākya*); that is to say, it refers to the path (*paddhati*).
The mention of both [terms] is for the purpose of clarifying their intended meaning.

And thus, the sense is that the authority of the Veda is logical because other defining characteristics are possible. By this, the intended meaning of the stated definition of scripture (*āgama*) is made clear.
Furthermore, he reveals the basis for the mention of "both" and its underlying existence with the words "herein."

Now, one might object: how then is the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to mere sentence-semblances (*vākyābhāsa*), which are either non-informative or convey a contrary meaning, avoided? [The answer is: It is by accepting that the second definition intends to exclude such cases, since it was stated in the *Paddhati* itself: "A sentence consists of words possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*sannidhi*)," followed by the statement: "By the term 'wordhood' (*padatvena*), non-denotability is excluded; by 'expectancy' and 'proximity,' the absence of syntactic connection (*anvayābhāva*) is excluded. Thus, on the basis of this, [the objection is resolved] through the absence of denotation and the absence of syntactic connection.

Keeping in mind the statement regarding the function of faultless words— beginning with “or [the charge of] non-communicativeness” and so forth— and following the method of explaining the intended meaning, he states the purport:
“In the case of being purposeless,” etc.
(Ākāṅkṣā-nirūpaṇam) The discourse on expectancy (ākaṅkṣāvādaḥ),
Part 3. Second, however, the statement "Scripture is a sentence free from defects" follows the *Brahmatarka*.
1. Here, the mention of "sentence" (vākya) is for the purpose of making the students understand the essential nature of words, sentences, and so forth.

For this very reason, in the *Paddhati*, the definitions of words (*pada*) and so forth are stated as follows: "In the second view, a word consists of phonemes ending in an inflection, or a sentence consists of words possessing expectancy, compatibility, and contiguity," and so on.
[This refers to the work] called the *Brahmatarka*.
The meaning is "the Brahma-tarka mentioned in the *Tattvanirṇaya*.

Now, one might object: "If it is sufficient to say simply 'word' (*śabda*) in the manner stated above, then the term 'sentence' (*vākya*) is redundant"; to this he replies: "In this context, the word 'sentence' (*vākya*)...
The intention is that, on this view, the term "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*) serves to exclude other defects that would otherwise be excluded by the term "sentence" as used in the *Paddhati*.
"Ending in case-terminations."
The meaning is that they end in *sup* (nominal) and *tiṅ* (verbal) case endings;
for in the rule "vibhaktaśca" (Pāṇini 1.4.104), both *sup* and *tiṅ* are designated as "vibhakti" (case ending).
This is based on the Pāṇinian sūtra "suptiṅantaṃ padam" (Pāṇini 1.4.14), which defines a word (*pada*) as that which ends in *sup* or *tiṅ*. This is the intended sense.
In this context, the plural number is used because it is intended to be illustrative.
The meaning is: "a word-ending phoneme," or "two such phonemes," or "such phonemes.
That is to say, the state of being a word consists in being a phoneme that ends in a case-ending.
Although the state of having an ending case-suffix (*vibhaktyantatva*) is never absent from phonemes (*varṇa*), the expression "phonemes" (*varṇāḥ*) is used for the sake of clarity.
In cases such as *rājapuruṣa*, the mention of "phonemes" is intended to exclude the status of being a word (*padatva*) from a collection of multiple words that ends in a case-suffix.
Its meaning is: those for which a case-suffix is precisely at the end (*anta*) are "ending in a case-suffix" (*vibhaktyanta*).

Regarding examples such as *rājapuruṣa*, some maintain that even though the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is elided in the middle, it was indeed present there. Others, however, say that its elision is for the very purpose of securing the status of being a "word" (*pada*) for that compound;

for since the aggregate [of the two words] is distinct from the case-endings produced from the two constituent parts of the two words, the aggregate of phonemes residing in the two words also possesses the quality of ending in a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta-varṇatva*).
Others maintain that the mention of "phonemes" (varṇa) is for the purpose of refuting the sphoṭa that is distinct from the phonemes. 5.
"Mutual expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) means that among the very words being employed, the words themselves possess mutual expectancy.

[Notes: 1. *tatra* – *ja-ka*. 2. *nisū* – *u*. 3. "For the purpose of refuting the view that phonemes (*varṇa*) are distinct from the word-sphoṭa" – *u*. 4. "The statement [ending with] '... – *rāja* – *u*. 5. "Phonemes," etc., does not exist – *u*.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*: "The word 'śabda' occurring in the root text refers to a sentence (*vākya*)."
Now, one might ask: what is this expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)? It cannot be inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), for it is absent in cases such as "bring the jar."
For a jar is not invariably concomitant with the act of bringing;
therefore, there is no contradiction with the commentary on the *Bhāṣya* which states that "a sentence consists of words that have no further expectancy.

This is because the *Candrikā* explains its meaning as follows: "A sentence is a collection of words that have no expectancy toward anything else, precisely because they possess full expectancy within themselves."
The plural number in the word *padāni* is intended to indicate a general plurality.

Here too, the purpose of employing the term *pada* should be understood as being similar to the previous use of the term *varṇa*: namely, to exclude the *sphoṭa* of non-sentential units (*avākya-sphoṭa*).

The expression "words" (*padāni*) is stated in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to those instances where the word consists of a co-occurrence of stem and suffix (*prakṛti-pratyaya-samabhivyāhāra*).
By the phrase "of words and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes sentence, expectancy, proximity, and the like.
"For this very reason" [refers to the following].

The meaning is: "precisely because it is for the purpose of explaining the true nature of words and so forth" (3), and "precisely because it is for the purpose of corroborating the Brahmatarka" (4). [This refers to] the term "mūla" (the root).
The meaning is that the phrase "nirdeśaḥ śabda āgamaḥ" (the instruction is the word, the tradition) is found in the root text (*mūla*).

Therein, in the *Paddhati* [commentary], in the section defining the sentence (*vākyalakṣaṇa*), he states the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in order to determine the nature of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), which was mentioned first: "But surely... (*nanu*).
The meaning is: what is this expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) of words?
It is [the absence of completion], because of non-existence. 6.
With the thought that this is because of mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*), he says: "For not... and so forth.
Or rather, it is also observed that bringing [the jar] is invariably concomitant with the jar;
by this, the claim that there is an invariable concomitance of the agent with the action, and of the action with the agent, is refuted.

For, in the absence of such a relationship between specific actions and specific agents, the two expressions "action" and "agent" would result in being mutually independent, as in the case of the pair "bring" and "jar."
The statement regarding the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "the lotus is blue" (*maṇau nīlaṃ sarojam*) is improper;

the point is that in those instances, there exists an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the blue color and the lotus, which are the objects intended by the speaker’s purport (*tātparya*).
(Definition of Expectancy) The Theory of Expectancy (Ākāṅkṣāvāda), Part 5.

Furthermore, in the case of the sentence "The water of the river is pure; a buffalo is roaming on the bank," there would be the undesirable consequence that the word *nadī* ("river"), which has expectancy toward the word *jala* ("water"), would also have expectancy toward the word *kaccha* ("bank"), since the bank is invariably concomitant with the river.
Nor is expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), as defined by Udayana and others, the prior absence of the cognition of a relation produced by the utterance [of a word] in the hearer.

For in the case of the sentence "The king's son comes; let the man be removed," there would be the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti): even when the word *rājñaḥ* ("king's") is expectant of *putraḥ* ("son"), if—due to a misconception regarding its intended meaning (*tātparya*)—there arises a cognition of its connection with *puruṣaḥ* ("man"), then at that time the prior absence of the cognition of its connection with *putraḥ* still exists. Thus, the definition would over-apply.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that even in the present context there exists an inseparable relation (avinābhāva) intended as the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākārakabhāva), characterized by the form that delimits the category of the word-meaning? To this, he says: "Oh, how pure! (aho vimalam).
Anticipating the objection that this might exclude the over-extension mentioned previously, he refutes it by saying: "Nor also... (nāpi).
The meaning is that *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) is the aforementioned prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) existing in the hearer.

Here, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such pseudo-sentences as "pot, objectness, bringing, action"— which have the same meaning as "bring the pot"— the qualification "produced by the utterance of those [words]" is applied to the cognition.
Some say that [the word "it"] is for the purpose of precluding the impossibility [of the definition] from the perspective of the speaker;
others say it is a statement of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The meaning is as follows: in the previously mentioned sentence "Aho vivalam," due to the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), there is sometimes no comprehension of the connection between the marsh (*kaccha*) and the river (*nadī*);

even though the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of that connection exists, because of the intention behind the utterance, there is no comprehension of the marsh being connected with the river qualified by water, and thus that prior absence does not exist [in this specific context]. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
The phrase "in this [context]" (*ityatra*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood that the words "and in the preceding sentence" (*pūrvavākye ca*) are also implied.

[Notes: 1. *ṇa sā* — *ca*. 2. The word *prasaṅgāt* is added — *ga*. 3. *pteḥ* — *ja*, *ka*, *gha*. 3. The phrase "to prevent expectancy in other cases" (*anyatra sākāṅkṣatvavāraṇāya*) is present — *u*. 4. *jalānvita nādyāḥ saṃ* — *u*.
Nor is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) the prior absence of the comprehension of the relation that constitutes the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*);
for since a prior absence is a cause of all effects whatsoever, it cannot be considered a unique cause specific to verbal cognition.
And this will be explained later.
As for what was stated in the *Maṇi*: "Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the non-termination of the denotative function (*abhidhāna*).

That which, in the absence of another, lacks the capacity to bring about the cognition of the connection of its own meaning with that [other], has precisely that [other] as its non-termination. And the lack of capacity to bring about the cognition of anything else is the prior absence of the cognition of the connection."

For this very reason, a word that has already produced the cognition of its own syntactic relation (anvaya) does not require [another word] at that time, because the prior absence [of that relation] no longer exists. However, in some cases, due to the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), there may be a comprehension of the connection with water; yet, even if the connection with the riverbank is not understood, it is possible that in another usage, through a misconception regarding the speaker's intention, the connection with the riverbank might again fail to be understood. Therefore, [the requirement for expectancy] pertains to the object of the speaker's intention.
The meaning is that since the cognition of the sequence of persons (*puruṣānvaya*) is not the intended object (*tātparyaviṣaya*), the previously mentioned fault does not apply.
The phrase "because it is impossible for [the sequence] to be unique to the word" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*);
for the prior absence of the comprehension of the relation (*saṃsarga*) still exists.
It should also be understood that for a sentence whose syntactic connection (*anvaya*) has already been produced, there would result the fault of being expectant (*sākāṅkṣatva*).
This will be explained [later].

The desire to state the [author's] own view regarding the refutation of intrinsic nature (*svarūpakhaṇḍana*) is found in the passage beginning with “Furthermore, regarding prior non-existence” (*kiñca prāgabhāvasya*) and so forth.
As for the phrase "in the gem" (maṇau):
The meaning is that this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in the section on words (*śabdakhaṇḍa*).

Now, if it is argued that "denotation" (abhidhāna) is the experience of syntactic connection (anvaya), and its "completion through semantic saturation" (aparyavasāna) means the realization of its meaning—since this [process] certainly exists in cases such as "karmatvam" (the state of being an object)—[the author] states the specific meaning of the word *aparyavasāna* as explained in the *Maṇi*: "of which... (*yasya*).

The meaning is as follows: when a word is presented, if the non-experience of the connection with its own referent (*svārtha*) is necessitated by the absence (*vyatireka*) of another word, then that very non-experience of the connection by that [first] word is "non-finality" (*aparyavasāna*). And that [non-finality] together with that [second word] constitutes "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*). (Note: The following technical notes regarding variant readings from the manuscripts are provided for the sake of completeness, as per the source text's inclusion.

1. śabdā-ga-ja-gha. 2. *anvaya* is added—ga. 3. *na* is added—ga-ja-ka. 4. *nubhā*—ga-ja-ka. 5. *masā*—ca. 6. *dhyeyam*—u. 7. *svarūpa* is absent—ū. (End of the section on the Definition of Expectancy)
The doctrine of expectancy (ākāṅkṣāvāda) [is as follows]:
For this reason, this [capacity] is distinct from the capacity of essential nature (svarūpayogyatā);
for the latter exists even when the effect has already been produced.
But this [expectancy] exists even prior to the production of the fruit (*phala*).
Nor is it impossible for there to be a gradation consisting of intensity and non-intensity within expectancy, on the grounds that there is no gradation in the absence [of the fruit] itself;
for such a gradation is established simply by the nature of the words being related or unrelated, and so forth.
And this [cognition] is the cause [of expectancy];
otherwise, if one were free from expectancy, there would be no cognition of the logical connection (anvaya) due to that error.
However, expectancy is not the desire to know the meanings of the words uttered together (*samabhivyāhṛta*).

Because it is observed that even a person who lacks a desire for knowledge— due to not knowing that knowledge is a means to achieve a desired end— still undergoes verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).
Furthermore, on this view, the cognition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣājñāna*) would not be a cause [of verbal comprehension],
since verbal comprehension is observed to occur even when there is no inquiry (*jijñāsā*).

That too is not correct, because it does not apply to metaphorical (gauṇa) and indicative (lākṣaṇika) words. For according to your position, their lack of expressiveness is not caused by the absence of the other [the primary meaning],
but rather is inherent in themselves.

Furthermore, it is possible that the word "bank" (ghoṣapada) alone does not require [the word "Ganges"] (gaṅgāpada), whereas the word "Ganges" (gaṅgāpada) does not [require the word "bank"] in relation to the word "bank."
Nor is it correct to argue that there is no lack of over-extension (*avyāpti*) when the term "non-indicator" (*ajñāpaka*) is substituted for the term "non-experiencer" (*ananubhāvaka*).
For inquiry (*jijñāsā*) consists of a desire for knowledge; and such a desire arises only when the knowledge in question is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), and not otherwise. Thus...

Furthermore, since verbal cognition is observed to occur even when there is no awareness that the object is a means to achieve what is desired— due to the deviation in negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra)— the meaning is that this expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is not the cause of verbal cognition.
"Secondary (gauṇa)" refers to the two cases "Caitra is a lion" and "a hamlet on the Ganges.
In that regard, according to the view of Maṇu, he clarifies the non-expressiveness of the words "lion" and "Ganges" with the words "for not in your position."
The passage beginning with "itaraviraha" is a restatement of the essential meaning expressed by the verse beginning with "yasya yena";
[the phrase] "svata eva" means "by itself alone."
The meaning is: "Precisely because it is caused by the unsuitability [of the word] in its own form.

The point is that, just as in cases such as "the jar is the objectness" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*), the lack of cognitive efficacy is caused solely by the unsuitability of the word's own form, and not caused by the absence of another word, so it is here.
Anticipating the objection that "because it is imperceptible, it cannot lead to the fault of over-extension," he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not).
The meaning is that it would contradict direct experience (*anubhava*).
The word division is *ajñāpakapada* (the word "non-informative"). [Note: Variants from manuscripts:
1. *dhat*—ga; 2. *desā*—ga-ja; *dasā*—ka; 3. *ditu*—ja; 4. *de iti*—ga-ja-ga; 5. the word "*pada*" is absent—ga.]

6. *jñā-ū.* 7. When there is knowledge of "you" (*tvajñāne sati*)—*u*. 8. Since this [definition] indeed exists—that "without which [x], that [y] lacks the capacity to produce cognition"—he clarifies this by stating "it exists"—*u*. 9. This is the meaning—*u*.
(End of the section on the definition of expectancy.)

Regarding the theory of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣāvāda*): even in the absence of other words, a word functions as a reminder; therefore, its lack of informativeness is not caused by the absence of other words.
Furthermore, since antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the cause of all effects, there would be no unique status for verbal cognition (*śābda*).

Nor should it be argued that in the case of verbal cognition (*śābdānubhava*), the antecedent absence of the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvayānubhavaprāgabhāva*) cannot serve as an uncommon cause because its existence is necessitated by the absence of subsequent words;
for this very reason, it has been specified [in the definition] by the phrase "without which.

This is because, although the antecedent absence of verbal cognition is necessitated by the absence of those other words due to their being cooperative causes, it nonetheless functions as a cause in the verbal cognition of a jar and so forth simply by virtue of being an antecedent absence.

Otherwise, even the prior absence of a jar would be a cause for the [non-existence] of the jar, by virtue of being necessitated by the absence of the staff and so forth. Nor is it correct to argue that although a word causes the recollection of its own meaning, it still does not make known the syntactic relation (*anvaya*), because that [making known the relation] alone is intended in the definition [of a word]. This is not tenable.
This is because, according to the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related), as will be explained below, there exists the capacity to recall one's own meaning as already related;

furthermore, even in the opponent's view (*paramata*), since the word-meaning is precisely the individual (*vyakti*) related to the genus (*jāti*) and the configuration (*ākṛti*), it possesses the capacity to recall the connection with the genus and so forth—this is the intended sense.
Now, an objection: "If that object which is presented by a word cannot become an object of experience through the absence of that word..."
The meaning of the definition is "having expectancy for that" (*tatsākāṅkṣatvam*).

And thus, since the state of being an object of experience for the riverbank (*tīra*) and so forth does not occur without the word "cowherd settlement" (*ghoṣa*) and so on, even words used in a secondary sense (*lākṣaṇika*) possess expectancy; therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the statement by Pakṣadhara and others. Anticipating this, the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*) states another fault—beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*)—and refutes it with the passage beginning "Nor [is it the case] that... (*na ca...*).
"By way of being a cooperative cause."
The meaning is: "by way of being an auxiliary factor for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*)."
Furthermore, the knowledge of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not the cause of verbal cognition; thus, there is no lack of commonality [with other means of knowledge],
because there is no evidence for such knowledge being a causal factor.
For it is not established by experience that prior to the verbal cognition there is no knowledge of the relation "this is mine" (*mamatva*);
otherwise, even in the case of a jar, its prior non-existence would have to be known as the cause [of its subsequent production].

Now, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not required as such, but rather by way of being the absence of a positive relation conditioned by the absence of others—a property common to both prior non-existence and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Thus, it is not a unique [probans].
This is because, in the case of a jar and so forth, [the probans] functions precisely as prior non-existence.
He raises an objection regarding the uniqueness of the word [as the cause] for the prior absence of the comprehension of a relation, by means of another perspective—beginning with "Now" (atha).
The mention of "prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*) and "absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāva*) is illustrative; "destruction" (*dhvaṃsa*) should also be understood [as included].
For this very reason, the statement defining the cause is made by way of its being an experience of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) conditioned by the absence of others.

Otherwise, having stated that the delimiting condition of the cause (*hetutāvacchedaka*) is simply "being the absence of the experience of positive concomitance" (*anvayānubhavābhāvatva*), one would not have said "caused by the absence of others" (*itaravirahaprayukta*).
This is because [the latter phrase] serves to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the state of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).

It is only when the intention is to define the cause as "the absence of relation to the experience of positive concomitance" (*anvayānubhava-saṃsargābhāvatva*) that the phrase "caused by the absence of others" becomes meaningful.

If it is argued that because destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is causeless, there is no commonality [of the definition] with it, then there would likewise be no commonality with absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Therefore, one should reflect that he will later state: "Nor at the stage of the destruction of the cognition of positive concomitance," and so forth.

Alternatively, let it be common to both as stated; since causality exists simply by virtue of being the absence of the experience of positive concomitance, the term "other" (*itara*) and other qualifiers are mentioned precisely to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to destruction.
But in the case of a jar and so forth, it is not thus; so he says: "In the case of a jar and so forth."
The phrase "of its prior absence" (tatprāgabhāvasya) is to be supplied [to the previous statement].
He clarifies what was stated by the words "for this very reason" (ata eva) with the word "then" (tadā).
[Notes: 1. *syāsā* — *ja*. 2. The word "pada" is added — *u*. 3. *tvena ta* — *u*. 4. The word "na" is added — *u*.
For this very reason, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) at the stage of the comprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*),

because at that time both antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) are absent; nor is there such over-extension at the stage following the destruction of the comprehension of the positive concomitance.
If it is argued that this is because, even though destruction exists at that time, it is not caused by the absence of anything else, we say no;
for if [non-existence] were a cause by virtue of a nature common to absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), then its own absolute non-existence would not be a cause with respect to itself.
[For example,] the absence of a verbal cognition subsequent to another verbal cognition is [not a cause] with respect to that verbal cognition.

In your view, the absence of another inference would be a cause [of the first inference] by virtue of being an absence of an obstacle (*pratibandhakābhāva*), just as it is for [the production of] an inference.

Furthermore, since you have accepted that the absence of an obstacle is a cause common to all effects and is itself merely a state of non-cognition (*ajñāna*), the causality of the cognition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣājñāna*) and its specific character (*asādhāraṇya*) would not exist.
[This refers to the phrase] "at the stage of destruction" (*dhvaṃsadaśāyām*).
The phrase "over-extension" (*ativyāpti*) is to be supplied.

Is the status of being a reason (*hetutva*), by virtue of its commonality with absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), intended to be common with its own absolute non-existence, or rather common with the absolute non-existence of other verbal cognitions?
Regarding the first [case], he says: "of its own absolute non-existence."
The last [author] says: "By the experience of another verbal [cognition]," etc.
"By way of being the absence of an obstacle."

The meaning is as follows: since "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatā*) is a defect in inference because the establishment [of the probandum] acts as an obstacle to inferential cognition, the absence of another establishment serves as the cause for inferential cognition by way of being the absence of an obstacle. Since verbal experience does not require [such establishment] and thus does not arise, another experience acts as an obstacle to the positive concomitant experience (*anvayānubhava*);
therefore, its absence would also have to be a cause by way of being the absence of an obstacle.
And as to what follows from that, he says: "and the absence of an impediment."
"Previously," it says.

The meaning is that at the stage when the recollection of the convention (*saṅketa*) and the presentation of the object (*padārthopasthiti*) occur, there is a further presentation of the words (*padānām upasthityantaram*).
[Note: The reading "anubhavapadaṃ na" is not found in the manuscript *u*.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Second Chapter, p. 12)

Furthermore, at the stage when all the words have been presented, prior to the verbal cognition, there is no non-existence (prāgabhāva) that is not caused by the absence of something else; thus, there is an over-narrow definition (avyāpti).
Therefore, expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) is difficult to define. To this, it is replied:

When the non-experience of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of a given word is caused by the absence of a certain form in another word uttered in proximity to it, then that specific form belonging to that [second] word with respect to that [first] word in relation to that connection is "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*).
In the *Paddhati*, it is said: "Expectancy is a desire to know (*jijñāsā*), which is a property of a conscious being;
because they are the objects of that [desire], word-meanings are said to possess expectancy. (1)

By the passage beginning with “because they convey that [meaning], the words also...,” it was stated that the expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) of words consists in their capacity to produce a cognition regarding the objects that constitute the subject matter of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*). With the intention that this "capacity to produce" does not mean the actual production of the result, but rather refers simply to the inherent fitness (*svarūpayogyatā*) of the words, the author extracts what was stated there and subsequently presents his own definition of expectancy.
Desiring first to state another definition that is inseparably connected with the definition set forth in the *Paddhati* due to its difficulty, he says: "Of which word," and so forth.
Since it is stated in the *Paddhati* that "the words [are those] in the *paddhati*," the term "of the word" (*padasya*) is used with the intention of referring to the majority of cases;
its meaning is "of whichever word.
By this, there is the inclusion of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), as well as great sentences (*mahāvākya*) and subordinate sentences (*avāntaravākya*).
That too is for the purpose of presenting that [object]; in the phrase "yatpada," the meaning is "the word *yat*";
and in the phrase "yadrūpa," it will be made clear later that it means "the presentation of the form of *yat*."
And thus, the analysis [of the compound] is as follows: "the state of not causing the non-experience of the connection of whichever word is present, and that which is this connection.
This is because it will be stated later, "in that connection";
therefore, it is the absence of the state of not causing the experience of such a connection.

And that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is either due to pronunciation, or due to intention, or due to the absence of the presence of a specific form residing in a word that stands together with another word; the meaning is that "possessing that" refers to such properties as being a verb-form (*kriyāpada*), being a noun-case-form (*kārakapada*), having the same case-ending (*ekavibhaktikatva*), and so forth.
(Definition of *ākāṅkṣā-niṣpanna*): *Ākāṅkṣāvādaḥ*, p. 13.

*Sākāṅkṣatva* (expectancy) is the state of being co-uttered with another word that possesses a form which is the counter-positive of the absence of that factor which causes a presented word not to produce the intended syntactic connection (*abhimatānvaya*). (Note: 1. The absence of the cause; 2. The form that has become the object of cognition.)
Up to this point:

the meaning of the connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: a word is "expectant" (*sākāṅkṣa*) because it is co-uttered with another word that is present in a form that serves as the cause for the causal factor of bringing about the experience of the intended connection of the word *upasthiti*.

For example, in the case of "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the fact that the word *ghaṭa* does not bring about the experience of a connection with anything else is caused by its lack of being a verb (*kriyāpada*) within the co-uttered word "bring" (*ānaya*). 4. # Ghaṭa.

Because it is observed to be so in cases such as "mānayanam" (the bringing of measuring), there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in the form of being a verb between that word "ghaṭa" and the word "ānayana" when they are construed together in the relation of bringing.

Likewise, the fact that the word "ānaya" does not cause the experience of its connection with the pot is caused by the absence of the factor of the object (*karmakāraka*) residing in the word "ghaṭa."
This is because we observe such usage in sentences like "Bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*).

Thus, it should be understood that when the word *ānaya* ("bring") is construed with the word *ghaṭa* ("jar"), the mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between them consists precisely in their being words expressing the same grammatical relation, namely, the object (*karman*).

In this context, if one were to state only that "the non-expressiveness of a word is caused by its lack of co-occurrence with another word," the definition would be impossible to satisfy (*asaṃbhava*).

In cases such as "bringing the jar" (*ghaṭam ānayanam*), although there are other words present, you maintain that [the sentence] lacks expressive power; therefore, that lack of power is not caused by the absence of those other words.
This is what was stated by the phrase "whatever form belonging to whatever word.
In the case of "the jar exists" (*ghaṭo bhavati*), even though the word "red" (*rakta*)—which shares the same case-ending—is not uttered, the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) [is still understood].

In the view that [the requirement] is simply "the absence of expectancy," since the property of having the same case-ending— which is the delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of the absence of the cause for not producing the cognition of the connection with redness in the word *ghaṭa*— is present, the expression "co-occurring" (*samabhivyāhṛta*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
However, according to the opinion that both [words] possess expectancy, the definition is simply "residing in the word *yat*" and so forth.
It will become clear later that a word uttered in proximity [to another] is not to be accepted [as the object of the relation].

As for the statement "in whose presence" (*yadanvaye*), it is intended to exclude both over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and under-extension (*avyāpti*): namely, to avoid over-extension in the case of a sentence such as "the pot, the objectness, the bringing, the effort," where there is no expectancy for a relation of action and object despite the presence of a relation, and to avoid under-extension in the case where there is expectancy for a relation of difference (*bhedānvaya*).
This will be made clear later.

1. *tāvacchedakānvayaviṣayībhūta* (the form that has become the object of the connection with the delimitor)—U. 2. *dupasthitaśabdāntara* (another word presented [in proximity])—U. 3. *upasthite* (presented)—does not exist—U. 4. *ṭāna*—U. 5. *neya*—U. 6. *tyādi* (and so forth)—U. 7. "Because of the proliferation of the faults stated for the position [of the author] of the *Maṇi* by the words 'Furthermore (*kiñca*)', etc."; thereafter, the passage beginning with "the word *yat*" (*yatpada*) exists—U-Naṃ. (Note: The symbols U and Naṃ refer to variant readings or notes from manuscripts U and Naṃ.)
And that form [of the word] consists,
in the case of connection with action, manner, or existence, of being a verb and so forth;
in the case of connection with relation, it consists of being the ending of a genitive case and so forth.
In the case of non-difference (abhedānvaya), there is identity of case endings;
in the case of the relation between the meanings of a base and its suffix, there is the status of being a base (prakṛtitva) and so forth.

For this very reason, in the case of "Bring the pot" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), the accusative case-ending in *ghaṭam*—which is a word denoting a factor of action (*kāraka*)—does not, in the absence of the verbal form *ānaya*, bring about the experience of the syntactic relation between the action and its object; thus, it stands in need of that [verb] for the connection between the action and the factor of action. To show where and in what form [this expectancy exists], he says: "And that... (*tacceti*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of words denoting a grammatical relation (kāraka) is intended.
Regarding examples such as "the king's servant" (rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ), he says:
"relational" (saṃbandha).
The meaning of the word "etcetera" (ādi) is the state of having the nominative case ending (*prathamāntatva*).
Regarding examples such as "the pot is red," he says: "non-difference" (*abheda*).
Accepting that in the defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), the non-inclusion of that [word] refers to the word itself, he says: "In the original... (*prakṛti*).

The meaning is that in expressions such as "ghaṭam" (the pot), there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) "ghaṭa"—which is the form of the pot—and the meaning of the second case ending (*dvitīyāvibhakti*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the secondness (*dvitīyatva*) and so forth are included.
Since it was stated that "being a verb" (*kriyāpadatva*) and so forth constitute its form, [the author] clarifies how this is so in certain places with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).

The meaning is: because the status of being a verbal root (*kriyāpada*) and so forth is precisely the cause for the failure to produce a cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) when other words are absent. [This refers to the phrase] "without a verbal root."
The meaning is that even when words such as "bringing" (*ānayana*) are employed without a word based on a verbal root (*kriyāpada*), [the relationship exists].
This refers to the state of action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*).

However, in the case of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*), since there is no expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatvāt*), there is no suspicion of under-extension (*avyāpti*) even in the absence of the same case-ending (*samānavibhaktitva*), which is the factor that necessitates the cognition of that [non-difference]. This is the intended meaning of the statement in the definition: "that with which [the object] is construed" (*yadanvaya*).
(Ākāṅkṣā-nirūpaṇam) Ākāṅkṣāvādaḥ, Chapter 15.

1. In cases such as "ghaṭaḥ" (pot), "karmatvam" (objecthood), "ānayanam" (bringing), "kṛtiḥ" (effort), and "iṣṭasādhanatvam" (being a means to a desired end), [there is no mutual expectancy]. 2. By the expression "ghaṭam ānaya" (bring the pot), [mutual expectancy is established].

Even though there is co-referentiality (*sahaikārthya*), because the words "pot" and so forth lack the status of being a word denoting an action or an agent (*kriyākārakapadatva*), they do not stand in a state of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*) toward that [word "fire"] in a relation of identity.
However, in a relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*), they are expectant because they possess identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktikatva*).

In the sentence "The mountain has fire; Devadatta has eaten," the word "mountain" (*giripada*), despite being proximate to the verbal form "eaten" (*bhukta*), does not have expectancy for it, as it is not an agent (*akāraka*).
However, even when [the agent] is not explicitly mentioned, there is still an expectancy through the word "Devadatta" itself for the sake of the action (*kāraṇa*).

[Objection: But even so, there is indeed a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in another sentence that has the same meaning as the stated sentence, because the property of being a verb (*kriyāpada*) that causes the experience of the aforementioned syntactic connection (*anvaya*) and so forth is absent there. To this, he says: "The pot" (*ghaṭaḥ*).

In the word "ānaya" (bring), because it is a verb (*ākhyāta*), there is an expression of the denoted meaning as "effort" (*kṛti*) when the injunctive suffix is elided; however, because in the theory of injunction (*vidhivāda*) it is observed that the meaning of an injunction is specifically "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), there is an expression of the denoted meaning as "injunction. Therefore, there is no [logical] connection with that [effort].
And thus, the sense is that there is no fault because [the object] is the very thing to be defined (lakṣya).

Alternatively, having established through the method of agreement that the status of being a verbal form and so forth is the cause for producing the experience of the intended syntactic connection, he establishes it by way of the method of difference with the words "ghaṭa" (pot).

But since there is also a motivating factor (prayojaka) even when [the term] is intended as a secondary definition (lakṣya) in another logical sequence, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti); thus he says: "abhedeti" (regarding non-difference).
By this, the purpose of the statement "that which has a positive concomitance" (yadanvaya) should be understood as explained.

Anticipating the objections of over-extension (ativyāpti) and non-extension (avyāpti) even in other sentences, he says "girih" (the mountain): where the aforementioned causal factor exists, there is the status of being a *lakṣya* (subject of definition) due to the presence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); where that [factor] is absent, there is no expectancy either, and thus it is not a *lakṣya*. Therefore, there is no fault.
"Of the verb."

The meaning is: "of a nominal word (*subanta*) that expresses an action. [Notes on variants: 1. This passage does not exist in manuscript Ga. 2. The word "tu" is added in manuscript Ka. 3. The word "tu" is added in manuscripts Ga, Ja, and Ka. 4. "ṇena giri" in manuscript Ga; "keṇa" in manuscripts Ja and Ka. 5. "ṇena" in manuscript Ga. 6. The phrase "iṣṭasādhanatvam iti" does not exist in manuscript U. 7. "ca" in manuscript U. 8. "nanu" in manuscript U.
In this context,
by the word "pada" (word), mere speech (*śabdamātra*) is intended as the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Therefore, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the mutual expectancy between a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*), or between two sentences (*vākya*).

Thus, by the word "pada" (word), only its presentation [to the mind] is intended. Therefore, since a mere word does not by itself bring about the experience of syntactic connection (*anvaya*), there is no room for the objection that it would be impossible [for a word to be a means of knowledge] because its lack of being an experiential cause is caused by the absence of other factors;
for in the case of the word "door" (*dvāra*) [in the sentence "dvāram"], it [is connected] with the word "close" (*pidhehi*).

In the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," although there is no explicit co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) between the word "should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) and the word "desirous of heaven" (*svargakāma*), there exists an intentional co-utterance—as in the case of a "silent verse" (*mauniśloka*). Thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

In the sentence "the pot becomes red" (*ghaṭo bhavati raktaḥ*), however, even though the word "red" (*rakta*) shares the same case-ending as the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*), there is no intentional co-utterance; thus, there is no over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*).
"And here" means: in the sentence that states the definition.
"Mutually" refers to the two sentences.
The meaning is "of the two residing in the Great Sayings" (mahāvākya).

Anticipating the objection that there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) regarding other worldly and Vedic sentences which lack co-utterance with other words and yet possess expectancy, he refutes it by saying: "In the case of 'dvāram' (the door), here..."
"One who desires heaven," it is said.

The meaning is that since it has been established in the seventh section of the third quarter of the fourth chapter— concerning the *viśvajit* sacrifice and others— that the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) must be supplied [to the injunction] because heaven is common to all,
he states "the jar," etc., having raised the objection that [the definition] would thus be over-extended (*ativyāpti*).
He brings together.

Regarding the statement on expectancy (ākāṅkṣāvāda), p. 17:
Alternatively, in that case, there is no expectancy at all regarding the word "red" (*rakta*).
For expectancy does not arise merely from co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*).
Rather, there is a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words that possess mutual expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*).

The conventional designation of "lack of expectancy" (*anākāṅkṣatva*) in that case is due to the absence of an intention (*tātparya*) toward the connection with "red. Through its connection with the action of coming into being (*bhavanakriyā*), the word "pot" possesses a specific expectancy toward the word "red."
"And because [the relation] exists [inherently]. However, the non-apprehension of the non-difference between the jar and redness is due to the fact that the word 'red' is not present [to the mind].
And on this view, regarding the definition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), the co-utterance of a qualifier is not required at all."

[Objection: In that case, it follows that *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) is nothing other than "intrinsic fitness," which consists in possessing a form that causes non-expressiveness when another word is absent.

To the question, "How can there be expectancy in the absence of co-utterance? he says: "For not... [na hi...].

The meaning is that, were it otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a lack of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) in cases such as "the door" (*dvāram*). [This refers to] "of those that possess expectancy."
Therefore, the intention is that there is an ellipsis (adhyāhāra) in such passages as "the door" and so forth;
[this refers to] the word "therein" (tatra).
The meaning is "having red feet.
By way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), that is, by being accompanied [by that quality];
thus, "arisen" (*utthita*).

And in this case...
The meaning is that the position is that there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the word *rakta*.
Since that [word] is also a thing to be defined (*lakṣya*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Thus, the point is that there is no suspicion of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *dvāram* and so forth.
One who takes pride in the definition stated in the *Maṇi*—that "expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the prior non-existence of experience conditioned by the absence of the other word"—raises this objection.
"Is it not so? [he asked].

The meaning is that [the capacity] consists in the possession of that specific characteristic— such as being a verb (*kriyāpada*) or the like— which serves as the causal factor for another word’s lack of expressive power, which is itself occasioned by its absence from that other word.
Furthermore,
since that [definition] would also exist in a case where the fruit has already been produced, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that instance.
If it is argued that this fault does not apply under the view that [the cause] is a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), we say no.
This is because we accept this as the desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).

As for the conventional designation of "having no expectancy" (*anākāṅkṣatva*) regarding that which has already produced its fruit, it is like giving instruction on trade to one who is dispassionate; for the listener has no further need for another comprehension of the connection (*anvaya-bodha*).
It is not, however, because the word itself lacks expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*).
Nor is there any lack of pervasion (avyāpti) regarding words used in a secondary sense (lākṣaṇika) and so forth;
for in my view, even words used in a secondary or metaphorical sense possess the capacity to produce valid cognition.
Now, one might object: "Even so, intrinsic fitness (*svarūpayogyatā*) is simply the state of being a cause, not the cause itself;
and if that were the case, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) would not be a cause of verbal comprehension. This is not so.
Since it is accepted that only the knowledge of syntactic expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as previously described is the cause [of verbal cognition], this is indeed the desired conclusion.

For this very reason, because the knowledge of the aforementioned semantic competency (*yogyatā*) is the cause specifically for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it possesses an uncommon (specific) causal status;
for the knowledge of causality regarding a jar or similar objects is not the cause [of verbal cognition].

The point is that even when the experience of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) has been produced, the status of being a verb such as "exists" (*asti*) and so forth does not depart from the sentence at that time either;
[this is because it is] independent [of such factors].

By this, the argument of Rucidatta and others— that even by that which has already produced a cognition of a relation (anvaya), there would arise the undesirable consequence of producing a second cognition of a relation—
is refuted; for non-expectation (*anapekṣā*) alone constitutes an obstacle, whereas if expectation (*apekṣā*) is present, the result is simply what is desired.
He states that the fault mentioned in the opinion of Maṇikṛt does not apply here: "And not... (na ca).
"Manmata" means "the mind's own."
The intention is that the investigation into the figurative function (*gauṇalakṣaṇavṛtti*) of words, which involves the aforementioned defects, will be refuted later.
[The opponent objects: "But even so..."
The meaning is that even though there is no fault in the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) [of the definition] to that which has already produced its fruit,
he clarifies this very point with the words "the aforementioned capacity," and so forth.
"No."

As for the objection that, if the desire-to-know (*ākāṅkṣā*) were the cause of [verbal] cognition, then even in a sentence where the fruit [of understanding] has already been produced, if another person were to point out that the word possesses a property that causes non-expressiveness due to the absence of something else, there would be the unwanted consequence (*āpatti*) of a further comprehension of the connection (*anvaya*),
that is not so; for the previous comprehension of the connection itself acts as an obstacle, and because the hearer has no further expectation.
(Ākāṅkṣā-nirūpaṇam) The theory of expectancy (ākāṅkṣāvāda),
page 19. Furthermore, there is no lack of evidence for the fact that the knowledge of that [expectancy] is a cause even in the case of verbal comprehension (śābdabodha).

Even when there is proficiency in the form of grasping the power of individual words (*pada-śakti-graha*), a word denoting a factor of action (*kāraka-pada*) does not convey a relational cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) without a verb. Thus, because there is no comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) without proficiency in the sentence as a whole in the form of a general cognition, otherwise a sentence would convey a relational cognition even for one who lacks proficiency in sentences.

If it is argued that, in this case, in the sentence "This son of the king comes; let the man be removed," there would be a cognition of the connection of both [the son and the man] with the word *rāja* (king), because the expectancy—defined as the lack of capacity to convey those respective connections due to the absence of the phonetic form (*rūpa*) found in the words *putra* and *puruṣa*—is present;
we say no, because there is a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*).

The intention of the objector is that when there is recollection of the word's power (śakti), there is no delay in the comprehension of the syntactic relation (anvaya-bodha) due to the absence of knowledge regarding that [power].
To show that in the absence of that [recollection], there is a delay in the comprehension of the syntactic relation, he says: "pada-śaktau" (regarding the word's power).
And Jayadeva has also stated: "Because there is no proof for its being the cause of expectancy, that cognition [of the sentence] is the cause."

By this, one should consider that Rucidatta’s statement— “Indeed, it cannot be said that even for him (the person who has not mastered the meaning of the sentence) knowledge [of the words] is the cause, because there is a lack of evidence for that”— is refuted.
This refers to “one who is unskilled in the sentence.”
The meaning is: "even for one who lacks proficiency in the linguistic analysis of sentences of the form described above."
Fearing that the definition just stated might be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*) with respect to other types of sentences, the following objection is raised: "But if this is so... (*nanvevam iti*).

The meaning is: if expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) consists in possessing a form that causes non-expressiveness conditioned by the absence of another word; [this property] resides in the words "son" (*putra*) and "servant" (*puruṣa*).
The meaning is: "the property characterized by having the nominative case ending. The word *rūpa* is a synonym for *dharma*.
"Both" [refers to the two].

Therefore, the intended meaning is that the definition stated therein is over-extensive (ativyāpta).
In the *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Second Chapter, p.

20): Even though there is expectancy in both cases, since the intention (*tātparya*) is grasped as applying only to the connection with the son, it is possible that there is no cognition of the connection with the person. And if the intention were grasped in both cases, it would result in an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
For this very reason, repetition (*āvṛtti*) is postulated in such cases.

Consider the sentence: "Oh, how pure is the river's water! Buffaloes are grazing on the riverbank. For a person who has heard only the words "of the river" (*nadyāḥ*) and so forth, the word "river" (*nadīpadam*) functions toward the bank itself because the word "water" (*jalapadam*) has not been heard.

Now, according to the system of Udayana and others, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is defined as the absence of the prior non-existence of verbal comprehension (*śābdānubhava-prāgabhāva*), which is caused by the lack of grasping the form [of the meaning] as you have described.

In his view, however, expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is that form which becomes the object of the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the non-existence (*viraha*) that causes prior absence (*prāgabhāva*). [He states the resolution by accepting the status of being the *lakṣya*: "In both cases."

The point is this: since the apprehension of *tātparya* (speaker’s intention) is a cause for verbal cognition, the absence of such cognition in other cases is due solely to the absence of that *tātparya*, and not due to a lack of *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy), which would otherwise result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Thus ends the section on "repetition" (*āvṛtti*).
The meaning is "of the word *rāja*";
[the suffix occurs] only after *kaccha*.

And thus, because water is not presented through its dependence [on another], it lacks the quality of being the object of a presentation that serves as the cause for the syntactic connection with a word ending in the genitive case; furthermore, even the word "water" ending in the nominative case remains semantically expectant (nirākāṅkṣatā). Therefore, there is no fault of under-extension (avyāpti) in that case.

As for the presentation itself, although semantic expectancy exists there, the absence of comprehension of the syntactic connection occurs due to the failure to grasp the speaker's intention (tātparya).

The point is that even in that case, if the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) is grasped, the comprehension of the connection in both instances and the repetition of the word "river" (*nadī*) are accepted as before.

Thus, since the existence or non-existence of the definition characterized by expectancy as stated by himself is untenable in every case—whether in what is defined (*lakṣya*) or what is not defined (*alakṣya*)—he now reveals the superiority of his own definition over the definitions stated by others, preceded by an objection:
"But surely... (*nanu*).
"Prior non-existence," etc.

and third, in my own view, however, expectancy, like proximity (*āsatti*), resides solely in the word.

For here, in the first view, fitness (*yogyatā*) consists in the absence of a sublation (*pramā-viraha*) of the connection that constitutes the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*). For [the contradiction] exists just as much in cases such as "one sprinkles with fire," where the lack of validity is certain, as it does in cases such as "one sprinkles with water," where the lack of validity is not yet certain.

And thus, in that case, since odor is simply the counter-positive of an absence that is incompatible with its connection to the object of apprehension, there is no over-extension; this is the meaning.
"For here," [he says].

(*tasmāt*). [This concludes] the refutation of the power of the speaker of the *Līlāvatī*.

Because there is no evidence for such an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*);

Now, it is not the case that the absences of [obstructing] gems and so forth function as causes by virtue of being absences of gems and so forth,

Nor do they function as causes by virtue of being the absence of an obstructer (pratibandhaka), because that would involve the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).
For only that which is the counter-positive of an absence that serves as a cause is a preventer; otherwise, even when a mantra is present, burning would occur simply through the absence of the jewel,

If it is argued that an effect does not arise merely from the presence of all its causes—since a jar is produced even when only a single stick is present—we say: not so. Furthermore, according to the view that "obstructiveness" (*pratibandhakatva*) consists in being pervaded by the non-production of the effect, the cause is the absence of that which is delimited by obstructiveness.

It has been stated that "the nature of being a staff" (daṇḍatva) is precisely the nature of essential fitness (svarūpayogyatā), which constitutes the delimiting factor of causality (kāraṇatāvacchedaka);
[this refers to] "of that" (tasya).
The meaning is: "of that which is delimited by the aforementioned form. [End of section on the view that the capacity resides in the word.]
Nor can the production of the effect, which consists in the collocation of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-samavadhāna*), be inferred [as the capacity];
for even when the auxiliary causes are not present in a staff, the conventional usage of that term [“capacity”] still occurs.
Furthermore, even when that [contact] is present in stone and other such materials, they are not conventionally designated as causes.

Nor can it be inferred that the nature of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*) is the non-interruption of a rule qualified by "not being otherwise established" (*ananyathāsiddhi*); for that [qualification] is already included within the very body of the logical reason (*hetu*).

With this very point in mind, it is stated in the *Sudhā*: "Therefore, one must admit that the causality of clay and so forth toward jars and other effects is something supersensible (*atīndriya*) alone, to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)."
"And that very [nature] is power."

However, by means of the perception that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is precisely the pervasion itself— characterized as a necessary rule and common to taste, form, and so forth— that is apprehended;
it is not the state of non-causality in the form of a power (*śakti*),
because that is eternally beyond the senses.

The point is that, since the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) must be stated as "invariably occurring prior [to the effect] while being established as non-otherwise" (*ananyathāsiddhaniyatapūrvavṛttitva*), it is precisely this [definition] that serves as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) in the form described above;
thus it is said in the *Sudhā*.

It should be understood that this occurs during the commentary on the verse beginning with "The Paiṅgi Śruti also says that it is indeed the existence of power [that is meant] by the term 'the Self' which grasps the moving and the unmoving" in the section [of the Brahma-sūtra] starting with "Because of the inclusion of the moving and the unmoving."

Now, one might object: "When fire and so forth exist, there is burning and so forth; when they are absent, that [burning] is absent. Thus, by means of a perception that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between fire and the like and burning and the like, the causality of fire and so forth toward burning is apprehended. Alternatively, by means of a perception that grasps the pervasion such as 'wherever there is smoke, there is fire,' causality is apprehended. Therefore, how can it be said that [causality] is an object of inference? It is precisely through this [pervasion] being otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*) that power (*śakti*) is established. To this, he says: "Regarding pervasion... (vyāptīti).

And it is not the case that the observation of concomitance (*sahacāradarśana*), being subject to deviation (*vyabhicārita*), can in any way be the apprehender of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in its nature as a rule (*niyama*). *Note: Variants from the manuscripts: 1. *vyabhicāritvaṃ* — Rā.; *na ca vyabhicāritvaṃ* — Ja.; *na ca vyabhicāritvaṃ* — Ga. 2. *tadavyavadhāne’pi tadavyava-* — Rā.; *tadavyavadhāne’pi tadavyava-* — Ga. 3. It should not be said that there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) if [the cognition] enters into the category of the apprehender as a necessary rule;
for, like collyrium and the like, it functions as an auxiliary to the perception that grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and thus does not depend upon non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*).
Furthermore, it is first inferred that water possesses the quality of quenching thirst by virtue of its being water;
however, in that case, the actual production of the result [of quenching thirst] cannot be what is inferred,
because that would be both contradicted and subject to deviation.
Rather, it is merely the state of being capable of allaying thirst;
and that does not yet consist in the nature of being a necessary antecedent established otherwise,
because that [nature] has already been known previously.

Otherwise, how could there be a grasp of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "water-ness" (*jalatva*)? [Objection: But surely it is incorrect to say that the pervasion itself is grasped, because neither the observation of concomitance (*sahacāradarśana*) nor the observation of restricted concomitance (*niyatasahacāradarśana*) can determine it. Anticipating this doubt, he provides the resolution: "Not so," etc.
The meaning is: "of that observation of concomitance."

With the intention that the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the inference that thirst is quenched by water is a proof for [the existence of] potency (śakti), he says: "Furthermore... (kiñca).
He refutes the possibility of an alternative explanation for the presumption (arthāpatti) with the words: "And in that case... (tatra ca).
The word "tāvat" (firstly) refers to the position that will be stated starting with "But what... and so forth;

The point is that, in that case, for one who has proceeded on the basis of another inference, the result—namely, the cessation of thirst—is perceived immediately after drinking water; furthermore, it is possible that in some instances there may be neither the proceeding nor the drinking.
Thus, [the reason] is "because of deviation" (vyabhicārāt).

The point is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because there is no evidence for the production of the aforementioned result in every instance of that which possesses the nature of water (*jalatva*), and because the production of the result is absent in water that has just arisen and immediately perished. [End of section on the view that [the cause] is capable.]
Nor can it be defined as "that which possesses an absence of effect caused by the absence of auxiliary causes" (sahakārivirahaprayuktakāryābhāvavattva),
because the term "auxiliary cause" (sahakārī) must be intended to mean "any cause other than itself," which would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya).

Because one who desires a fruit cannot engage in action without wavering due to the fear of the absence of future auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), [the opponent's position fails]. For, by that much alone, your proposed definition— namely, that "the cause is the connection with a subsequent time of the prior non-existence of the effect"— would imply that one must first know the causality [of the auxiliary] before knowing that the absence of the effect is brought about by the absence of the auxiliaries.

Because it is impossible to know [it], and because it would follow that a staff or similar object would not be a cause in a state where there is no conjunction with the [water], causal power (*kāraṇatva*)—which is of the nature of a capacity (*śakti*) beyond the senses—is [the cause]. Having raised an objection regarding the nature of being the cause of the cessation of thirst by way of another alternative, he refutes it, saying: "Nor also... (*nāpi*).

The meaning is as follows: being characterized by the absence of the causal complex (*sahakāri-viraha*)—that is, being produced as qualified by a connection with a subsequent moment due to the absence of the causal complex—and possessing that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the effect in the form of satisfaction, constitutes the state of being the cause for the allaying of thirst.
To that extent, your proposed definition [is met].
However, because a prior non-existence possesses another prior non-existence, in that case...

The meaning is that there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a jar and the like, because it lacks the nature of causality as stated by you—namely, the state of being characterized by the absence of the effect in the form of the prior non-existence of the jar, which is itself occasioned by the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
[This occurs] when the staff and so forth are not considered causes.
In that case, even though prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) exists, it cannot be the case that [the effect's non-arising] is not caused by the absence of auxiliary causes;
nor is this a desirable conclusion,
for [the effect] would always be present there.
The meaning is that [it is so] because of the conventional usage of "causality" (hetutva).
Therefore... [tasmāt].
The meaning is that, by virtue of its capacity (*śakti*), nothing other than the cause for the allaying of thirst can be logically possible. (Note: Variants in the manuscripts include:

"Or [it is] the object of inference"—thus is the proof of *śakti* (potency). [Additional text: "The cause of jars and so forth"—this is redundant. "Equal"—this is redundant. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava*, Second Chapter, page 62. 1. Or [it is] the object of inference—thus is the proof of *śakti*.

for even in the case of a staff and the like, there is no necessity with respect to the individual instance (*vyakti*),
and if the necessity were with respect to the universal (*jāti*), it would lead to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a donkey [could be considered a cause].

For in beginningless saṃsāra, it is indeed possible that there is no rule regarding the immediate precedence of something belonging to the class of donkeys following something belonging to the class of jars.
Nor [can it be established] because the state of occurring immediately prior is not invariably fixed.

With the intention that the existence of *śakti* (potency) is established by the fact that otherwise the non-causality of donkeys and the like would be inexplicable, he says: "Furthermore, otherwise... (4).

The word "if" (ced) implies the following: immediately thereafter, there would be no absence of causality for a donkey and so forth with respect to a jar and the like; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
To the question "Why would it not be so?", he says: "In the case of the donkey and so forth," etc.
Because the state of being antecedent is not fixed.
The phrase "its absence in the case of a donkey and so forth" is to be supplied.

Is it intended that there is no causal status for a donkey and so forth because of the lack of necessity regarding its existence at a temporally remote prior moment, or rather because of the lack of necessity regarding its existence at an immediately prior moment?
He clarifies the over-extension [of the definition] to the first case, such as a donkey and so forth, with the words: "For it is possible..."
He states the final [position]: "Nor even... (nāpi).
The phrase "by way of being indeterminate" (*aniyatattvena*) is to be supplied as before immediately after this.

[Regarding the term] *eva*: it does not exist in Rā. and ṇa. [Regarding the term] *ṇatvena anu-*: it exists in ja. [Regarding the phrase] *na hy anaudo*: it exists in naṃ. and ja. Śaktivādaḥ, Part II, p. 63.
[Objection: Because sacrifices and the like, which are separated by an interval, would consequently fail to be causes of heaven and other results;
if it is argued that there is no such interval for the sacrifice when it is accompanied by the *apūrva*, we say no.

Since the sacrifice's status as the cause of heaven is first established through prior cognition, and the *apūrva* (unseen potency) must subsequently be postulated, it is impossible for that [potency]—which is not immediately contiguous—to enter into the definition of causality;
otherwise, the *apūrva* itself would have to be the expressed meaning [of the word].

In this case, causality consists precisely in a supersensible power (*atīndriya-śakti*). With respect to that power, being of the same genus as its own substratum and having no intervention by the effect is the pervader (*vyāpaka*). And since, as in the case of sacrifice or eating with respect to satisfaction, it is impossible for [the sacrifice] to have no intervention by its own nature with respect to heaven, there must be non-intervention by means of an operation (*vyāpāra*), just as in the case of experience with respect to memory.
The phrase "it must be stated" implies that the conception of something unprecedented (apūrva) is logical.
[Regarding the term] "sāpūrvasya": it means "of that which possesses the apūrva."
The meaning is "of that which is accompanied by the unprecedented" (apūrva).
"That" refers to this.
The meaning is that it would be separated by something unprecedented;
thus, it would have to be expressed.

In your view, since it is precisely the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) that is denoted by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers—and not, as in the Guru’s view, the *apūrva*—the *apūrva* cannot be the denotation of the optative suffix and so forth.

If the meaning of the injunction were the causality residing in the sacrifice, characterized by the state of occurring immediately prior to heaven, then the *apūrva* would also have to be the denotation of the optative suffix and so forth, rather than something to be inferred through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). This is the sense, lest it constitute a departure from established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*).
It is indeed power alone.
And thus, since that [capacity] is absent in donkeys and the like, there is an absence of causality; this is the sense that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor does it follow that there would be non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of sacrifices and the like; therefore, he says: "And that... (*tāṃ ca*).

And the meaning is "the capacity" (śaktim). [The phrase] "its own substratum"—[the rest of the sentence follows]. This has also been stated in the *Sudhā* [commentary] with the words beginning "atīndriyam eva" (only that which is beyond the senses), and so forth. (Second Chapter, p. 64)
If it is objected: "In that case, if power (*śakti*) is causality (*kāraṇatva*), then that [power] would not be a cause;
and consequently, power would not be conducive to burning," we say no.

This is because causality itself, like [the property of] being a cause, is a substratum of conduciveness, which consists in being the counter-positive of a prior non-existence that is pervaded by the prior non-existence of the effect.

However, some [object]: "If [the absence of an obstacle] were a cause by virtue of being the absence of an obstructer (*pratibandhakābhāva*), then because of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), you have stated that the cause is the collection (*kūṭa*) of absences such as the [absence of] a magnet and so forth. Thus, you have effectively stated that the causality belongs to these various non-concomitant absences.
Furthermore, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a staff located in a forest; therefore, [you] said '[of that which is of the same class as its own substratum]'."
This also [is the case].
The meaning is that this also establishes the existence of a supersensible power (*atīndriya-śakti*), because it would otherwise be impossible to account for the causality of donkeys and the like.
Anticipating an objection to the view that power (śakti) consists in the nature of causality, he refutes it: "But even so..."
"In the pervaded" (vyāpye).
The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is to be understood as temporal (*kālikī*).
The point is that, just as a cause such as a staff possesses such a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), its power (*śakti*) likewise possesses it as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
He states the proof of power through another method by means of an indirect reference: "But some... (*kecit tu*).
"Mutually."

The meaning is as follows: since the absence of the jewel and so forth must first be known to be an "absence of an obstructor" (*pratibandhakābhāva*), there can be knowledge that those absences are causes;

and once the status of being a cause is known, there can be knowledge that they are obstructors in the sense of being the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of the absences that constitute the cause; and once that is known, there can be knowledge that those absences are causes by virtue of being absences of obstructors.
Thus, because of this mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), you have asserted that the collection of absences (*abhāvakūṭa*) constitutes the causality.

And so, to the question "What follows from this?", he states his own intended probandum: "And thus... (tathā ca). [The following is the commentary on the verse: 1. The theory of power (*śaktivāda*)—page 65: The postulation of power is by way of the hypothesis that the infinite properties residing in each respective [substratum] serve as the delimiters of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*);
otherwise, even for you, the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) would not be established.
They say that the cognition of a qualified entity is established by means of infinite, inherent relations of its own nature alone.

Furthermore, if one accepts that the absence of the jewel qualified by the absence of an excitant is the cause [of combustion] while denying *śakti* (potency), then— since it would be possible for the non-performance of the *sandhyāvandana* and other rites,

when conjoined with the absence of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), to be a cause of hell— even if that [non-performance] were removed, the unseen merit (*apūrva*) resulting from the rite would not be established.

In this way, even the *apūrva* produced by the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices would not be established; for it is logically consistent that the cause of results such as heaven is simply the absence of the self characterized by the prior non-existence of the sacrifice together with its constituent parts, as demonstrated through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). [The phrase "abhāvakūṭasya" means] when there is causality consisting of a collection of absences.
The meaning is that, otherwise, there would be no regard for the parsimony of conceptual construction (*kalpanālāghava*);
this applies to you as well.

Regarding this position, the seed of dissatisfaction should be understood as follows: since there is no room for postulating a [separate] power (*śakti*) based on the principle of "otherwise inexplicability" (*anyathānupapatti*), because—as will be explained—the absence of obstructions (*pratibandhakābhāva*) can be subsumed under a single category such as being a "qualified injunction" (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) and the like, and thus this fault does not apply to that alternative view.
Nevertheless, there is no fault, because this position is introduced since it is possible to level that same objection against the opponent by following their own method.

thus, it includes the *apūrva* as well.
