[This refers to] the non-existence of that [obstruction], which is the cause of the absence of obstacles to those qualities; [and it is] to be accomplished by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Even though there is no absence of the qualificand due to the self's permanence, the absence of the qualified [entity] is possible through the absence of the qualifier in the form of prior non-existence.
Nor should it be suspected that the infinity of the result would follow from the infinity of this qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*);

for, by the force of scriptural testimony which declares a result with a limit, one must assume that the aforementioned qualified absence—just like the *apūrva*—has the inherent nature of producing a result that is itself limited.

Moreover, even in a case where the body of Devadatta or another person has been perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) but is not subsequently experienced again through another perception, inference (*anumāna*), or other means, the memory of that body nevertheless arises.

Even though the self of the sacrificer who performs sacrifices such as *iṣṭāpūrta* is permanent, because he has already performed the sacrifice and so forth, there is an absence of that [sacrifice] therein; thus, [the non-existence of the qualification] is caused by the absence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇābhāvaprayukta*).
The state of being qualified [by the absence] is indeed easily obtained;
the sense is that it is like the existence of the absence of a jewel (maṇi) etc., qualified by the absence of an excitant (uttejaka), when the jewel etc. exists and the excitant is present.

If it is objected that, since the sacrifice itself is the opponent of its own prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), then upon the destruction of the sacrifice—which perishes immediately—the prior non-existence would re-emerge, and thus the absence of the qualifier (the sacrifice) could not occur;
we say no, because just as the sacrifice is the opponent of its prior non-existence, so too is its destruction the opponent of that same prior non-existence.
Anticipating the objection that there is a disparity regarding the absence of an obstructing factor, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not).
It is "with a limit."
The meaning of such scriptural passages as, "He who drinks Soma becomes indeed immortal, as long as Indra, as long as Manu, as long as Āditya," is as follows.
To show that there is likewise no possibility of doubting the infinity of the fruit, he states another counter-argument with the words "Moreover" (api ca).
In order to establish the non-existence of the qualifier "the absence of occurrence," it was stated that [the object] is not experienced again by another perception or by inference and so forth.
(Regarding the position that [the self] possesses power:
The theory of power (śaktivāda), page 67.

Furthermore, with respect to memory, let the absence of the self—qualified by the prior non-existence of the experience of that [object] and persisting until the occurrence of the memory—be the cause, as established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Having accepted that an action is the cause of memory, one postulates a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in order to account for it.
And in this case, there is not even the slightest room for the suspicion that the result consists of the nature of memory.

For, just as in the case of the theory of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the absence of a result is logically established simply due to the deficiency of the auxiliary conditions consisting of similarity, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and reflection.

If, in that case [of the recollection of heaven], one establishes—on the grounds of parsimony—that the very experience of the sacrifice, which has an established causal status regarding the recollection of heaven, is the cause by means of a positive *apūrva* (unseen potentiality) as its mediating factor, and thereby explains the absence of the effect from the absence of that [cause]; then here too, in the case of burning, one should establish—on the grounds of parsimony—that fire itself, whose causal status regarding burning is already established, is the cause by means of a positive power (*śakti*), and explain the absence of the effect from the absence of that [cause].
Why, then, resort to the postulation of the absence of an obstructor qualified by the absence of an activator as the cause?

Therefore, the absence of an obstructing factor (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is not the cause; rather, it must be stated that the absence of burning at the time of obstruction is due solely to the absence of power (*śakti*). Thus, power is established.
[Question: Why? [Answer: It means "because of this. He states that the fault mentioned previously does not apply here: "And not here" (*na cātra*).

Having caused the opponent himself to state the resolution for the two *pratibandī* (counter-objections), he says "if indeed" (*yadi cet*) here as well, indicating that it is the same in this case too.
[From the *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava*, Second Chapter, page 68:

Objection: On the view that [burning] is due to a power (*śakti*), since the previous power has perished, how can burning occur again when the obstacle is removed or when an auxiliary factor (*uttejaka*) is present?

If it is argued that a new power is produced by those two [factors], then the status of the absence of an obstacle as a cause—even though it is not a recurring entity—is equally true for you as well. Reply: This is not so.

Just as dullness may occasionally occur in an axe despite its existence, or as there may be an absence of inference in a case of perceptual certainty following doubt despite the presence of the causal complex, or as there may be a lack of fruition for an *apūrva* despite its existence, or just as there may be occasional dullness in a capacity despite its existence— so too, one must postulate a specific state characterized by dullness (*kaṇṭhībhāva*) in that [capacity].
For it is said in the *Sudhā*: “Because by the word ‘individual’ (*vyakti*), what is intended is a particular state of the power (*śakti*) itself.”
Furthermore, regarding the four positions you are about to state— which are not accepted by you—
he anticipates an objection against the position that [the cause] possesses causal power (*śakti*) and refutes it with various examples, beginning with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).
For it has been said: "Indeed..."

Having stated that "power exists as the unmanifest (*avyakta*)," he provides the answer to the question "What is its unmanifest nature? with the words beginning "by means of sound" (*śabdena*).

"As will be explained."

Or else, there is a triad of absences regarding the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation— [namely, the absence of the qualifier, the absence of the qualified, and the absence of their relation].
This is the position of those who maintain that [the word] possesses [denotative] power (*śaktā-vatti-pakṣa*).

Nevertheless, the status of an obstructer (*pratibandhakatva*)— such as that of a jewel (*maṇi*) and so forth— is established in common worldly experience as the nature of being a destroyer of some property conducive to the effect.
It would not be so; therefore, the existence of *śakti* (potency) is established by the fact that otherwise the obstructive nature of gems and the like could not be accounted for.
Furthermore, the jewel is not the obstruction itself— consisting as it does in the disruption of what is conducive to the effect—
but rather, the person who employs it is the actual obstructer.

It should be stated that the conventional usage of the term "obstructer" (*pratibandhaka*) with respect to the jewel (*maṇi*) occurs either through metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) or by resorting to the suffix *ka* in the sense of "that which possesses. This is because there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*) against its primary [application]. Furthermore, in accordance with the usage "obstructed by the jewel" (*maṇinā pratibaddha*), it is more appropriate here as well to understand the suffix *ka* as having an agentive (*kartṛ*) sense in the word "obstructer."

The meaning is that this will be explained in the subsequent refutation (*uttarabhaṅga*), which states that the cause [of non-obstruction] is either the absence of the very object to be qualified—the obstructing form—which exists [at that time] due to a difference in the delimitors of its counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*); or the absence here of the magnet and so forth, which are qualified by the absence of the enhancer located in another place; or the absence of the relation between the qualifier and the qualified.
Regarding the suffix having the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
The meaning is: "of the suffix ṇvul prescribed for the agent" according to the rule *ṇvultṛcau*.

Therefore, it is improper to assert that very thing [obstructiveness] without *śakti*. To this he says: "Furthermore... (*kiñca*). Furthermore, if the absence of a jewel and so forth were the cause [of the non-arising of an effect], then the jewel itself could not be considered an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*).

In common worldly usage, there is no application of the term "obstacle" to the absence of a cause—such as the absence of a staff—which is of the nature of the absence of a cause, nor to the performance of a prescribed act, which is of the nature of the absence of a prohibited cause that would otherwise result in demerit.

Therefore, the existence of *śakti* (potency) is established through: (1) the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the inference of causality based on observed positive and negative concomitance; (2) the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the non-causality of things such as a donkey; (3) the objection based on the analogy of the *apūrva* (unseen merit); (4) the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the well-known worldly status of things like a magnet as an inhibitor; and (5) the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the nature of inhibition as you yourself have defined it.
Thus ends the fivefold [classification] of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) regarding capacity.
And likewise, even by you, the nature of an obstructer must be stated as consisting precisely in the disruption of the capacity that serves as the cause, and so forth.
Concluding by restating everything previously mentioned in its essential form, he says: "Therefore," etc.

By the phrase "apūrvādi" (beginning with the *apūrva*), the inclusion [of other factors] is intended by the word "ādi. However, because the parsimony of postulation (*kalpanālāghava*) mentioned in the passage beginning with "some say" is seized by a lack of conviction (*aruci*), its inclusion was not made.
The fivefold [classification of] presumption (*arthāpatti*) regarding capacity:

1. *Smādanvaya* (according to the Rāṇaga school). 2. The passage beginning with "tvadabhimata" is absent in the Ja manuscript. 3. The phrase "iti bhāvaḥ" is added in the U manuscript. 4. The reading "skāragra-u. or "3 8" appears in the U manuscript. (The objection regarding the non-exclusion of the cause from the luminous [subject]).
*Śaktivāda*, Part II, p. 71. Now begins the refutation of the fourfold theory regarding the causality of the absence of an inhibitor.

Furthermore—in your view, a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) does not exist apart from the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and their relation (*sambandha*). Consequently, even the absence of an inhibitor qualified by the absence of an activator (*uttabhaka*) would, in some cases, be of the nature of the absence of the qualifier, in some cases of the nature of the absence of the qualified, and in some cases of the nature of the absence of the relation. Because of this lack of uniformity (*ananugama*), it cannot serve as a [single] cause. If one seeks uniformity by asserting that these three absences possess a single power (*śakti*), then the existence of that power is established.
Now follows the refutation of the view that the absence of an obstructer is a cause. (7)

Having stated the objection— that the non-production of burning is accounted for simply by the absence of visible causes, such as the absence of a gem qualified by the absence of an inciter— and having refuted it by pointing out its contradiction with scripture and other authorities, as well as its conflict with five types of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), [the author] now says "Moreover" (*kiṃ ca*), with the intention that the status of such an absence as a cause is itself untenable, which would otherwise justify the denial of *śakti*.

Having stated that "the ancients [hold] that the cause [of the non-production of fire] is the absence [of the rubbing], conjoined with the absence of the stimulant in the gem," and having refuted that by saying, "this qualified [absence] is not a distinct entity;

otherwise, this absence would be a recurring [single] factor," and so forth, he himself states the refutation by extracting all of that [from his own position] in the passage beginning with "In your view... and so on.
"By way of being a single possessor of power."

The meaning is: "by virtue of possessing a power conducive to a single effect. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Second Chapter, p. 72) (Note: Variants indicated: 1. *ubhayatra rūpapadaṃ na* — Rā.; 2. *vārthā* — U.; 3. *yena tada* — U.)

Nor should it be argued that the absence of the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation are not subsumed under the concept of "contradictory to the qualified" (viśiṣṭavirodhitva), because in those cases where neither the qualifier, nor the qualified, nor their relation exists, there is the cognition that "the qualified does not exist."
For "being the counter-correlative of a qualified entity" must be stated as either consisting in the absence of that qualified entity or being pervaded by it.

Since both of these are non-universal (ananugata) due to the non-universality of the qualified counter-correlative itself, the absence [of such a qualified entity] would likewise be non-universal. However, if the qualified entity were universal, its absence would be universal by its very nature; so what is the point of this elaborate effort?

[Objection: But then, even for a jewel that exists by its own nature, at the time when an illuminator is present, there exists an absence [of the jewel] as delimited by the absence of the illuminator;

for an absence differs not only through a difference in the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), but also through a difference in the delimiting property of the counter-positive (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). [Reply:
Anticipating the objection that the same [property] mentioned by Śaśadhara serves as the unifying factor, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not).
He clarifies that these three possess a distinguished state of opposition with the words: "Where... (yatra).
"Followed."

The meaning is as follows: if [non-existence] consisted of the triad of the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation, then non-existence itself would possess a threefold nature, resulting in a lack of commonality (ananugama). Alternatively, whether it consists in the absence of those [three] or in being pervaded by their absence, it remains non-common. However, "if there were commonality" refers to the following.
The meaning is: "But if one accepts that the qualified [object] is a distinct category of entity (padārthāntara) following upon the triad beginning with the qualifier.
[This refers to the phrase] "by means of the distinction" (kṛsṛṣṭyā).

The meaning is that there is a subsumption by way of being a qualified counter-correlative; "counter-correlativity" [is attributed] through the conceptualization that it consists in the nature of absence.

Having thus refuted the position of the three types of non-existence favored by Śaśadhara according to the method set forth by Maṇi and others, he now raises the objection regarding the position of an additional non-existence favored by Udayana and others: "But then... (nanu tarhi).
"Not at all, when the counter-positive differs."

Although, in cases where there is a difference between counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), a difference in the delimiters of counter-correlation (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is necessary— such that difference [of absence] arises solely from that [difference in delimiters]—
nevertheless, the meaning is that just as the difference between counter-correlates is pervaded by the difference between absences, so too is the difference in the delimiters of counter-correlation.
(Prabhāsya-hetve-pracaṅga) Śaktivāda, p.

73: Otherwise, how could there be a valid cognition (*pramā*) of the absence of a person delimited by isolation (*kaivalya*), in the form "there is no isolated person," even while the person who possesses a staff is present?

If it is argued that, whether the stimulant (uttambhaka) is present or absent, the absence of the gem (*maṇi*) alone—pervading both the time when the stimulant is absent and the time when the gem is conjoined with the stimulant—is the cause, we say no.
In my view, since the counter-positive of the delimited absence (*avacchinnābhāva*) is a distinct entity (*padārthāntara*) qualified [by the stimulant], the gem itself is not its counter-positive.

Furthermore, in your view, when the qualified [entity] exists, the cognition of the absence of the qualified must, according to the maxim *saviśeṣaṇe hi* (for [the cognition of an absence] regarding a qualified [object] [depends on the cognition of the absence of the qualifier]), have as its object the absence of the qualifier; thus, the lack of pervasion (*ananugatatva*) remains as it was.

The point is that this absence, which exists even while the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is present, must be understood—following the direction of Maṇi’s argument—as being either distinct from the triad beginning with prior absence (prāgabhāva), or as destruction (dhvaṃsa) itself, or as the postulated absolute absence (atyantābhāva).
"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "And thus... (tathā ca).

If the jewel is not present during the state of neutralization (*uttambhaka*), then because both the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*)—which consists of the absence of the neutralizer—and its delimited subject (*viśeṣya*) are absent, the absence of the jewel is caused by those two. However, if the jewel is not present when the neutralizer is present, then there is an absence of the subject; and in the state where the jewel is accompanied by the neutralizer, the absence of the subject is caused by the absence of the delimiting factor, which consists of the absence of the neutralizer. This is because the jewel that persists through these states is not the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of that [absence].

And thus, since even the non-existence (abhāva) favored by you is itself unreal (alīka), of what could there be causality such that the power [of causes] would be denied? This is the intended meaning.
He states the very same fault mentioned by Maṇi: "And in your view... and so forth.

Otherwise, how could there be the uncontradicted cognition: "Only the crest has perished, but not the person"? Furthermore, how could that which does not contradict the existence of the substantive possess the nature of its non-existence?
And there is no absence of that absence [of the qualifier], because it is contradictory to the mere existence of the qualifier.
Furthermore, since this very jewel was previously qualified by the absence of the stimulator, an absence [of the fire] delimited by that [time] is also impossible.

Nor should it be argued that although the jewel and so forth were previously qualified by the absence of the stimulator, there is now an absence qualified by the absence of the stimulator because the stimulator is absent at present; for if that were so, the qualification by the absence of the stimulator at the present time would have to be stated as the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*).
And that is incorrect;
for [according to] the view of Udayana, that [non-existence] never occurs when the gem is in conjunction with the stimulant— this is the meaning.
How could it be otherwise?
The meaning is that the cognition of the absence of a qualified entity (viśiṣṭābhāvabuddhi) has as its primary object the absence of the qualificandum (viśeṣyābhāva).
He clarifies that the cognition of the absence of the qualified entity has the absence of the qualifier (viśeṣaṇābhāva) as its objective content by asking: "And how? (kathaṃ ca).
Regarding the phrase "the existence of the qualifier":
And how so? This is the connection [of the question].
He states that such a conceptualization of non-existence is also contrary to the established tenets of Nyāya: "Furthermore, of this very [self]... and so forth.
The meaning is that it refers to the very absence of that jewel of which it is spoken.

Prior to the presence of the magnetizer (uttejaka), its absence is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedaka); or, at the time of the magnetizer's presence, [the absence is different].
Regarding the first case, he says: "from the magnetizer."
Having raised a second objection, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not).
He explains this with the word "idānīm" (now).
The meaning is "in the state of being stimulated.
[This refers to] "present-time" (idānīntana).
The meaning is "at the time of the stimulator.

[Note: Variants include *viśiṣṭasyaiva naṣṭā* (ka), the absence of the word *tu* (naṃ), *kabhāvena* (naṃ), *kābhāvena* (ga), and *hyuttejakābhāva* (naṃ). This is the objection regarding the cause of manifestation (*prabhāsya-hetv-aprasaṅga*).

The theory of power (*śaktivāda*) [is untenable], because it would lead to the fallacy of an unestablished conclusion (*aprasiddhānta*) by admitting the existence of an absence (*abhāva*) qualified by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*).

Furthermore, since that [absence] is a purely positive entity (*kevalānvayin*), it would exist even prior to the presence of the inciter (*uttejaka*); consequently, burning would occur at that time as well.
Furthermore, even if something exists, there would have to be some absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is distributed (*vyāsajya*) over the delimitation by a non-existent property;
and that is not accepted.
[The term] "residing in different loci" (*vyadhikaraṇa*)...
The meaning is that the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is non-co-located (vyadhikaraṇa);
[this is stated] because [otherwise] it would result in a contradiction with one's own established tenets (apasiddhānta).

Just as the absence of "horn-ness" (śaśīyatva) is never admitted in a horn because it [the property of being a rabbit's horn] is never present there, so too— out of fear of the undesirable consequence that one would have to accept an additional type of absence characterized by a locus determined by a non-overlapping property (vyadhikaraṇadharma)— on the ground, in the case of the cognition "there is no jar on the ground," one must accept an absence whose locus is determined by a property distinct from the jar itself; this is made explicit in the definitions of inference and their commentaries.

Similarly here as well, since the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*)—consisting of the absence of the present stimulator (*uttejaka*) existing in the gem when conjoined with a stimulator—is found only elsewhere and never exists here, it follows that the absence [of the stimulator] would be one whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) resides in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Therefore, the meaning is that by accepting such an absence, one falls into the fallacy of proving what is already established (*aprasiddhānta*).
If someone were to say, "Let such a non-existence (abhāva) also exist," he states the fault in that case as well: "of that" (tasya).

The meaning is: [the absence] consists of an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a property residing in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇadharma), namely the absence of the stimulator as delimited by the state of being a stimulator.
And he states an over-extension [of the argument] with the words "furthermore" (kiñca).
Regarding the term *vyāvajyeti*:

in the case of a pot and a sentient being (*ghaṭasatva*), by the force of the cognition that "the pot and the cloth do not exist," there would also have to be an absence distinct from those mentioned, whose counter-positiveness is delimited by duality and whose counter-positives are the existing pot and cloth.
Since the cognition is satisfactorily explained by the absence of either one alone, such an unauthentic absence is not accepted there by the Naiyāyikas; this is the meaning.

To one who argues that such a non-existence (abhāva) may indeed exist, he states another fault: "Moreover, in this way... [etc. [Notes: 1. tāko-ka.ga.ja; 2. nā vya-u; 3. ttambhakā-u; 4. rūpapadaṃ na-u; 5. atirikto 'bhāvopi-u]
Furthermore,
in this way, since the jar would be non-existent at the time of its redness due to being delimited by its dark color, there would be a contradiction with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Nor should it be argued that even if the jar is non-existent as "darkness," there is no such contradiction because it exists as "jar-ness."

If that were the case, since recognition would be explained as having as its object the non-difference delimited by potness (*ghaṭatva*), there would follow the consequence of a difference delimited by blackness (*śyāmatva*), which would entail the [simultaneous] presence of both difference and non-difference—a position you do not accept.
Likewise, by delimitation through respective moments (*kṣaṇa*), difference would follow, resulting in the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Similarly, even within a single moment, difference and non-difference would exist by way of being delimited by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and its absence.
Moreover, it is thus.
The meaning is that one accepts the non-existence [of a thing] as being caused by the absence of a delimiting factor (avacchedaka) for an object that is indeed existent.
Recognition.
The meaning is that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is the [cognition] "that which was dark is this very same one that is red.
Regarding the phrase "difference and non-difference" (*bhedābheda*):
The meaning is that there is non-difference in terms of being a jar, while there is difference in terms of being dark; thus, it refers to both difference and non-difference.
"At that moment" (tatkṣaṇa) [is the phrase].

The meaning is that because there is no possibility of difference when each moment is delimited by the non-existence of preceding and succeeding moments—as established by the cognition "it is not [the same] at this moment"—there would be momentariness.
Thus, there is both difference and non-difference.

Since there is the existence of the monkey's conjunction with the branch of the tree and the non-existence of that [conjunction] at the root, there would arise— based on the cognitions "the tree does not possess the monkey's conjunction at the root" or "the tree does not lack the absence of the monkey's conjunction at the tip"— both a difference from that which possesses the conjunction and a difference from that which possesses the absence of the conjunction in the tree, delimited by the conjunction and its absence respectively.

The meaning is that, likewise, in a locus where there is an absence of conjunction, there would result both the non-difference from that which possesses the absence of conjunction and the difference from that which possesses conjunction.

The term ‘pika’ exists—[as indicated by] -u. 10. [This is] with the delimitation of the cow (gāvacchedena)—-u. @---------------------------------------------------------------------------- (The non-application of the rule regarding the cause of manifestation) Śaktivādaḥ, page 77. @--------------------- -------- --------

Furthermore, even at the time when the counter-positive exists, this absence cannot be either destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) or prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), because those two do not exist at the same time as their counter-positives. Moreover, since destruction is infinite, it would still exist even at the time when the stimulant is removed; consequently, if the jewel were present at that time, burning would result.
For this very reason, it is not an absolute non-existence;
since that [non-existence] is beginningless and endless, it would exist even at the time of an obstacle, and thus burning would occur even then.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that for the absolute absence of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭātyantābhāva*), the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of either the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) serves as the condition of proximity (*pratyāsatti*)? And thus, during the state when the qualifier is present, because the absolute absence is not proximate, there is neither the production of burning nor its cognition? If this is argued, we say no; for among those [conditions], there is no single form (*ekarūpa*) that serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the status of being a condition of proximity.

Or rather, let those very things which are not [universally] concomitant, yet possess proximity (*pratyāsatti*), be the cause of burning; what is the use of postulating a distinct entity (*bhāva*)? Now, one might object: in cases where the locus of the negation (*viśeṣya*) exists, the absence that is admitted through a difference in delimiters (*avacchedaka-bheda*) is indeed a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), and not a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Lest the aforementioned fault should occur, he says: "Furthermore" (kiñca).
The phrase "because of the consequence of burning" is an elliptical expression;
it should also be understood that this is because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of a cognition of non-existence at that time as well.
Having adopted the position of absolute non-existence, he raises an objection to ward off the fault stated therein: "But surely... (nanu).
"In them" means:
Although only two— namely, destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)— were suspected,
nevertheless, by accepting a fourfold division based on the distinction between the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) in the form of qualifiers and qualificands, it was stated "among them" (*teṣu*).

Consequently, the lamp is indeed perceived while it exists, and thus it is established that it illuminates itself. [The opponent's view: Even if the lamp illuminates itself, it does not illuminate other things such as jars. [The proponent's reply: That is not so. [The opponent's view: If the lamp illuminates itself, then it must be both the agent and the object of the action of illumination. [The proponent's reply: This is not a fault. [The opponent's view: If the lamp illuminates itself, then it would be perceived even when it is extinguished. By the very statement "situated in the midst of water," it is already evident that [the subject] does not possess a nature different from its prior form; therefore, the phrase "like a jar" is stated to establish its earthen nature (*pārthivatva*).
[The opponent claims this argument is] "unproving" (*aprayojaka*).
The word "inference" (anumāna) is the subject [of the sentence].

Now, one might ask: "In that case, on what basis is it established that a liquid substance is fiery? With the intention of answering this by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), he says: "And that..."
He gathers them.

Just as water gathers particles of earth by means of its cohesiveness (*piṇḍībhūtatā*), so too molten gold does not gather anything; this means that it is not water because it lacks the unique property of water characterized by viscidity (*sneha*) and oiliness (*cikkaṇatā*).
Nor [is it fire].
And that liquid substance is not composed of earth.

That substance possesses color and possesses fluidity; furthermore, it is composed of fire (*taijasa*), because, while being distinct from [substances] other than earth, it possesses color—this is established by the mental perception that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrahakamānāsiddha*). (Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava, Śaktivāda, Part 1, p. 134)
"You are radiance."

That is not so. For the mark (*liṅga*) you have described—namely, the non-transformation of color—is accounted for simply by the presence of some obstructing factor that prevents the transformation of color; it does not establish the "gaseous nature" (*taijasatva*) of the substance possessing liquidity according to your stated method—that the obstructing factor must extend as far as liquidity itself, such that the possession of color by that which possesses liquidity [proves gaseous nature].
Furthermore, another established obstructing factor is possible in this case.

The meaning is that this liquid substance is not incompatible with the burning—characterized by reduction to ashes—that occurs in the portion of the earth-element conjoined with its own supporting medium, whereas it is indeed incompatible with that [burning].
If that is so, why is that substance not of the nature of air and so forth? To this he says: "and because it possesses color."
Regarding this, he states the reason: "because of possessing fluidity."
The sense is "like water";
and [it is] also composed of fire.
The word "substance" (dravyam) is to be supplied [as the subject].

Now, one might object: since neither the obstructiveness [of light] nor a color of a different genus from the adventitious fluidity (naimittikadravatva) is observed in another instance of fire (tejas), how can the substratum of this [fluidity] be conceived as being of the nature of fire? To this, he says:

the meaning is that it is established by the aforementioned inference—which proves conjunction with a fluid substance—assisted by the reasons of its opposition to burning, its adventitious fluidity, and its having the nature of color.

Regarding the first inference, he refutes the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*) by showing that the stated reason is unestablished (*aprayojaka*) because it can be explained otherwise (*anyathopapatti*) even in the absence of the proposed probandum; he does so with the words beginning "tvadukta" and so forth.
Now, one might object: "Is there not simply no other substance devoid of fluidity that could act as such an obstacle? To this, he says: "And it is possible..."

"What is that unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) and what is its nature? Since it is not observed as an obstructing factor anywhere, [the author] clarifies this by means of an example, beginning with the word *karakā*. [The commentary continues: "Because of the statement that [the rain] would be given by him...

(susya-dadyu-ktātteḥ-padhā-thotti-sanam). (Note: The textual variants provided are: 1. *tasya* is redundant according to Rā., Ga., Naṃ., and Su.; 2. the word *hi* is absent in Rā. and Su.; 3. *nnaprati* in Rā. and Su.; 4. *papra* in U.)
*Śaktivāda*, p. 135:

Just as there is natural fluidity in hailstones (*karakā*), so too in the case of a diamond (*vajra*)—which is earthy (*pārthiva*) yet conjoined with extreme fire—there is a color distinct from its previous color; and likewise in gold, there is a color distinct [from that of other metals]. This occurs precisely due to a specific *bhoktṛ-adṛṣṭa* (the unseen merit/demerit of the enjoyer).

Otherwise, one would have to postulate that just as there is another hard constituent part in hailstones that acts as an obstacle to fluidity, there must also be another liquid constituent part in the diamond that acts as an obstacle to the transformation of its color.
In that case, if another entity distinct from diamond and so forth is sublated by non-apprehension, then here too, if fluidity distinct from its yellow substrate is sublated by non-apprehension—

just as you yourself have accepted that even though fluidity is not seen in other types of fire, it arises in gold, which is of the nature of fire, due to the connection with a specific unseen [merit] through contact with fire.
Furthermore, let it be that fluidity itself is the obstructing factor;
however, that fluidity belongs to yellow earthy substances,
because it is already established [as such].

And because they share a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatva*). [Objection: But it is observed that the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is employed only when the collection of visible causal factors (*dṛṣṭasāmagrī*) is complete; it does not perform any function [on its own]. To this, he says: "And it is accepted" (*svīkṛtaṃ ca*).

The observed capacity to obstruct the transformation of color belongs to water only through its fluidity (dravatva), not directly; for this is seen in exactly the same way in the case of a jar situated within water, as otherwise one would fall into the error of postulating an unseen factor (adṛṣṭa). As for hailstones (karakā) and the like, they are accepted as such only because there is no other recourse; therefore, he says: "Furthermore, let it be... (kiṃ cāstu).
"Yellow Earth," it is said.
The meaning is: "by you, [the earth] has been accepted as the supporting substratum.
Regarding the phrase "because it is established":

this means that both the locus (dharmin) and the property (dharma) are known through valid cognition, and because there is a connection with the nature of the related [property], and because fluidity—which is intended to be the obstructing factor—resides in a single common locus.

1. *ca* is added—Ka, Ja, Naṃ. 2. *vyagatamevāstu*—Rā, Ga, Su; *vibhāgāntaramevāstu*—Ka, Ja. 3. *vādṛ*—U. 4. *na syāt*—Kk, Thya, U. 5. *stvapāti*—U. It is not, however, [the case that] what has gone away (*vyagata*) is [to be] postulated along with the substratum (*dharmī*), because it is [already] established and because it would involve a difference of locus (*vyadhikaraṇatva*). *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Second Chapter, p. 136) (Note: The variants provided indicate differences in the reading of the commentary text.)
Otherwise, for the sake of the transformation of color in water that is being boiled,
one would have to postulate a conjunction with another liquid substance.

[Objection: But surely—if the liquidity of earth were the preventer of the transformation of color (*rūpaparāvṛtti*) in that which is co-located with it, then the liquidity of lacquer and the like would also be such [a preventer]. [Reply: No, because of the parity [of the argument]:

if the fire you accept as being "mobile" were the preventer of the transformation of color in a yellow substance with which it is conjoined, then it would likewise be so in a cloth or other object conjoined with it.
As for the resolution through the postulation of a specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*), that applies equally to the present case as well.
But it does not proceed by means of support.
The meaning is that it is considered to be the fire as intended by you;
[this is stated] "with respect to the locus" (dharmiṇi).
The meaning is that this is because its non-perception has already been established;
and also because [the two terms] belong to different loci (vyadhikaraṇa).

The sense is this: if fluidity residing in a different substratum were to obstruct the transformation of color in another substance by means of an obstruction consisting of earthy form—since it has already been stated that no such thing is observed here either—and since the principle that "when an explanation is possible through what is already established, one should not postulate what is unestablished" applies equally here, [the opponent's view fails].
He raises an objection based on the position favored in the *Kusumāñjali* and other works, beginning with "But surely... (*nanu*).

With the intention that, if non-obstructiveness were established merely by observing the behavior of certain individuals, then the same would apply even to the support for what you yourself accept, he says: "tvad... (your...).
[Objection: But surely its very nature is that of being an obstructer precisely when it acts as a supporting factor; to this he says: "By its own nature," etc.

Thus, when "being conjoined with a liquid substance" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), there is either liquidity (*dravatva*) or being conjoined with such a substance. [Notes: 1. *Ṣṭambha* (Rā., Ka., Ja., Naṃ., Su.); *ṣṭambhaka* (Ka., Ja., Naṃ., Su.). 2. *Kvathya* (Rā., Ga., Ja., Naṃ., Su.). 3. The word *paṭa* is added in Ka. 4. *Papa* (Rā., Su.). 5. *Lālā* (Ka.). 6. The phrase *na iti* is absent in Rā. and Su. 7. *Syāt* (Ka., Ja., Naṃ.). 8. *Gata* (U.). 9. The meaning is: "because they subsist in different loci" (*abhinnādhikaraṇavṛttitvāt*).
Now, [it may be objected]: "Is it not so that—[this is an addition]—the apprehension of the object (*padārthopasthiti*) arises from the statement of the capacity (*śakti*)?
(Śaktivāda, p. 137)."
Furthermore, let it be granted that some distinct substance acts as the obstructer;
even so, how can that [substance] be fire?
For, by the very fact of its being opposed to burning—which proves its difference from earth—it is all the more established that it is different from fire.

For the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (dharmin) as a liquid substance does not—by necessity—exclude earthiness (*pārthivatva*) which is co-located with liquidity; rather, it establishes fireness (*tejastva*), which is non-co-located with liquidity, such that the proof of "being other than fire" on the grounds of its opposition to burning would be contradicted by both the establishment and non-establishment of the subject. This is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be grasped due to the lack of recognition of any instance of rapidly moving fire.

Previously, it was stated that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) or non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) by means of the passage beginning with "or [the reason] is established even without [the probandum]. Now, even while granting that point, he states—beginning with "furthermore" (*kiñca*)—that it is improper to assert its luminosity (*tejastva*) by way of elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*).
It is an impediment.
The meaning is that it is an obstacle to a form dissimilar to its prior form. [This applies] to the state of being other than fire (*tejonyatva*).

The sense is that, because it functions as a support (*upaṣṭambha*), the liquid substance you favor cannot be fire, since it would contradict burning—just like water; for such a formal argument (*prayoga*) is possible, whereas fire, being conducive to burning, lacks that contradiction.

[Objection: But in this way, there would be a sublation by the means of knowledge that grasps the subject (dharmin) as being conjoined with a liquid substance, as previously stated; therefore, he says: "For not... (na hi).
"Touches" (spṛśati) means "makes known through inference" (anumāpayati). The meaning is as follows:
if such a substance is established through both its proof and its non-proof, then establishing its absence by means of its being established as fire alone is contradicted;
and if it is not established, then because its very locus is unestablished, establishing its difference from fire is contradicted.
To the question "Why does it not touch?", he says: "Melted," etc.
Because the portion that is mobile [and] supported is characterized precisely by its opposition to solidity— [Notes:
1. *dravadravyatva* (liquid substance-ness) — ka, ja; 2. *drava* (liquid) is added — ka; 3. *vā vinā* (or without) — u; 4.
Thus / by the words beginning with "extreme" etc., there is the following — u; 6. *ktatvasā* — u; 7. *bhyām iti* (by the two) / thus it is — u.]
Otherwise,
let that part be composed of earth alone; for,
having accepted the means of cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*), the resolution of the suspicion of contradiction is equal in both cases.
2. There is a contradiction [in the opponent's position] if they do not accept that it is distinct from fire;
"otherwise" means...
"Contradiction."

In response to the doubt—“How can that which has the nature of being liquid (druta) possess the nature of earth (pṛthivītva), since liquidity is opposed to combustibility?”—the resolution is provided as follows: just as the doubt “How can it have the nature of fire (tejastva)? is resolved by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (dharmin), so too is this resolved. The meaning is that, in the same way, one may likewise establish its status as water (apnitva) by relying on the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject.
"In both cases."
The meaning is: in the state of being earth and in the state of being fire.
The point is this:

if it is argued that the fluid portion—postulated as being opposed to burning—is understood to be fire because its nature as a substratum is established by the means of cognition that apprehends it (*dharmigrāhakamāna*), then let that portion be of the very nature of earth.

Nor should it be said: "How can it have the nature of earth, given that earth is not opposed to burning, whereas this [fluid portion] is opposed to the supporting substance (*upaṣṭambhakadravya*)? [For the reason is as follows:]...

This being the case, since fire also possesses the quality of obstructing burning, and this particular portion likewise possesses the quality of obstructing burning, how can it be considered fire? For the two cases are identical.

If it is argued: "Surely, by the very cognition of the subject (*dharmī*) in the previously stated inference beginning with 'extremely hot' (*atyantānala*), the fiery nature (*tejastva*) of the liquid portion is established; thus, even though it is not perceived in other fires, its quality of being opposed to burning (*dāhavirodhitva*) is accepted here alone"—then [we reply]: in that case, by that same cognition of the subject, its earth-nature (*avanitva*) is also established; therefore, since the logic is the same, its quality of being opposed to burning, even though not seen in other types of earth, would have to be accepted here alone as well.
Therefore, if fluidity is not established, then luminosity is not established.

With the thought that the proof of the liquid portion being earth or the proof of its being other than fire is sublated by the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*), he raises an objection: "But surely... (*nanu*).
[This is] the beginning of the *Śaktivāda* (Discourse on Potency), page 139:
"But surely, the status of being composed of light (*taijasatva*) is not established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*)."

When the liquid portion has been established according to the aforementioned method, there arises the doubt as to whether that portion is earth or fire. In this regard, since the property of "earth-liquidity" (pṛthivī-dravatvatva) is over-extensive (atiprasakta), being present even in the liquidity of lacquer and the like, one would have to postulate that the specific "earth-liquidity" residing in the supporting substrates of gold, silver, copper, and so forth—which serves as the delimiting factor for the prevention of burning—is the [required] property; thus, there is the fault of conceptual complexity (gaurava).

If it is argued that "fluidity in fire" (tejodravatva) is indeed lightness (laghu), and thus, through the assistance of the principle of parsimony (lāghava-tarka), the very means of grasping the subject (dharmigrāhaka) functions as far as establishing its fiery nature—this is not so;
for since fluidity in fire is unestablished prior to the operation of the relevant means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the principle of parsimony does not present itself.

Furthermore,

in the Vedic injunctions such as "one should cook a kṛṣṇala," and in the scriptural accounts of gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa*, there would be no mention of the body being measured [by a scale] or the weight being measured at a thousand *palas*, nor would there be any mention of hearing [the sound of the scales].
The logical connection is that [this] is the statement regarding hearing and so forth.
O King, gold, silver, clothing, or whatever else is desired,
[should be given] until it becomes equal to oneself or even greater than oneself.
Having weighed all that on a scale, one should give it to a person of the twice-born caste.
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
There, on one side of the scale, [they should place] a person who has bathed well and is wearing clean clothes; then,
on the other side of the scale, the eminent brahmins should place gold that is spotless, equal or even greater in weight.
Thus, according to the Smṛti of Matsya.

Likewise, in the Matsya Purāṇa, in the section concerning the gift of the golden wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*) and so forth, it is stated: "One should have fashioned a cow and a calf out of pure gold;
the best [cow] is made from a thousand *palas*, while the middling one is made from half of that."
The Kāmadhenu is proclaimed to be half the size of that [smaller one].
The meaning is that this is because of such a traditional teaching (smaraṇa).
[The term] "kṛṣṇala" [is used].

The phrase "golden razor" is either a restatement of what is already established by the meaning of the Vedic injunction— "one desiring long life should offer a caru-oblation of ghee to Prajāpati consisting of a hundred kṛṣṇalas"— or it is a restatement of what is obtained through a direct scriptural command,
or it refers to the statement from another recensional branch (śākhā): "one should cook [the oblation] with kṛṣṇalas."

For this very reason, in the second quarter of the tenth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], it is stated: “In the case of the *kṛṣṇala* [gold seeds], there is no cooking because the purpose is lost,” and so forth. This is because the scripture (*śruti*) declares that [the *kṛṣṇala*] is to be offered as a gift. Furthermore, since the word *pākya* (to be cooked) is derived from the verbal root *pac* with the suffix *yat*, it signifies that which is fit for cooking. However, in the present context, because the purpose is absent, the cooking is omitted. Thus, the text concludes:

“...from the root *pad* (to go), the suffix *ti* [is applied], and then the suffix *san* [is added]. (Note: The bracketed portions indicate the reconstructed grammatical analysis of the term *pākya*).
Śaktivādaḥ, p. 141:

Furthermore, in that context, the word "gold" (suvarṇa) does not refer exclusively to the supporting substance (upaṣṭambhaka), because if it were incapable of denoting its own primary meaning, it would result in the fault of metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).
Even for that [word], since it is possible [to apply it], it would have multiple meanings.
By this [it is shown]:
"Where there is yellowness, heaviness, and redness upon heating— by whom can the status of 'gold' be denied to that which is well-known in the world?"
"And that substance which appears here as possessing uninterrupted liquidity—this is what is designated by the term 'gold' in the treatises.

In this context, since there is an absence of effects such as the arrangement of constituent parts in the *kṛṣṇala* gold-particles, it follows that they do not undergo heating (*apāka*). However, because the scriptural injunction would otherwise be rendered meaningless, heating must necessarily be performed in the form of mere warming (*ūṣmīkaraṇa*).
The sense is that this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*):
The meaning is: in the context of the argument concerning [the soul] being limited by the body.
Furthermore, does the word "gold" (suvarṇa) possess denotative power (śakti) even with respect to the supporting medium (upaṣṭambhaka), or not?
Regarding the first alternative, he says: "because [it would be] impossible for it to have another [meaning]."
The last [author] says: "Because that too is possible."
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of having various meanings":
The sense is that this is improper according to the principle that "the same logical reason cannot have multiple meanings.
By the word "etena" (by this), [he means:]...
The meaning is: by stating that gold is not a distinct substance [from its properties].
The word "refuted" (nirasta) is to be construed [with the preceding].
The meaning here is: in this object, yellowness, heaviness, and the redness caused by heating are perceived; [the opponent argues] "of that" (tasya).
Regarding that locus of yellowness and so forth, as to which [instance] has the primary designation of "gold-ness" and which has the secondary, he says: "uninterrupted," etc.
"Avacchinnadravatvam" (delimited fluidity) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. "Dāha" (burning) is to be supplied as a qualifier of the object (*vastu*).
The similarity of words—the similarity of the word "suvarṇa"—also applies to the supporting substance (*uṣṭambhaka*).
Just as the word "sweet" primarily applies to taste, yet the sound of a lute is called sweet and the sound of a flute is called sweet, so too is the meaning here.

"Because it has been demonstrated. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (Second Chapter, p. 142) [Notes on variants: 1. *vatviha-rā.su.*, 2. *ta-ja.naṃ.su.*, 3. *tyādya-u.*, 4. *nyathā-u.*, 5. *vā nyāyaiścā-u.*]
Even when a difference between entities is established, a similarity of words may still apply,
just as both the nature of a flavor and a sound can be called "sweet."
Thus, what was stated by Līlāvatī is refuted,
because the distinction between entities is itself unestablished and because it has been shown that scriptural usage applies only to that which is earthen.
Because it is possible for them to have a single meaning, and because it is illogical for them to have multiple meanings.
Furthermore, let it be granted that the liquefying portion which prevents burning is fiery in nature;
nevertheless, that portion must necessarily reside within the fire itself,
and not within the supporting portion consisting of gold, silver, copper, and so forth, because of the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).

— By means of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*) occurs generally only with respect to that which is connected with something else that is capable [of connection].

Furthermore, in the sentence "there is smoke," the verbal cognition occurs only when there is a knowledge of the function (vṛtti) of the word "smoke" as indicating (lakṣaṇā) fire; otherwise, it would be an inference. Thus, regarding the aspect of the relation (anvaya), if there is no knowledge of that [relation], how can the relation itself be verbal? [Objection:
But was it not stated previously that if the relation is impossible, then the cognition of it cannot be verbal?

Regarding what was stated—that the word-form and the instrument [of cognition] possess proximity with respect to the positive concomitance (anvaya)—he raises an objection: neither of those two proves that the apprehension of the word’s power (śaktigraha) is a cause for the positive concomitance, because that [concomitance] is established in quite another way—namely, "And not the positive concomitance... and so forth.
"Even by way of error."

If the word were the cause of verbal cognition and the means of connection (*pratyāsatti*) only insofar as it exists as a real entity in its own right (*svarūpasatya*), then a misconception regarding the word would not occur through a misconception regarding that [word]; yet such a misconception is observed.
Therefore, the cognition of that [word] itself is the cause in this case.
The meaning is that this very proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is indeed known in that context.

There is a reading, "because of the observation of both verbal valid cognition and error in some cases," which intends to show that even in the case of grasping the expressive power of incorrect words such as *gāvī*, a valid cognition is observed.
But some say that there is apprehension of a valid cognition by chance.
Having thus established two erroneous proponents among the six previously mentioned (5) by means of reasoning (6),

and now desiring to state four further arguments, [the author] says "Moreover" (kiñca), [intending to show that] because it is established elsewhere, the knowledge of that [power] is also necessary in the context of power (śakti), even in the aspect of positive concomitance (anvaya).
The object of verbal cognition is the object of the knowledge of the word’s power (śakti) with respect to its own object, because it is the object of the cognition produced by that [power].
Nor is this unestablished,
for even the opponent admits that the knowledge of the word’s power is a cause with respect to the aspect of the word-meaning.

Nor is there an absence of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta). He states another argument—beginning with "api ca"—on the grounds that in the case of inference regarding an imperceptible object (parokṣānumāna), there is a rule that whatever is the object of the produced cognition is also necessarily the object of the producing cognition. (Note: 1. *ityādi* — *Su.Rā.*; 2. *yat* is absent — *Naṃ.U.E.*; 3. *śakti* is added — *U.E.*; 4. *śābda* — *Naṃ.U.E.*)
5. *dhyepyukta*—Naṃ-u. 6. *bhātaṃ*—Naṃ-u. The word *abhrāntaṃ* is struck through with a line—E. 7. *dbhānaṃ*—Naṃ. 8.
*na ca* and so forth do not exist—Naṃ-u-E. (In the case of *anvidhāne*, there is water.)

Furthermore, 1) in the case of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), there is a rule that the relation which constitutes the object of the resulting cognition must be an object of the cognition that produces it. Consequently, the *anvaya* (logical concomitance), which is the object of the resulting verbal cognition, arises from that [verbal cognition].

2) For indeed, the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—which consists in the specific form of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of fire and smoke and which operates commonly with respect to both the subject (*pakṣa*) and its others—has the relation between the mountain and fire as its object in a general sense.

Furthermore, if the knowledge of the word’s power (śakti) regarding the aspect of syntactic relation (anvaya) were not a cause [of verbal cognition], then why would there not be a cognition of syntactic relation from a collection of words such as "ghaṭaḥ karmatvam ānayanam kṛtiḥ" (pot-ness, object-ness, bringing, effort), just as there is from a collection of words such as "ghaṭam ānaya" (bring the pot)? This is because the word has power with respect to its word-meaning, and thus there is the recollection of that meaning; since that recollection produces a recollection of unconnected word-meanings, and because factors such as semantic competency (yogyatā) exist among those word-meanings.
It is stated that [the object] is "indirect" (parokṣa) because the connection with an object possessing conceptual content (savikalpaka) is not the object of non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpaka).
Since it might be argued that the word "necessarily" (niyamena) is unestablished, he clarifies this by saying: "For it happens... (bhavati hi).
The term "sāmānādhikaraṇyaviśeṣa" means a specific type of grammatical coreferentiality.
The meaning is "invariable co-referentiality" (avyabhicarita-sāmānādhikaraṇya).
It is the object in a general sense.
The point is that otherwise, from the perception of smoke on a mountain, there would be the undesirable consequence (apatti) that no cognition of fire on that mountain could arise.

He states—“Furthermore, if...”—that even the fact that there is no such comprehension in cases like "The pot is the object" (ghaṭaḥ karmatvam) serves as proof that the knowledge of the word's power (śaktijñāna) is a cause even for the factor of syntactic relation (anvaya).
Because there is no cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) due to the absence of the necessary causal complex, he says: "of the word" (*padasya*).
The meaning is "to be accomplished by that," namely, to be accomplished by the recollection of power (*śaktismṛti*).
[The term] "unconnected" (*ananvita*)...
The meaning is: "of the recollection of the word-meaning which does not have the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as its object.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (Second Chapter, p. 190) (Note: Variants noted: 1. *cāpa* for *ca*; 2. *tadajñātaśakti* for *tadajñātaśaktiḥ*.)

Nor should it be said that there is no expectancy regarding that [general form], because with respect to the ignorance of the general capacity for positive concomitance, it is precisely the ignorance of the general capacity for positive concomitance— not the ignorance of the specific positive concomitance— that is the governing factor for bringing about the expectancy for a specific positive concomitance.

Nor should it be argued that such a collection of words— as in "a stone fragment, like a sprout"— is inherently unfit for the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya*) by way of the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakabhāva*), because no such cognition of relation is ever observed from them. For, in this case, when an expert who has heard the sentence "The pot, the objectness" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*) experiences the recollection of the nominal suffix, the verbal root, and the finite verb, a cognition of syntactic relation arises.

If one observes the linguistic usage of an elderly person who is being prompted to act, a child who has acquired proficiency [in language] through such instances as "the jar is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*) would not subsequently attain an understanding of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
In the phrase "of fitness, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and proximity (*satti*).
"Knowledge of the general" (*sāmānyājñāna*) means knowledge of the general concomitance (*anvayasāmānyajñāna*). Regarding "of the ignorance of capacity" (*śaktyajñānasya*):
the sense is that, accordingly, the knowledge of capacity must necessarily be accepted for the sake of establishing the existence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
He raises the doubt that there is no fitness—namely, "If not," etc.
"Śīla" means ethical discipline.
The meaning is that just as a fragment of stone is not suitable for a sprout, so it is in this case.
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is "unfitness for its own nature";
this is what is meant by the word "nāma" (indeed).
"Ghaṭa" is the name;
"dvitīyā" is the second case ending;
"ānaya" is the verbal root for bringing.
The meaning is that the word consists of the forms of lost verbal roots, nominal stems, and verbal suffixes, [which are understood] through the recollection of these;
thus it is called "anvaya" (syntactic connection).
The meaning is: "of the cognition of the relation [consisting in] the bringing of a pot as the object";
[this applies] only in such cases as these.

For one who does not know that the cause of linguistic usage consists in the name and case-ending being recalled, the expression "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*) has the meaning "the pot as object" (*ghaṭakarma*);
the expression "bringing is the effort" (*ānayanaṃ kṛtiḥ*) has the meaning "bring [it]" (*ānayanaṃ kuru*).
This refers to one who possesses the knowledge that [the word] is expressive (*śakta*).
The meaning is: "therefore [the cognition arises] from such sentences as 'the jar is the object' (ghaṭaḥ karmatvam).
By this very [explanation], the absence of expectancy (ākāṅkṣābhāva) is also refuted. (In the case of the injunction, water [is the object]).
And it is not the case that the cognition of a relation [between word and meaning] occurs by virtue of an auxiliary factor consisting in an error regarding potency (*śakti*);
for even when hundreds of auxiliary factors are present, that which is inherently incapable does not produce its effect.

Therefore, that [word] is indeed inherently capable; with respect to a child, it brings about the cognition of the positive concomitance (anvaya) because it is accompanied by the auxiliary factor consisting of the knowledge of its power regarding the aspect of positive concomitance.

But for another person, it does not do so because it lacks that [auxiliary factor]; thus, the status of the knowledge of power as an auxiliary factor regarding the aspect of positive concomitance is established.
Furthermore, it is your view that even the knowledge of the power (*śakti*) regarding the referent-part of a word is a cause of the cognition of that power by way of the recollection of the referent.
However, for that recollection, the knowledge of the relation in the form of the power as "power" is not required;

for even in its absence, we observe that the recollection of an elephant-driver produced by the sight of the related object—the elephant—is caused precisely by a cognition of the relation-part having "being a relation" as its qualifier.
However, it is precisely as a relation that knowledge is required.

Thus, for one who has the recollection of "ether" (ākāśa) from the sentence "ether exists" by virtue of the word "ether" being inherent in it, there might arise a cognition of syntactic connection (anvaya-dhī) even with respect to the word "ether," despite its [apparent] unsuitability [as a subject]. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And not... (na ca).
"That" [refers to that].

The meaning is that it refers to a sentence such as "the pot is the object" (ghaṭaḥ karmatvam). And since one might ask what follows from this in the present context, he says: "with respect to a child."

They say that the fact that the cognition of the capacity is not otherwise established as a capacity is the proof for its being a cause of the positive concomitant cognition—this is expressed by the words "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*).
They [say], "This is our opinion."

The sense is that, according to the established doctrine (siddhānta), the recollection of word-meanings is not admitted to occur between the cognition of the word’s power (śakti) and the cognition of the sentence-meaning.
To the question, "Let it be so; what follows from that?", he says: "And if this is the case... (evaṃ ca).
The meaning is: provided that the knowledge of the word’s power (*śakti*) functions as the cause for the recollection of the word-meaning by virtue of being a relation (*sambandha*).
[Notes on variants: 1. *nasya saha-naṃ.su.rā.ga.* 2. *śabdadhī-naṃ.su.rā.ga.ka.* 3. *śasya-su.rā.* 4. *ayogyeti / ityasti-naṃ.u.* 5. *syānyathā-naṃ.u.*
Even for a person devoid of linguistic proficiency, there would arise the cognition of the existence of space.
Nor is it possible to suspect that the [word "space"] is inherently unfit for its own meaning when joined with a noun, a case-ending, and a verb.

If it is argued that, since the recollection of space is established by a cognition having "relation-ness" as its qualifier, a cognition of it as a power (śakti) is required for the sake of actual experience (*anubhava*), then my desired conclusion is proven: namely, that a cognition of power is required in that very instance for the sake of the experience of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*).
Thus, in the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), there is not only the aforementioned set of six [objections];
furthermore, verbal cognition occurs only when there is knowledge of the word-meaning relation (*vṛtti*).

Regarding indirect cognition, there is a rule that the object of the resulting cognition must be the object of the cognition that produces the relation; however, in cases such as "the jar" (*ghaṭaḥ*) and "objectness" (*karmatvam*), no cognition of a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) arises.
Since the recollection of word-meanings can be established even otherwise, there would be no need for the cognition of the existence of space through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

The sense is that [the cognition would arise] even without the cause consisting of the knowledge of capacity (*śakti*), because all other causes, such as the recollection of the word-meanings, are present.
To the objection that there is no cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) due to the absence of compatibility (*yogyatā*), he says: "And not here... (*na cātra*).
The meaning is that the statement "space exists" is [the third]. In that case, [it is as follows].

The meaning is as follows: according to the view that [the word] has for its object the experience [of the meaning] as qualified by the relation [of syntactic connection], since that [relation] cannot apply to a mere isolated meaning (*kevalapadārtha*), it is stated that the cognition of the expressive power (*śaktijñāna*) regarding the relation itself is required precisely for the sake of that experience; this is what is meant by "in the case of the qualified" (*anviteti*). Furthermore, for the sake of existence, there is a dependence upon the knowledge of power in that very same place; thus, all four arguments are established.
The ten arguments for *anvitābhidhāna* (the theory that words denote meanings as already related).
The meaning is that in both parts [of the denotation], the expression of the word-meaning and its relation occurs solely through the knowledge of the word’s power (*śakti*).
This passage is clear.

In the theory of *anvitābhidhāna*, there is a set of ten arguments consistent with what was previously stated. [18] Now follows the difficulty of avoiding [this position] through the counter-argument regarding the manifestation of individuals (*vyakti*). [19]
Now, an objection: the counter-argument regarding the individual (*vyakti*) included within the group of six is not tenable;
for if the knowledge of the word’s power (*śakti*) were not a cause with respect to the individual, just as it is not with respect to the universal (*jāti*), then— [Response:
Now, the counter-argument regarding the individual is difficult to avoid. (19)

Now, an objection is raised: "In the theory of the 'crippled power' (*kubja-śakti-pakṣa*), it has been stated that power is useful when known with respect to an individual word-meaning (*padārtha*), but exists merely by its own nature (*svarūpasat*) with respect to the syntactic relation (*anvaya*). Thus, the difficulty regarding this position remains firm. Furthermore, in that context, the fact that the syntactic relation is verbal and that the cause—the word—is proximate, would not be tenable without the knowledge of power. Therefore, even if these two supporting arguments are established, power [is required] just as it is in the case of a universal (*jāti*)."

Even in the case of an individual (vyakti), it is argued that the [word's] power is useful when there is a cognition of that individual as qualified by [the universal], but not when the individual-aspect is unknown; just as this is said, so too it applies to the aspect of the relation (anvaya). What has been stated as a proof for this is incorrect. With the intention that—by way of a parallel argument regarding the universal and the individual—the power [of the word] would likewise be useful as something known in the aspect of the relation within verbal cognition, he raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely).
Regarding the established doctrine of the theory of word-potency (padaśaktivāda), he states what was said in the *Maṇi*: "In the individual [form]... (vyaktau).

Regarding the aspect of the individual [word-meaning]—@--------------------------------------------------------------------------- 1. It is precisely preceded by the knowledge of the *śakti* (denotative power) that there is the denotation of the related [meaning] (*anvitābhidhāna*). Thus it was previously stated...

If it is argued that since the capacity to motivate [the application of a word] is possible for that which is known simply as "capable" (śakta), it is cumbersome (gaurava) to postulate another motivator in the form of being an individual instance (vyakti) related to a genus (jāti) known as "capable" (śakya), then [we reply]: even in the case of *samanvaya*, there is the same cumbersomeness mentioned in the *Anuvyākhyāna* regarding the postulation of another motivator.

Now, it might be argued that for one who knows "the word *go* is potent with respect to cowness (*gotva*)," it is proper that the universal (*jāti*) should serve as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by way of being the object of that cognition, precisely by taking the individual (*vyakti*) which serves as its qualifier, according to the maxim of "not [apprehending] the qualified without having apprehended the qualifier. This is because the universal cannot be presented without the individual. [The author replies: The connection [of the argument] is as follows: if the potency (*śakti*) and the knowledge of that potency are causes for the knowledge of an individual qualified by the universal, then there is the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) insofar as the potency must exist as a real entity (*svarūpasati*) with respect to the individual portion [of the object].
To the question "How so?", it is said: "the genus, the dress," and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is meant that just as the reality of being a cognition (*jñānatattva*) is the operative cause when the cognition of the genus "cow-ness" (*gotva*) is to be produced—since the genus is the denotable object (*śakyārtha*) of the word "cow"—likewise, when the cognition of the individual cow (*govyakti*) is to be produced, it is the reality of being a cognition itself [that is the cause], since the individual is also the denotable object of the word "cow."

The meaning is that since it is possible for [the universal] to be the motivator (prayojaka), one must abandon that [universal as the denotation] and instead postulate another motivator— such as being an individual instance related to the universal of cowness— which is known to be the denotatum (śakyārtha) of the word "cow" and so forth.
"By another instigator."

Just as in the case of the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), other [theories] also involve "complexity" (*gaurava*)— namely, the complexity mentioned in the *Anuvyākhyāna* cited in the discussion of the six proofs (*sādhaka-ṣaṭka*), which consists in abandoning the established causal factor of being known as the word's denotation (*śakyatva*) and instead postulating another causal factor, namely, having a connection with a word-meaning known as the denotation.
The term "*Anuvyākhyāna*" is used here to demonstrate that this [point] is grounded in the original source (*mūla*).
In the established doctrine of the theory of word-potency (*padaśaktivāda*), he raises an objection according to the direction set forth in the *Maṇi*: "But surely... (*nanu*).
When it is known that "the word 'cow' (gopada) is denotative of cowness (gotva)," cowness is the object as the qualificand (viśeṣya).

For this very reason, in that cognition, the delimitor (avacchedaka)— which is synonymous with the differentiator (vyāvartaka)— is the individual cow, and it is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) with respect to the universal (jāti).
Because without that [individual], the universal (*jāti*) is not perceived.
(The individual is the means for the manifestation of the universal.)
If it is argued that in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*),
this is not so— since the presentation of word-meanings occurs even without it— that is not correct.

In the case of the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*), which is a cognition produced by a mark (*liṅga*) consisting of linguistic usage directed toward the related object, there is the presence of the relation (*anvaya*) because the application of the rule [of co-occurrence] exists therein. However, since such cognition does not necessarily occur elsewhere—for instance, in the cognition of words such as "eternal" (*nitya*), where although the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is perceived, the individual cow (*gavādivyakti*) is not—there is an absence [of the rule] even with respect to the individual.
Thus, even though the individual and the relation are equal [in terms of being objects], it is cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a discrepancy between them.

And thus, according to the maxim that "there is no cognition of a qualified object without its qualifier having been apprehended," the knowledge that "the word *go* is denotative (*śakta*) with respect to cowness (*gotva*)" takes both the individual cow and cowness as its objects. Therefore, it is logical that both the universal and the individual function as delimiters (*avacchedaka*) by virtue of being objects of such knowledge;

consequently, it is correct to hold that the knowledge of the denotative power with respect to the individual portion, just like that with respect to the universal portion, is the cause for the knowledge of an individual as qualified by a universal.
But in the case of positive concomitance (anvaya), it is not so;
he clarifies this with the words "that [is] tam" (2).

Since it is intended to establish that only the sentence produces direct experience, it follows that in the case of an isolated word, its status as a mere reminder is established simply because the causal complex for experience is absent.
