for this alone is what is meant by "being cognized by the same cognition," namely, that the intellect occurs elsewhere than in the cause whose effect-ness is delimited by other types of intellect.
"Constructed by means of individuals."

The intended meaning is either that [the universal] such as "cowness" (gotva) consists of a specific property residing in individuals such as cows, or that it consists of existing in multiple individuals.
He himself provides an example, saying: "Just as..."

In the inference for God—"The earth and so forth have an intelligent cause because they are effects, like a pot"—the fact that the earth and so forth are produced by an intelligent being, established by the reason of "being an effect" residing in the earth and so forth, necessarily implies that this production by an intelligent being is by one possessing eternal intelligence; for without the eternity of that intelligence, the status of being an effect residing in the earth and so forth would be impossible. Furthermore, in the world, regarding effects such as pots, there is an apprehension of the causal relation based on the cognition that they have an intelligent cause, specifically through the property of being an effect which is pervaded by being produced by an intelligent being; it is not, however, through an inference of having an intelligent cause that includes the element of eternity.
Nevertheless, the meaning is that it is just as there is the establishment of specific properties in the case of earth and so forth.
To the question, "What would be stated by this as the restrictive factor? he says: "For it is precisely this," and so forth.

He clarifies what was stated as "this" with the words "that which": the meaning is that from the knowledge of the power residing in the genus (*jātiśaktijñāna*), which is the cause having as its counter-correlative the effecthood delimited by the nature of being a verbal cognition of a genus (*jātiśābdajñānatvāvacchinnakāryatāpratiyogikakāraṇatā*), there arises a cognition of the object as qualified by the genus (*jātiviśiṣṭe buddhiḥ*). 1. *śaktatvāt tā*—Naṃ.; *śakteḥ tā*—Ja.; *śakyatvāt tā*—Rā., Su. 2. *tathā*—Ga., Ka. 3. *tvena*—Bu., Rā., Su.

4. [The reason] is "being produced by [something] possessing power" (śaktimat-kāryatva). 5. "Being a cause" does not exist in the Rā. [manuscript]. 6. "Being produced by that which possesses pure intelligence" is established—[this is] *siddhyati*—in the *Naṃ.* and *Siddha-ū.* [manuscripts].
7. Of which—*yasyāḥ*—in the *Naṃ.*, *U.*, and *@* [manuscripts]. (This concludes the previously mentioned proof.)
It is said:
When a relation is apprehended with respect to a relatum presented under a certain form, that cognition of one relatum under that form makes known the other relatum;
thus, rather than overstepping the general causal relationship already established in cases such as inference, it is not proper to postulate an entirely new and extraordinary [causal] principle.

Even in the case of the inference of God (*īśvarānumāna*), although one may accept that the word's denotative power (*śakti*) resides in a specific individual qualified by being produced by an intelligent agent, the cognition of that power functions as the cause for the cognition of the individual qualified by the universal (*jāti*) precisely by virtue of being a cognition of the power residing in the universal.

In that context, there are two restrictive factors (*niyāmaka*) that prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): either the state of being qualified by that [universal], or the state of being cognized by the same single cognition (*ekavittivedyatva*).
He refutes both of those as well with the words: "in whatever form..."

When smoke and the like are presented in the form of "smokeness" (dhūmatva) and so forth, that relation which is apprehended—namely, the relation characterized by pervasion (vyāpti) defined by fire—is grasped as a relation determined by [fire].

It is established that through that form, the cognition of one related term in the form of smoke makes known the other related term characterized by fire; this is the case both in the instance of inference and in instances such as the recollection of an elephant or its foot.

In the same way, in the case of verbal testimony as well, when the related term in the form of the word "cow" is presented in the form of "cow-wordness" (govadatva), [the relation] is determined by the individual cow qualified by cowness (gotva).

Since the relation characterized by *śakti* (potency) has been grasped, it is logically established that the cognition of one related term in the form of the word "cow" (*gopada*) makes known the other related object, namely the individual cow qualified by the universal (*jāti*). Thus,

when the causal relationship is possible precisely between the cognition of the word "cow" as the cause and the cognition of the object— the cow qualified by the universal— as the effect, [the following applies] regarding the cognition of the individual qualified by the universal:

The meaning is that there is the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) in postulating another causal complex consisting of the knowledge of the universal and the knowledge of the power, when [the effect] can already be accounted for by the nature of the knowledge of the universal and the power.
By stating "in its own meaning" (*svārthe*) and "in the manifest" (*vyaktau*), [the author] implies:
"The power of words is experienced as residing both in their own meaning and in that which is associated with it (*anvita*).
Therefore, they denote the associated; otherwise, one would have to assume an unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*)."
Even though there is no sublation regarding the universal, one must assume a separate causal complex for the individual as its own referent, because of the prolixity mentioned in the *Anuvyākhyāna*.

Furthermore, why could it not be the reverse: that the causal efficiency (*kāraṇatā*) resides in the cognition of the word’s power (*śaktijñāna*) with respect to the individual (*vyakti*), while the effect (*kāryatā*) resides in the verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*) whose object is the individual qualified by the universal (*jāti*)? Thus, according to the verse, the power of words is experienced as residing in the individual which is the own-meaning (*svārtha*) conjoined with the universal; therefore, words denote the individual as conjoined with the universal.
The intended meaning is that [the word] conveys an individual endowed with a genus;
otherwise, one would have to postulate a different causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Now, one might object: "Even when the cognition of an individual is obtainable through other means, the assumption that the cognition of the word's power (śakti) toward the individual is also a cause [of that cognition] involves an equal degree of complexity (gaurava). To this, he says: "Furthermore, in this way... (kiṃ caivam iti).
The meaning of the word "evam" (thus) is that, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), only the cognition of the capacity for either one part [of the meaning] is the cause.

If it is argued that there is a disparity— since the universal (jāti) has a form constituted by the individual (vyakti), the manifestation of the universal is not possible without the manifestation of the individual,
whereas the manifestation of the individual does not require the universal—
then it would follow that the principle of the "cognizability of both universal and individual by a single cognition" (ekavittivedyatva) is violated.

This is because the meaning of the term "cognized by a single cognition" (*ekavittivedyatva*) consists in the fact that a cognition arises with respect to something other than the non-cause which stands in the relation of being the counter-positive of an effecthood delimited by being a cognition of another [object].

[Objection: "But surely, since the individual (vyakti) is a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) of the universal (jāti), by the maxim *nāgṛhītaviśeṣaṇa* (one cannot grasp the qualified without first grasping the qualifier), the cause [of the cognition of the word-meaning] must be precisely the knowledge of the word's power with respect to the universal. [Reply: This is not so. For the individual is also a qualifier of the universal; thus, the maxim *nāgṛhīta* applies only in cases where there is a sequential presentation (kramikopasthiti). However, in a case where the universal and the individual are cognized through a single act of awareness (*tulyavittivedya*), that maxim does not apply. He states another defect [in the opponent's view] with the words "evam" (thus).

The point is that this undesirable consequence arises because the Prābhākaras themselves accept that the knowledge of the word’s power (*śakti*) is a cause even for the cognition of the generic form (*anvayāṃśa*). Having accepted the maxim "not [cognized] unless grasped" (*nāgṛhīta*), he states another defect: "Moreover, 'shaven'... [etc.].
(As previously stated regarding the limbs of the argument:
The theory of potency (*śaktivāda*)—page 225. Thus, causality [is established] by virtue of the cognition of the potency of word-meanings.

Since it would follow that the effect is defined as verbal cognition whose object is a word-meaning associated with another [meaning], the knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) residing in the associated meaning would not be the cause.
Furthermore, the apprehension of the denotative power (*śaktigraha*) does not occur with respect to "cowness" (*gotva*) in its abstracted form;
for it is not established that "cowness"—as excluded from horsehood and other such properties—is the denotable object merely through the cognition that "whatever is possible [is denotable].

Rather, the apprehension of the denotative power occurs with respect to "cowness" as qualified by an individual instance (*vyakti*). Thus, the maxim "that which has an unapprehended qualifier [cannot be apprehended]" is not reversed in this case.

Nor should it be argued that because the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*) is inherently distinct, the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) occurs once cowness is known as being intrinsically excluded from others; for even in the cognition "cowness is the denotable object," there is no mention of exclusion from others. Or, if such exclusion were mentioned, that very exclusion would itself become the ground for linguistic application (*pravṛttinimitta*).
Furthermore, the apprehension of the power (śakti) regarding "cowness" (gotva) does not occur when [the object] is known as "cowness-ness" (gotvatva).

This is because, since there is no other "cowness-ness" apart from its being present in cowness while being absent in everything other than cows, the individual instance (vyakti) would have to enter into [the cognition] twice—once as the locus and once as the property—within that very "cowness-ness.
[The phrase] "in cowness unqualified by the individual" means this.
Anticipating the objection that [the universal] is excluded from others by its very nature, as previously stated, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not).
Because it is not mentioned.
The meaning is that there is no such form [of cognition] as "cowness is that which is excluded from horses and so forth.
"That very [form]" refers to this.

The meaning is that the exclusion of others (*itaravyāvṞtti*) alone must be the ground for the application of the word "cow" (*gopada*), because of the maxim that "that which is not grasped as a qualifier [cannot be grasped as a qualified object]. The intention is that it is not "cowness" (*gotva*) as qualified by the property of being excluded from others.

1. *Viśva* is added—Ga, Rā, Su; 2. *syābhāvena*—Nṛ, Ja; 3. *tago*—Naṃ, U. Furthermore, if this were so, then the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *gaṅgā* and others toward the riverbank and such, as well as the metaphorical indication of the word *maṇḍapa* toward a person associated with a specific type of house—which is preceded by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*)—would not be possible according to your view. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (Second Chapter, p. 226) (Note: The manuscript variants provided at the beginning indicate textual variations for the preceding commentary.)

In that case as well, it would simply have to be that the "bank-ness" and "man-ness" alone are the objects of indication (*lakṣya*), while the bank and the man are understood either by the maxim of "the unperceived qualifier" (*agṛhītaviśeṣaṇanyāya*) or by virtue of being cognized in a single act of cognition, without recourse to indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, if the individual (vyakti) were impossible [to denote], there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) therein.

Nor should it be argued that even if the individual instance (*vyakti*) cannot be denoted, there is still a syntactic connection with the meaning of the case-ending because the individual is conveyed by the base (*prakṛti*) through being cognized by a single cognition;
for if that were the case, then priority (*pūrvatva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*) would also be mutually connected [with one another] simply by virtue of being cognized by a single cognition—
this is what you intend.
The connection is with the word "characteristic" (lakṣaṇā).
[The term] "based on conventional usage" (rūḍhipūrvaka) [is used].
Since the word *maṇḍapa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as a specific type of house, the meaning is that it is preceded by that [conventional usage].
He states the two restrictive factors mentioned by the opponent even in the case of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), beginning with the words "nāgṛhīta" (not ungrasped).
Regarding the phrase "vibhaktyartha" (the meaning of a case-ending): [it refers to the fact that the suffix *sva* denotes the sense of a case-ending].
The meaning is that in expressions such as "bring the jar" (*ghaṭam ānaya*), there is a syntactic connection with the case-meanings, such as objecthood (*karmatva*).

This is because *su*-inflected case endings convey their own meanings as connected to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*); furthermore, since an individual instance (*vyakti*) cannot be denoted [directly by a word], it lacks the status of being the meaning of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) such as "jar."

If it is argued that the syntactic relation of the case-meaning occurs with the object intended by the primary sense (*prakṛti*), we say no; for this would result in the abolition of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication), and because it involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). This is the underlying intention.

Although it has been stated that the expressive power (*śakti*) indeed resides in the qualified [individual] as before, and thus the individual (*vyakti*) also possesses the status of being denotable (*śakyatva*), there is no fault [in our position] because of the following two possible interpretations: either (1) because the cognition of the expressive power is not the cause with respect to that [individual] part, and therefore the individual is not considered denotable; or (2) because of the view that the expressive power resides in the genus (*jāti*) alone, while the cognition of the individual occurs through its being cognized in a single act of awareness (*ekavittivedyatva*).
"For if that were the case," etc.
(Note: 1. *Tagam* - *Rā.su.naṃ*. 2. *Ktyanvayo* - *Ja.ka*. 3. *Tinajā-naṃ-'na'* is marked as corrupt by a line - *E*. 4. *Vāsya doṣasyā* - *U. naṃ*.
End of the previously mentioned section.)
In the Śaktivāda (p.

227): Since the syntactic relation [of the case ending] is possible [directly], there would be no need for a reciprocal secondary signification (viparītalakṣaṇā) whereby the preceding and succeeding nominal stems would respectively refer to the meanings of the succeeding and preceding nominal stems.

Moreover, in the primary usage "Bring the previous one," there would be no syntactic connection of the other [object] with the case-meaning, nor would there be its connection with the action, which depends upon that [case-meaning].

Furthermore, if the word-meaning were merely the universal (jāti), then from the word "cow" there would be no cognition of an individual qualified by that universal. Nor can it be argued that such a cognition arises simply through being cognized in the same act of consciousness (samānasaṃvitsaṃvedyatā); for this is not the case regarding the aspect of the qualification itself.

When there is a syntactic connection with the meaning of a case-ending based merely on being cognizable by a single cognition, if one first employs the word *pūrva* (prior) with an intention contrary to its literal sense— namely, through indirect indication (*viparītalakṣaṇā*) to mean "bring the other"— then there would be no indication of the meaning of the subsequent word by the nominal stem *pūrva*. This is because, even without indication, it is possible for the objecthood denoted by the second case-ending to connect with the meaning of the subsequent word— which is itself cognizable by the same single cognition as the meaning of the prior word— and thus the intended meaning "bring the other" is established.

In the same way, even in the case of "bring another," the meaning "bring the previous one" is established according to the direction already stated; for the meanings of the words "prior" (pūrva) and "subsequent" (apara) are mutually dependent and thus cognizable by a single cognition. Nor is this an undesirable consequence.
Because it contradicts all Tantric and worldly [conventions],
he states the sublation even while granting the opponent's position, beginning with "Moreover" (api ca).

In a case where the primary meaning is employed first—such as "bring it"—without any intention toward a secondary (lakṣya) sense, there occurs an application of the case-ending heard after the preceding nominal stem to express its objective case-role (*karmatva*) in relation to the object denoted by the subsequent word;

for this satisfies your stated condition for the application of the case-meaning, namely that the meaning of the preceding word and the meaning of the subsequent word are cognized by a single act of cognition.
To the question, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", he says: "Dependent on that."

And likewise, when it was previously said "bring the first," there arose the contingency of bringing the other; therefore, by saying "not [the other]," the contingency of bringing the first is indicated.
Even in that case,
if it were so, there would be the abolition of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*).

Furthermore, according to the principle already stated, if the expressive power (*śakti*) and the cognition thereof reside in the genus (*gotva*) as qualified by a particular individual, then the verbal cognition (*śābdadhī*) produced by that [power] would also have as its object an individual qualified by the genus *gotva*, with the genus itself serving as the qualifier.
Yet such is not experienced;
for by the word "cow" (*gauḥ*), there is the apprehension of an individual qualified by the genus *gotva* alone.

Therefore, if the cognition of the power resides in the universal aspect alone, there arises the contingency of postulating a separate causal complex; if it resides in the individual aspect alone, there arises the contingency of the opposite—that the cognition of the power is the cause; this constitutes a counter-argument based on positive concomitance (*anvaya-pratibandī*).

If the individual were to enter [into the denotation] twice at the time of grasping the word-potency (*śakti*) in respect to "cowness" (*gotva*), there would be the undesirable consequence of redundancy.

Furthermore, if words such as *go* (cow) were to have their potency (*śakti*) reside solely in the universal (*jāti*), it would follow that words such as *gaṅgā* (the Ganges) would have to possess indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in respect to the bank (*tīra*) and so forth.

If the syntactic connection with the meaning of an inflectional suffix (*vibhakti*) were based merely on being cognizable by a single cognition, then it would follow that even the suffix *para* in expressions such as *pūrvamāna* (measuring first) would be subject to that same consequence.
Regarding the term "non-conceptual" (nirvikalpaka):

The meaning is as follows: since a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) qualified by a universal is known by a single act of awareness (*ekavitti-vedyatā*), it possesses the individual (*vyakti*) as its object; likewise, if the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) were also known by that same act of awareness of the universal, it would follow that the cognition also possesses the relation of qualification as its object. Consequently, non-conceptual cognitions that do not have the relation of qualification as their object would be abolished. This has been stated according to the view that non-conceptual cognition exists.
But regarding the view that those [entities] do not exist, he states another fault: "Moreover, it has been said... and so forth.
The meaning is: "by the logic stated in the passage beginning with 'there is no apprehension of power in the case of the class [of] shaven-headed [monks]' (muṇḍite gotve na śaktigrahaḥ).
The phrase "produced by that" means "produced by the power.
To the objection "let it be so," he replies: "and not so."
Restating what was previously mentioned in brief, he concludes with the words "Therefore": "Therefore... [and so forth].
[This concludes the section on] the figurative sense (*bhākta*), the individual (*vyakti*), and the basis for the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*).

The theory of capacity (*śaktivāda*) [faces] eight defects: (1) the impossibility of cognizing the aspect of the qualification by the universal (*jāti-vaiśiṣṭya*); and (2) the undesirable consequence that the word "cow" would produce a cognition of an individual qualified by cowness as its qualifier (*vyakti-viśeṣita-gotva-viśeṣaṇaka-vyakty-dhī-prasaṅga*). These constitute the eight defects.

the Refutation of the Indication of the Individual as Stated by the Bhāṭṭa School // 24 //

The Bhāṭṭas, however, maintain that because it is impossible to grasp the denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to an individual due to [the faults of] infinity and deviation, the genus (*jāti*) alone is the denoted meaning; the individual qualified by the genus, on the other hand, is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣyā*).
Now follows the refutation of the Bhāṭṭa-asserted indication of the individual (*vyaktilakṣaṇābhaṅga*).

Having restated the view that the cognition of the individual (vyakti) arises either through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) or by implication (ākṣepa), and therefore the denotative power (śakti) belongs only to the genus (jāti) which cannot be obtained otherwise, he refutes it with the words: "The Bhāṭṭas, however..."
"Endlessly."
On the view that the word’s expressive power resides in the individual, it is impossible to grasp that power with respect to each individual because they are infinite in number.

Furthermore, if the power were grasped in relation to a single individual, the grasp of power would be fallacious, since we observe that upon hearing the word, another individual is also presented to the mind.

Because that [cognition] arises even without that [universal], and because it is therefore impossible to grasp the word-potency (*śakti*) in an individual, the meaning is that the potency of words such as "cow" is grasped only in a single genus (*jāti*), such as "cowness" (*gotva*), which is common to all individuals.
How then, one might ask, can the cognition of an individual arise from the word? To this:
He states the two positions: "having characterized," etc.
And it is "obtainable by implication."

The meaning is that it is implied by the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Thus, since the base (*prakṛti*) functions as the locus, just like the bank of a river, its connection with the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is logical.
Alternatively, some say that since the individual (vyakti) is obtainable through implication (ākṣepa), no denotative function (vṛtti) need be postulated for it.
That too is not correct;

for, as stated above, since the capacity (śakti) for denoting the individual in its own right is possible, to accept indication (lakṣaṇā)—which consists of an indirect or mediated relationship—would involve the excessive complexity (gaurava) mentioned in the *Anuvyākhyāna*.
Although Maṇḍana Miśra, in his own view, stated that the individual is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) and thus set forth the faults of the theory of implication alone—saying:
"No one would wish to speak of a universal if it were a non-entity;
for they [the qualifiers] are indeed qualifiers of the individual, which is what is to be indicated because of its permanence."

Having cited this verse by Maṇḍana as a point of consensus (*saṃmati*) and having introduced the position that the individual (*lakṣya*) is the denotation as Maṇḍana’s own view, [the author] refuted it.
Nevertheless, because Maṇḍana was a disciple of Bhaṭṭa, it was stated that "the Bhāṭṭas, however, say that the individual is the denotation.
Furthermore, in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, the position that the individual is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) is clear according to the Vārttika school.
And it is also stated in the *Śāstradīpikā*:
"Or rather, a definition (*lakṣaṇā*) must be accepted; therefore, the universal (*jāti*) is the denotation.
Regarding the position that it is a definition, he says "if this is so" to show that the previously mentioned fault does not apply.
"Natural functions."
The meaning is: because it is the object of the operation whose form is characterized by residing in the nominal stem (prātipadika).
[Regarding the term] "ākṣepa" (implication):...

The meaning is that because the individual (vyakti) is inseparable from the universal (jāti), the cognition of the individual arises through a sequence of reflecting upon the pervasion (vyāpti) and so forth, immediately after the cognition of the universal derived from the word.
The point is that it is unproven that the universal and the individual are cognizable by a single act of consciousness.
He states the intended meaning of the three quarters [of the verse] situated where there is no further commentary: "In its own meaning" (svārthe).
In the reading "uktarītyā" (in the manner stated), the meaning is "in the manner stated in the previous refutation."

He explains the meaning of the word *anyathā* (otherwise) found in the fourth quarter of the verse, "Otherwise, there would be [only] a conceptual construction," with the words: "paramparā" (succession). (Note:
This refers to the sequence of figurative usage (*bhākta*), individual manifestation (*vyakti*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*).)
Śaktivādaḥ, Part II, p. 231:

Furthermore, since the preceding words within a sentence function as indicators (lakṣaka), and according to the view that an indicator does not produce cognition, it would be impossible for the individual (vyakti) to be cognized.

Furthermore, it is observed that the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of a word such as "Ganges" occurs toward an object like a riverbank only when that bank is presented under a form other than its own primary meaning—such as the form of being a "riverbank" (*tīratva*). But in this case [of the cognition "cow"], the individual is not presented under any other form apart from the universal;
for in the cognition "cow," both the universal and the individual are indeed manifested.

Even in cases such as "The curd must be protected from crows," the indication (lakṣaṇā) occurs precisely with respect to that which is presented through the property of damaging the curd and so forth, rather than through the property of being a crow.

Furthermore, even in cases such as "Look at the cow" or "The cow stands," [the connection exists]— meaning it takes the form of a mediated relationship (*paramparāsambandha*) consisting of the connection with the genus (*jāti*) which is itself connected to the word.
It is stated that this was mentioned in the *Anuvyākhyāna* in order to indicate its foundational status (*mūlārūḍhatā*).
The thought that the derivation of such meanings as "sudhā" and so forth should be inferred by the students themselves is due only to the fear of making the book too voluminous,
and not because they are unintended by the author of the work.
Since the original authors themselves stated, "This work also contains many meanings," no contradiction should be suspected.
The syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "because [the word] cannot bring about the experience of the manifestation (*vyakti*) by way of being indicative (*lākṣyaka*).
Why is this so? Because it refers to the position of those who hold the view that "an indicative word (*lākṣaṇika-pada*) does not produce direct experience."
He states the fault mentioned by Maṇi with the thought that there can be no definition because of the absence of the seed of a definition, beginning with "Furthermore" (kiñca).
Anticipating the objection that the definition might be subject to deviation because [the word "crow"] is present in another form [as a bird], he says: "from crows."

He states that not only is there an absence of the seed consisting in the manifestation [of the word] in another form, but also that the seed of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—which consists in the recollection of the impossibility of the primary meaning—is absent: "Furthermore, [the word] 'cow'... and so on.
He states the two defects consisting of the abandonment of what is established and the acceptance of what is not established: "Furthermore, in which [case]... etc.
[From the *Tarkatāṇḍava* with the *Nyāyadīpa*, Second Chapter, p. 232]

When a genus (*jāti*) is capable of being construed [with a word], the cognition of an individual qualified by that genus occurs even without reflecting on an impossibility of direct application; therefore, there is no secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in such cases.

On the contrary, in instances such as "the cow is eternal" or "cowness is a genus," the cognition of the genus arises precisely because the construction of the individual is impossible; thus, it is only in those cases that secondary indication exists.

Furthermore, since the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) occurs through the practical usage of bringing, leading away, and so forth with respect to an individual (*vyakti*), and since there is an abundance of both usage and cognition in instances such as "the cow is lost," "the cow is tall," "the cow is white," "the cow has a dewlap," "the cow is many," "the cow goes," "bring the cow," and "tie up the cow"—

it is a sound principle that the secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) resides in that individual, while the primary power (*śakti*) resides in the genus (*jāti*), which is the opposite of that [individual].
For indeed, destruction and so forth do not exist in a genus.

Furthermore, there would be no established definition such as "the state of possessing activity" being the definition of substance due to under-extension (*avyāpti*), nor "being the substratum of existence" due to over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

This is because, in the case of substances and other categories, the property of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*)— which is restricted solely to its respective individual instances— would fail to include the objects to be defined, resulting in under-extension.

Since existence, when resting in each [individual], does not reside in qualities, actions, and so forth, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) consisting of an inclusion of things distinct from the definiendum (*lakṣya*).
Therefore, if one does not accept a universal that follows after [individuals], there would be the collapse of all conventional usage.
It is replied:

Is it being said that in the absence of a recurring universal (*anugata-jāti*), the presentation of all individuals—whether as the objects of a word's denotation (*śakya*) or as the locus of pervasion (*vyāpya*)—is simply impossible? Or is it that even if such a presentation were possible, there could be no "comprehensive inclusion" (*kroḍīkāra*)? For, in the absence of a single [universal] such as "cowness" (*gotva*) or "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*), the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śakti*) or pervasion (*vyāpti*) through the synthesis of all individual cows and so forth would be impossible.
The first proponent states another fault regarding the absence of an accompanying universal (*anugatajāti*), beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*).
Because [the definition] does not apply to space and so forth, he says: "because of non-pervasion" (avyāpteḥ).
Since [the definition] also applies to qualities, actions, and so forth, he says: "because of over-extension" (ativyāpteḥ).

By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), it is understood that there would be no established distinction between universals (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*) regarding [categories] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) and earthness (*pṛthivītva*);
nor would there be an established distinction such as some words having a single referent while other words, like "akṣa," have multiple referents.

The underlying sense is that this [distinction] depends on whether the grounds for the application of a word (*pravṛttinimitta*) are one or many, thereby accounting for the state of having a single referent and so on.
To the question "Why should it not be so?", he clarifies the sequence with the words "tattad" (each respective).
Because it is under-extended.

Not the first [alternative]. For in your view, by means of a single universal (*sāmānya*) serving as a cognitive proximity (*pratyāsatti*)— which is the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the pervasion of denotability (*śakyatva*), just like "cowness" (*gotva*)— in my view as well, at the time of grasping the pervasion of the word-potency (*śakti*) and so forth through instruction, repeated observation of usage, and so on, there is the possibility of the presentation of all past and future instances that are pervaded by the potency, by means of a single similarity (*sādṛśya*) which has as its locus specific individual cows already presented and which has as its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) all past and future individuals.
However, this is the distinction:
in your view, the universal (*jāti*) resides in things past and so forth;
in my view, however, similarity is related to each respective object by way of being its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), just as [negation] is related to destruction and the like.
"Regarding 'pervasion and so forth'..."

The "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is the meaning of the first term (*ādipadārtha*). The phrase "by repeated observation, etc."—where the word "etc. (*ādi*) also connects with what precedes—refers to the apprehension of the connection between that [term] and its referent through instruction such as "this is a cow," through the linguistic usage of elders such as "bring the cow," and through means such as analogy (*upamāna*) and lexicons (*kośa*).

The meaning is: at the time of grasping causality, by means of repeated observation; at the time of grasping pervasion (vyāpti), by means of observing positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); this is "at the time of grasping causality.
Regarding "by similarity" (sādṛśyena):
similarity is a distinct category of entity (padārthāntara).
The intended meaning is that [the word] does not have a form constituted by a genus (jāti) that is concomitant [with the individual].

By the phrase "pervasion and so forth" (*vyāptyādi*), the inclusion of the individual cause (*kāraṇavyakti*) is intended. He says, "But this much is the difference," in order to indicate that there is no distinction regarding their capacity to bring [the object] to mind (*upasthāpakatā*).
The meaning is that this alone is the distinction.

How can past entities and the like possess the property called "counter-correlativity" (pratiyogitva), given the absence of a substratum? To this, it is said: "like destruction (dhvaṃsa) and so forth."
Prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the first category [of absence].
The point is that if it were so [that all absences were prior non-existences], then destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and the others would not have it as their counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
[The objection that] there would be a grasping of universals such as "cowness" and so forth [is answered by saying:

the theory of universals (jātivāda) is indeed logical; for even though it does not depend on those [individuals], it brings them to mind by virtue of being a proximity (*pratyāsatti*), just like a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
On the contrary, in your own view, since the past and so forth are non-existent, it is illogical for them to be the substratum of a universal (jāti).
If it is objected: "But in your view, since similarity is not [identical to] the past and so forth, the relation consisting of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva) is manifold; what does that matter?
For there is no rule that in a single cognition only one relation can be the cause," [we reply:
because such a rule is absent in cases such as a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana-jñāna*) or in cognitions like "the pot is colored" (*rūpī ghaṭa*).

Now, one might object: "How can similarity—which does not depend on the past and so forth, but depends solely on that which is present before one—bring about the recollection of the past and so forth? To this, he says: "And it is logical," etc.
"Like a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

This means that just as in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and in the presentation of [objects] such as a piece of sandalwood, a latent impression—though residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth—functions as a proximity for the eyes and other sense organs; it is in this same way [that the object functions].
And this has been stated by relying on his own philosophical position.
In the view of the opponent (paramata), however, it should be understood that [the cognition] is like [the case of] knowledge (*jñāna*).

It should be noted that even for a cognition in the form of memory—such as the memory of "that-ness" (*tattā*) and so forth—which is inherent in the self (*ātmasamaveta*), its status as a causal proximity (*pratyāsatti*) for visual perception and the like in recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is likewise established.

He states "on the contrary" (*pratyuta*) to show that, in the very position that accepts generality (*sāmānya*) as the causal proximity, the required presentation (*upasthiti*) is difficult to establish.

Now, an objection: the property of being the counter-correlative of similarity residing in a subject (dharmin) present before one is not a single, recurring [entity] in all cases, such as those that are past and so forth.
If that were the case, since it would be possible for "cowness" (gotva) and the like themselves to function in that way, what is the point of this postulation?
Furthermore, it would be swallowed by the defects of the "recurring" (anugata) position that will be stated later.

Therefore, as many counter-correlatives (pratiyogin) there are, so many instances of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva) there also must be, and thus they are distinct from one another. And in that case, how could [the cognition] simultaneously present infinite objects that serve as counter-correlatives through infinite relations consisting of the absence of those counter-correlatives and their corresponding positive correlates (anuyogitā)? With this in mind, he raises an objection: "But surely... (nanu).

He states that the multiplicity of relations is not an obstacle when there is simultaneous presentation, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), by means of the passage beginning with "But what [is the case]... and so forth.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (Second Chapter, p. 264) [Note: The provided text contains fragments of commentary and manuscript variants.]
This is because there is a distinction between the various types of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) and the essential natures (*svarūpa*) of the pot and so forth.

Furthermore, even in your own view as one who maintains the non-difference of inherence (*samavāya*), since the inherence of "cowness" (*gotva*) and other universals exists even in horses and the like, the mere relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) exists in all loci such as time (*kāla*). Therefore, you must admit that it is specifically *viśeṣaṇatā*—in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*)—that serves as the regulator for cognitions such as "this is a cow."

Accepting that in the case of a cognition having a collective object (*samūhālambana*), the distinctness of the various contacts with the jar, cloth, and so forth is evident, he clarifies this in the cognition "it has color" and so on, stating: "the jar," etc.

The meaning is: of the sense-object contacts consisting of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), and inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*).
And he states that this plurality of relations exists even under the view that generality (*sāmānya*) is a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), by saying "furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*).

Regarding the universal "cowness" residing in the object present before one, there must be stated either an inherence (*samavāya*) with past and other individual instances, or a relation of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), or else a relation consisting in being its own qualifier (*svaviśeṣaṇatva*) by virtue of the universal being a qualifier that differentiates the individual.
Regarding these, he states the first [option]: "by inherence."

On the view that inherence (*samavāya*) is one and not manifold like conjunction (*saṃyoga*), there is only a single relation between the universal (*jāti*) and all its individual instances; thus, the simultaneous presentation of all [individuals] would be possible.
Nevertheless, just as all cow-individuals are presented by means of "cowness" (*gotva*), there would also be the presentation of horse-individuals and so forth.

This is because, since the inherence of cowness is one, the inherence of cowness exists in horses and other animals as well, according to the principle stated previously regarding the non-cessation of inherence.
2. The second [author] says: "The support."
"At the beginning of time," etc.
And thus, the intention is that by means of "cowness" (gotva), there would also be the presentation of space and time.
With the thought that the third alternative remains, he says: "svarūpa... (its own nature).
Regarding the phrase "such as 'cow' (gaur) and so forth":
The meaning is that it must be stated [as] "that which determines the cognitions whose objects are all cows, whether past or future."

Now, an objection: only when the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) are present can there be knowledge of the relation consisting in the absence of those counter-correlates; and only when there is knowledge of that relation can the counter-correlates be present. Thus, it follows that for the knowledge of the counter-correlates, the knowledge of the counter-correlates itself is the cause.
[The inclusion of beds and so forth] is thus [an example of] the doctrine of birth (jātivāda).
It is the same [in this case], for that [universal] is indeed infinite in the form of those respective individual instances (tattadvyakti).

And that relation, being existent by its very nature (*svarūpasat*), is the proximity; it is not [proximity] as something cognized. Thus, our avoidance of the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) is also the same for both of us.

[Objection: But surely, just as in your view the universal *gotva* (cowness) resides in the individual cow standing before one, in your [opponent's] view that individual does not possess the status of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of its own internal similarity; how then can there be an apprehension of it from that [similarity]? [Reply:

This is not so, because in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), that individual is apprehended through the very same means—such as sensory contact—as the "this" (*idam-aṃśa*) portion [of the object].

Since the relation is of the nature of the thing's own essence (*svarūpa*), the relation, existing as the very essence of the thing, is itself the cause for the apprehension of the counter-correlative.
"It is not known [by that cognition], such that it could have itself as its substratum;
otherwise, this same fault would apply to you as well"—with this intention, he says: "And that... (sa ca).

The meaning is that [the relation] is of two kinds: the nature of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) and the nature of the relation between the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and the sub-correlative (*anuyogin*).

It is incorrect to claim that similarity is established through the proximity of a universal (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*), whereas similarity is established through the proximity of resemblance (*sādṛśyapratyāsatti*).

It is logical that the relation of the universal "cowness" with the individual present before one, as well as with individuals not currently perceived, is exclusively of the nature of being a qualifier.

In this regard, since the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is connected to the object present before one by means of that very same form, it is also connected to past and other [objects] by that same form; thus, it brings forth the manifest individual present before one and the past and other individuals simultaneously.

However, [the opponent] raises an objection with the thought: "But how could similarity bring forth everything simultaneously? For there is a difference in form (*vairūpya*): it is related to the object present before one as the locus (*dharmin*), whereas it is related to past and other objects as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
The phrase "in my view" (*manmate*) means "in the view of the Logicians" (*tārkika*).
"Welcome! he said.
The meaning is that the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitva) does not belong to the similarity residing in the individual present before one;
rather, it belongs only to the subject (dharmitva).
Counter-correlativity, however, exists only in that which is unperceived and so forth.
"Of her," it says.
The meaning is "of that which is present before one";

[it is] "like the 'this'-portion" (idamaṃśa). 1. *tve* is the correct reading, but not *na* (as in *naṃ.* and *ja.*); 2. *viśeṣyarū-* is the correct reading, but not *u.naṃ.*; 3. *ndhaḥ tenai-* is the correct reading, but not *u.naṃ.*; 4. *ndha iti* is the correct reading, but not *u.naṃ.*.
Furthermore—
just as Trivikrama touches the upper world with one foot and the lower world with the other,

so too does [the cognition] touch the past and so forth through the relation of being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*), and even the object present before one through the relation of being a substratum (*dharmitva*).
And there is no such lack of uniformity,
because the nature of being a determiner, which conforms to both [cases], is of a single form.
Moreover, the term "proximity" (*pratyāsatti*) is used merely in the sense of being a cooperative factor (*sahakāritva*), like collyrium and other such aids.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Paddhati* that the cognition of the past and so forth occurs through the power of cooperative factors such as repeated observation.

In this case, it is only the aspect of "that-ness" (*tattā*)—whether as a refinement of the eye, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), or a cognition—that constitutes the proximity, while in the aspect of "this-ness" (*idamaṃśa*), it is simply [sensory] contact and the like.

The point is this: just as a single act of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) concerning both objects arises through two relations— since worldly proximity (*laukikannikarṣa*) serves as the means of immediate contact—

likewise, a single cognition having as its object both that which is present before one and everything else arises precisely through the two relations of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*).
Now, even so, a relationship of a single form is not obtained; therefore, he says: "Moreover" (api ca).
"Both."
The meaning is that [similarity] possesses the property of being a relatum (*nirūpakatva*) with respect to both that which is present before one and that which has passed into the past, etc.
The intention is that similarity must be determined by both the locus (*dharmī*) and its counter-correlate (*pratiyogī*).
It is stated that [similarity] is "concomitant" simply because the property of being a relatum exists both in what is present before one and in the past, etc.
However, one must not be deluded into thinking that a single entity exists by way of distributed occurrence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*);
for if that were the case, it would be impossible to exclude a recurring universal (*anugatajāti*).
Now, an objection is raised: "But even the property of being a qualifier (nirūpakatva) is not of a single form;
since it appears in some cases as the locus (dharmin) and in others as the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), it is manifold.
Furthermore, there is the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of merely following the word [as a common denominator]. To this, he says: "Moreover... (api ca).
If it is argued that perception, which grasps only what is present and proximate, how could it grasp a pervasion (*vyāpti*) whose locus is the past and so forth?

[The author] says "In the *Paddhati*, etc. having extracted the meaning of the statement: "Because it is frequently observed that through the power of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), other capacities of the sense organs (*karaṇa*) are manifested."
The intention is that this statement serves as a supporting argument because, according to the direction to be explained, it culminates in similarity (*sādṛśya*).
Therefore, the swallowing of universals (*jāti*), individuals (*vyakti*), and so forth, constitutes the doctrine of universals (*jātivāda*). (Page 267)

For even in the Nyāya system, there is no primary status as a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) for a recurring universal (*anugatajāti*), mental impression (*saṃskāra*), ascertainment (*vyavasāya*), merit born of yoga (*yogajadharma*), or a defect (*doṣa*) which is the cause of error.
Nor is there a relation between merit born of yoga and so forth and the past and so on.

Furthermore, even in the *Paddhati*, the intended meaning is that the sense organ, aided by impressions produced from repeated observation and the like, grasps the past and so forth as the counter-correlates of similarity residing in the individual present in contact with it; thus, there is no abandonment of the "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) mentioned in the *Anuvyākhyāna*.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving even what is dissimilar;
furthermore, it would contradict your own statement that "similarity is the mediating factor.
To the question, "Why then should mere universal-proximity (*sāmānya-pratyāsatti*) be accepted? he says: "For not... [etc.].
It is called "volitional formations" (saṃskāra).
The term "saṃskāra" (mental impression) refers to knowledge (*jñāna*),
because it is accepted that knowledge itself serves as the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) in recognition and similar processes;
or else, the mention of "saṃskāra" is made according to the view of the Prābhākaras and others.

Because the determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) is in close proximity when an external object is made the object of perception through subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), it is called "determinate.
This refers to the quality born of yoga (*yogajadharma*).
Because it possesses the nature of a proximity (pratyāsatti) in the case of cognitions such as those that are eternally inferable;
thus, it is primary.
The meaning is that it consists in the state of being related to both, just like the worldly means of contact (*sannikarṣa*) such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
To the question, "How does the sentence in the *Paddhati* support the stated meaning? he says: "In the *Paddhati* also..."
The meaning is that even etymological derivation is understood through similarity alone, as stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna* beginning with "ityādi"; otherwise [it would not be possible].
The meaning is that there is an absence of the intention to express similarity.
Regarding the phrase "by one's own words":

The word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) is to be supplied [to the previous sentence]. The meaning is that this contradicts the statement found in the *Śabdapariccheda* section of the *Paddhati*: "It is the individuals themselves that are denoted; however, in the acquisition of the linguistic convention, similarity serves as the basis."

Nor should it be said that it has been stated that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the basis for the apprehension of the word’s power (*śakti*) alone, but not for the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Second Chapter, p. 268) [Notes: 1. *di-saṃ* – Naṃ., Ja., Ga., Rā., Su.; 2. *ktya* – U., Naṃ.]

If it is argued that even so, since the gavaya is also the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) of similarity to a cow, its presentation would also occur [in the cognition], then for you too, in the case of an analogy, there would be the cognition of another animal similar to a cow as being denoted by the word "gavaya.
Furthermore, when there is the instruction "this is a cow," there would be the cognition of other universals (jāti), such as substanceness (dravyatva) and so forth, residing in that cow.

And if, through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāpa*), there is similarity (*sādṛśya*) of that which is internal—this is the sense, namely, because the principle is the same—then, since similarity functions either as a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) or as a proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it brings about the presentation of all its own qualifiers (*svanirūpaka*) in some way or another; thus, when the presentation of all things, including those past and so forth, has been admitted, [the objection] "not... [does not apply].

He clarifies the objection regarding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) stated in the *Sudhā*—namely, that "since similarity to a cow exists even in a horse, it would follow that the word 'cow' could be applied to it as well" and so forth—by means of the passage beginning with "But surely... (*nanu*).
The meaning is "resembling that which stands upon a cow-horn" (goniṣṭha).
[This occurs] in the case of a simile (upamitau).

In the view that an analogy arises for one who has heard the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) "the *gavaya* is like a cow" and, having gone to the forest, perceives an individual object qualified by similarity to a cow, such that the resulting analogy concerns the fact that this specific object is denotable by the word "gavaya"— the application [of the definition] is as follows: even upon seeing some other animal distinct from a *gavaya* that is similar to a cow and qualified by a certain degree of similarity to a cow, there would arise an analogy regarding its being denotable by the word "gavaya."
Even regarding the teaching of direct perception, he brings forward an over-extension for the opponent with the words: "This [is]... and so forth.
When a cow-individual is present before one, upon the instruction "This is a cow," one grasps that it is denotable by the word "cow" as delimited by cowness (gotva).
That would not be the case;

rather, the meaning is that the cognition [of the object] would be expressed by "substantiality" (dravyatva), which is a broader category (bahiraṅga) encompassing "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, or indeed by "earthness" (pṛthivītva) and the like. He states the resolution precisely with those words: "If, however... (yadi ca).
*Avāpa* means insertion;
*udvāpa* means extraction.

If, upon grasping the primary application (*autpattika-graha*) of the word "gavaya" to something merely similar to a buffalo and so forth, one were to engage in worldly transactions such as "Bring the buffalo," there would be an extraction (*udvāpa*) of the word "gavaya" and an insertion (*avāpa*) of the word "buffalo"; however, that [extraction and insertion] would not be possible.

In the *Sudhā*,
the non-mention of the first alternative stated in the *Paddhati* is because it was already stated in the *Paddhati* itself.

because both methods mentioned in the *paddhati* are possible even in the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*) due to the same underlying logic; furthermore, by the statement in the *Sudhā*, "By this, the apprehension of the relation of cause and effect and so forth is also resolved," the method stated regarding the apprehension of potency is extended by analogy to the apprehension of pervasion and the like.
For this very reason:
"Indeed, even scripture, when there is a general perception, can only lead one to understand a particularity through direct perception;
otherwise, how could there be a grasp of the capacity [of words]?"
"From this very reason" means: because the two methods mentioned in the *Paddhati* are indeed possible for the apprehension of the word's power (*śakti*).
The verse beginning with "The scripture also... is located in a portion of the text slightly preceding the verse that mentions "the apprehender of pastness and presentness.
It is an ancient commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna* titled *Sannyāyaratnāvalī*.

Although, according to the reading, the expressive power of words is grasped with respect to past and future objects when they are perceived by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) in their general form— and thus that [power] belongs precisely to the witness-consciousness because it brings about the presentation of the past and so forth—

nevertheless, since there is also the existence of the witness-knowledge in its general aspect, the term "witness" is used. Even so, this does not exclude the presentation [of the object] through visual perception by means of the efficacy of the auxiliary causes.

For this very reason, with the intention that even in that case it was stated "by way of a general form," there is no fault in citing the remaining portion of the sentence after discarding certain parts from those things perceived by the witness through their general forms. (Now follows the sub-section: *ata-jāve-śavyādi-grasanam*)
Regarding the discussion on the theory of universals (jātivāda) on page 289:

The justification for the apprehension of power (*śakti*), pervasion (*vyāpti*), and so forth, even in the absence of a concomitant universal (*anugatajāti*):

Regarding the second position, the meaning is that since there is no manifestation of everything by way of being the determiner of similarity (*sādṛśya-nirūpaka*), and since the manifestation of the past and so forth must be stated to occur through the witness (*sākṣin*) alone, the witness is accepted as the bringer of objects such as the past for the sake of the linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and other suffixes; this is the intended sense.

The meaning is as follows: even if one were to suspect that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) could be dispensed with because the presentation of past and other cow-individuals could be achieved through the proximity of universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*), the witness-consciousness must nevertheless be accepted;

for in the linguistic analysis of verbal suffixes such as the *laṅ* (imperfect) and *luṅ* (aorist), the presentation of the past and so forth is indispensable, and thus the witness-consciousness must necessarily be accepted.

Thus ends the demonstration that the apprehension of power, pervasion, and so forth is possible even in the absence of a corresponding universal (*anugata-jāti*). Now begins the counter-argument regarding the universal "golden pot-ness" (*svarṇaghaṭatva*) and so forth. (Chapter Two, p. 290)
Furthermore, even in your own view, the universal "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) is manifold, being pervaded by universals such as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth.

Likewise, the universal "high-pitched-ness" (*tāratva*) is also manifold, being pervaded by universals such as "ka-ness" (*katva*) and the universal "being the *caitra*-universal" (*caitratva*), since otherwise there would be the fault of "crossing over" (*saṅkara*).

Similarly, the universal "manifestness" (*udbhūtatva*) is also manifold, being pervaded by universals such as "white-ness" (*śuklatva*), since otherwise there would be the fault of "crossing over" with universals such as "blue-ness" (*nīlatva*).

Now, the counter-argument regarding [the universal] "being a golden jar" and so forth. (30) To establish that the apprehension of a word's power (*śaktigraha*) is possible even according to the opponent's view by means of a non-uniform property (*ananugata-dharma*), he provides an introductory remark: "Furthermore, in your view... and so on.
The logical connection [is established] by these very [words], "not indeed" (naiva eva).
He causes confusion.
*Saṅkara* (intermixture) is the coexistence in one place of two things that exist by way of mutual exclusion.

In this case, since *tejas-tva* (the nature of fire/luminosity), which exists in light and so forth while excluding *ghaṭatva* (the nature of a jar), is present in a golden jar along with *ghaṭatva*, which exists in an earthen jar while excluding *tejas-tva*; and since, according to the opponent's view, gold itself possesses *tejas-tva*, there would be the fault of intermixture (*sāṅkarya*). Therefore, to avoid this fault of intermixture, [the category of] "earth" must be accepted as manifold.

And thus, because the property of "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva), which is pervaded by "fire-ness" (tejastva) and so forth, does not subsist elsewhere once "fire-ness" and the like have been excluded, there is no overlap (sāṅkarya).
He states this according to the view that the universal "pot-ness" and so forth does not exist in things such as golden pots: "tāratva... and so on.
"Being born in Caitra."
The meaning is: "by means of the genus that delimits being produced by Caitra.

Since the genus of "high-pitchedness" (*tāratva*) and the genus that delimits being produced by Caitra both exist in Maitra’s high-pitched *k* sound and in a mat made by Caitra respectively, there would be a confusion (*sāṅkarya*) [of the two genera] in Caitra’s high-pitched *k* sound;
therefore, in order to avoid this, they must be asserted as distinct.

The meaning is that, in order to avoid the confusion (*sāṅkarya*) resulting from the coexistence of manifestedness (*udbhūtatva*) and blueness (*nīlatva*)—where both a non-manifested white color and a manifested blue color exist within a jar or similar object possessing a manifested blue color—it must be stated that these are indeed distinct [universals].

291: And thus, just as in that case—despite the multiplicity of potness and so forth—there is the conventional derivation of words such as "pot," and the pot possesses the property of being pervaded by its shards; [so it is here].
Just as there is the causality for fetching water and so forth,
as well as the cognition conforming to the form of a jar,
why should it not be the case that, despite the multiplicity of individual cows (*gotva*), there is likewise [a common] linguistic convention and so forth?
Nor should it be argued that there is no confusion (saṅkara) because "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) resides in the shape, color, parts, and conjunctions [of the pot];
for this would lead to the fallacy of confusion with a genus produced by the action of either one [of the two factors] and so forth.
[Objection: But surely, "pot-ness" is one and the same in all pots composed of earth?
Even in the case of golden jars, there is only one [universal] everywhere;
however, in your view, "cowness" and so forth are many.
If it is argued that there is no fault because there is no multiplicity of "jar-ness," we say no.

Since this disparity is irrelevant even though the lack of pervasion (*ananugatatva*) is common [to both cases], and because the objection that there would be no derivation of words such as "tāra" due to the multiplicity of qualities like *tāratva* cannot be avoided;
he raises an objection according to the view of a certain school: "And it is not the case that..."
"Pot-ness," it is said.
There is no confusion.
The meaning is that there is no coexistence [of properties] such as "being fire" and so forth within a single substratum.
The term "from another" [is used].

For in the Nyāya system, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is of three kinds— arising from the action of one, arising from the action of both, and arising from another conjunction— and thus three distinct universals (*jāti*) that delimit these respective causal capacities must be admitted in conjunction, according to the logic of the grass, the flint, and the gem. Consequently, the universal produced by the action of one [of two conjoining objects] exists in the conjunction between a hawk and a post, even while excluding the universal "pot-ness."
Pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) also exists in that [state], as does the disjunction produced by the action of two shards resulting from the abandonment of that [pot].
Furthermore, both exist in the conjunction of one shard with another shard produced by the action of either one; thus, there is an overlap (*sāṅkarya*).
In this same way, an overlap should be understood to exist even with respect to universals (*jāti*) and so forth, which are produced by the actions of both.
Furthermore,
because there is the cognition that "the large pot moves," wherein the property of potness (*ghaṭatva*) is perceived as co-located with dimension (*parimāṇa*), action (*karman*), and so forth.

And if there is an unification of properties such as high pitch (tāratva) by virtue of their residing in that which delimits the obstruction to the direct perception of their own kind, then here too, let there be an unification of individual cows by virtue of their being related to a similarity that is unified [as a single concept].

Moreover, in your own view, just as the production of words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*), "denotable" (*abhidheya*), "corporeal" (*mūrta*), "produced" (*kārya*), "having the nature of being" (*svarūpatva*), "being a universal" (*jātitva*), and so forth occurs despite the lack of a commonality (*ananugama*) among these properties, and likewise their respective appropriate pervasions (*vyāpti*) and so on [are established],
why should it not be the same in this case as well?
Furthermore, properties such as "knowability" (jñeyatva) and so forth are not also pervasive [in this sense],
because that would entail their being universals (jāti);
nor is such an undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) accepted.
Because it also subsists in universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth.
He states the sublation by perception (*pratyakṣa*) which apprehends [the universal] as residing in a substance (*dravyaniṣṭhatva*), beginning with the word "sthūla" (gross).

Furthermore, regarding the point that "highness" (*tāratva*) is manifold, which was intended by the use of the phrase "there would be no production of words such as 'high' (*tāra*)," etc.—anticipating the objection that there is a commonality (*anugati*) in those cases, he says: "And if... (*yadi ca*).
"Of the same class" (sajātīya).
This has been explained in the discussion on the eternality of words;
[the term] "anugata" [means] "concomitant."
The meaning is: the state of being related by similarity, which exists everywhere as the property-bearer (dharmin) and the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), following the direction previously stated.

Now, one might object: "But even similarities, though they possess various relations, function in exactly the same way; for the mere persistence of a word leads to over-extension. With this intention, he says: "Furthermore... (api ca).
Corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is the possession of a dimension delimited by a specific magnitude (*iyattā*).
Being an effect (*kāryatva*) is being the object of volitional effort (*kṛti*).
"Appropriate for each respective [occasion]."

The meaning is that whatever is to be known is existent (*sat*), whatever is expressible is an object of cognition (*prameya*), and so forth, according to their respective fitness; "here too" refers to this same principle.
The meaning is that even when there is a following after the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), there is the acquisition of the linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) for words such as "cow" and so forth.
He raises an objection according to the direction stated in the *Maṇi* and other works on the chapter concerning purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*): "But surely... (*nanu*).
[Regarding] gold, jars, and so forth—this is the discussion on universals (*jāti*).

[Page 293] Now, an objection: are not properties such as "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) and the like merely forms of universals, such as "cognitiveness" (*jñānatva*), "denotableness" (*abhidheyatva*), "dimensionality" (*parimāṇatva*), and "productness" (*kṛtitva*)?

If it is argued that because adventitious properties (*aupādhika-dharma*) are not distinct from their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and those [adjuncts] are thus found to be co-extensive (*anugata*) in things such as jars through a series of relations, then here too— by way of similarity (*sādṛśya*)— let there be either the universal "cowness" (*gotva*), which resides in each individual alone, or a similarity related to multiple individuals, which is co-extensive with all cows, just as the cognition residing in the speaker is co-extensive with the word.
"Conditioned by limiting adjuncts."

The point is that since knowability and so forth are not distinct from cognition and so forth, knowability and the rest are simply the nature of cognition itself. [This is expressed by the term] "successively" (paramparā).
The meaning is: by way of a relation consisting in having as its object that which is inherent in itself.
[This refers to] the property of subsisting in only one [locus].

The universal "cowness" (*gotva*), which resides in any particular cow-body present before one, is connected to all cows through a mediated relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting in being the locus of cowness, which is the substratum of similarity whose counter-correlate is that [particular cow].
Thus, the derivation and usage of the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) is possible.
Alternatively, similarity itself is connected to the infinite individual cows related to it through the relation of being related to it; thus, the derivation and usage [of the word] is established.

The cognition residing in the speaker, which has as its object the speaker's own cognition and which, being common to all [referents] by virtue of their connection with itself among the multiple objects, serves as the basis for the derivation of that word *tat* which bears the technical name "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*).
Since it is well known that pronouns denote whatever is present in the mind,
the meaning is "nevertheless. Furthermore,

by means of a counter-argument (*pratibandhī*) against the "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) residing in eternal substances as accepted by the logicians (*tārkika*), he says— "Moreover, in the case of absolutely..."— in order to establish the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) and so forth even for a category of properties that are not co-inherent (*ananugata*).
The meaning is that it is excluded [from others], even though there exists another differentiator (*vyāvartaka*).

(30) Now, it might be argued that since it was stated that a property consisting of an adventitious attribute (*aupādhika-dharma*) is not distinct from its substrate (*upādhi*), there is no loss of essential nature (*svarūpa-hāni*) when particulars are subsumed under a specific genus residing in the substrate—which serves as the constituent of the adventitious property—by means of a transitive relation. Now, let it be granted that in the four aforementioned cases such as the golden jar, since there is no inclusive property (*anugata-dharma*), the apprehension of capacity (*śakti*) and so forth must occur through non-inclusive properties due to the lack of any other alternative. Because there is an absence of proof and an absence of any means of establishing it— this being the underlying thought:
"How can one who has attained the state of ashes be desired to possess humanity once again?"
