Keeping in mind the sentences from the *Sudhā* commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna* regarding the Vaiśeṣika system—beginning with "Thus, etc."—the author first demonstrates the non-eternality of the universal (*jāti*) through specific perception (*viśiṣṭapratyakṣa*), by means of the following: perception whose object is the production and destruction of a thing qualified by a universal; reasoning concerning the production and destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyin*); scriptural texts that indicate the production and destruction of the universal; perception grasping the production and so forth of the universal alone; and Śruti. He states this with the words beginning "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*).
This representation of the form of the cognition of the arising and destruction of a limited measure and blue color—as "this is gross," and so forth—[is what is meant].
Thus, "because of experience."

And since this [cognition] has both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*)—such as "pot-ness" or "cloth-ness"—as its objects, it has been stated that the production and destruction of the universal are indeed perceived directly.
(Note on variants: 1. *nīlam utpannam iti nāsti* — Naṃ.Ja.; 2. *paṭa utpannaḥ ghaṭo naṣṭaḥ paṭo naṣṭaḥ* — Ga.; 3. *eva* — Naṃ.Ja.Rā.Su.; 4. *tyayena* — Naṃ.U.; 5. *lam utpannam i* — U.E.)

Nor should it be argued that this cognition regarding a qualified object is possible through the mere production of the individual substrate, rather than through the production of the qualified entity;
for the opposite view could equally well be maintained.
Furthermore, it would follow that cognitions such as "a gross object has arisen" would likewise [be erroneous].

Furthermore, just as in a substance the destruction and production of blue and red colors occur through baking, so too, while the substance itself persists, the destruction and production of "copper-ness" and "silver-ness" are observed through the application of medicinal substances and the like. Now, one might object: this experience has as its object an individual qualified by a universal; it does not have both the jar and jar-ness as its objects, because it takes as its object the production and destruction of both, as in the thought, "the jar and jar-ness have been produced."
And thus, he raises the objection that [the reason] might be otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) by saying: "If not... (*na ceti*).

Is it because, when the [cognition] can be accounted for by having only one of the two as its object, it is postulated as having both as its objects only due to the complexity of the assumption (*kalpanā-gaurava*), or rather because there is a sublation (*bādha*) regarding the qualifier—as in cases such as "the man with the staff does not exist"?
Regarding the first [alternative], he says: "Because the opposite is also possible."
The meaning of "even by [the view of] mere birth, arising, and so forth" is that even in this case, parsimony (lāghava) is possible;
on the contrary, this alone is logical.
With the intention that "the qualified [subject] would not reach the qualifier due to the maxim that 'one whose power is exhausted does not qualify'," it was stated: "because it is easy to say."

Now, one might object: since the primary factor is the qualificand, it is more appropriate for cognitions such as "origination" to have that qualificand as their object, rather than having as their referent a subordinate attribute (dharma); to this, he says: "It is gross."
Thusness.
The meaning is that it has as its purpose the production of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*).

Now, one might object: "Since we observe the cessation of qualities such as blue even while the substance itself persists, it is not logical to conclude that the same applies there [in the case of the self]. To this, he says: "Furthermore... (kiṃ ca).

Since the theory of cooking within the seed (*pīlupākavāda*) lacks authoritative proof, contradicts the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that will be mentioned as a valid means of knowledge, and has already been refuted in the *Sudhā* during the very discussion on the rejection of universals (*jāti*), the theory of cooking within the pot (*piṭharapākavāda*) alone is accepted; with this intention, it was stated: "only while the substance exists."

In the second case as well, is it the experience of the universal (*jāti*) in the locus where the individual (*vyakti*) has perished that constitutes the sublation, or is it the experience of it in another individual? (Regarding the phrase *ata-jātau-bākam*: [The word "etc. (*ādi*) is not present in the manuscripts Na and Ja; the reading *cānyathā* is found in U and E.]

Regarding the doctrine of the universal (*jāti*): [It is argued that] even when the individual substance (*puruṣa*) has perished, and even when the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) has perished like a staff, the universal is still perceived in that very same location;
whereby the cognition of its production and so forth would have as its object merely the production and so forth of the substratum (*viśeṣya*).
However, experience [of the universal] occurs in other individual instances even in the case of dimension (*parimāṇa*) and so forth.
The assumption that the universal is not experienced there due to the absence of a manifesting individual instance applies equally to dimension and the rest as well.
Furthermore, the eternality of the universal has not yet been established.
Because there is no recognition (pratyabhijñā) such as "this very thing is that same cowness," whereby a discrepancy in terms of magnitude and so forth might arise; rather,
the cognitions "this is a cow" and "this too is a cow" have similarity as their object, just like the cognition "this is fat" and "this too is fat."
Furthermore, [the objection is raised]: "How can that which is inherent in it [the substance] arise prior to it, or after its destruction?
He refutes the first [alternative] with the words: "And not... (na ca).
He states the second [point]: "In another individual," etc.

Now, one might object: "Even though the universal (jāti) continues to exist when the destruction of an individual occurs, there may be a lack of perception due to the absence of a manifester (vyañjaka). To this, he says: "The manifester," etc.

Now, one might object: since permanence is not established for [qualities] such as dimension (*parimāṇa*), the assumption that non-perception is caused by the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is groundless;
however, this is not the case for a universal (*jāti*). To this, they say: "And even now... and so forth.

Now, [an objection might be raised]: "Is it not the case that the eternity of the universal (*jāti*) is established by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) or by a continuous cognition (*anugatamati*)? Therefore, since recognition is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by its very nature, it is not subject to doubt. Anticipating this, the author clarifies what was stated in the *Āsudhā* (the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā-vimarśinī*), saying: "It is just like 'this is that very same thing' (*tadevedamiva*)."
[Objection: But surely, how can that which has an unoriginated birth not be eternal?
[For there is] the contradiction with the following inference: "Birth is eternal, because it is an entity without beginning, like space. To this, he says: "Furthermore... (kiṃ ca).

Alternatively, having stated the perceptual evidence for the non-eternality of the universal (*jāti*), he now sets forth the arguments stated in the *Sudhā*— namely, "the subject of dispute is possessed of destruction, because it is inherent in a substrate that is possessed of destruction, like color and so forth"— with the passage beginning with "Furthermore" and ending with "it would follow our own position."
Because it is a rule.
The meaning is that it is observed to be so in the case of the qualities and actions of a whole (*avayavin*).

Furthermore, since non-existence is a fixed state, how could potness and the like be beginningless or eternal?

Furthermore, if a genus (*jāti*) were to exist as a distributed entity (*vyāsajyajvṛtti*), like duality and so forth, then—just like those—it could not be cognized without the cognition of all its substrata. Consequently, if one were to relinquish a substance intended merely for "fire" (as in the case of the *agnīṣomīya* injunction), the meaning of the scriptural injunction "one should give a cow" would remain unfulfilled if only a single individual cow were given. Thus, the purpose of that scriptural rule would not have been accomplished.

Now, one might argue that the very fact of being a universal (*anugatatva*) is a sublation of the genus' impermanence; therefore, it is more reasonable that cognitions such as "the jar is destroyed" have only the individual (*vyakti*) as their object. To this, [the author] refutes even the notion of being a universal, while illustrating the words of the *Sudhā*: "A property that resides in many is not perceived in the cognition of each single instance, as is the case with duality and so forth. Yet, humanity (*naratva*) and the like are perceived in the cognition of each single instance; therefore, they are not universals. He states this with the words "Moreover... (*api ca*).
Does the universal (jāti) exist by not being fully exhausted in each individual instance, or by being fully exhausted?
Regarding the first [alternative], he says: "Of the universal," and so forth.
The word division is *apratītiḥ syāt* (there would be non-comprehension);
the meaning is that there would be no comprehension. [The example is] *agnimātra*.

For on the full moon day, a triad of rites known as the Āgneya, the Upāṃśuyāja, and the Āgnīṣomīya is performed. Among these, regarding the substance in the form of a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) prepared upon eight potsherds— as referred to in the scriptural statement, "That which belongs to Agni, consisting of eight potsherds, is not omitted on the new moon and on the full moon day"— it is offered by means of the mere dedication to Agni with the thought, "This is for Agni, not mine."

The point is this: even when the Āgneya sacrifice, which consists of renunciation, has been performed, the scriptural injunction stating, "He offered the cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma at the full moon," remains unfulfilled; for if that were the case, since the purpose would have been achieved through the Āgneya alone, it would follow that the Agniṣomīya sacrifice would never be performed.
For, just like deityhood, cowness (*gotva*) also exists as a distributed whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*);

and if it were to be fully present in each individual, then because it would not be fully present in each [individual] by way of subsisting in every single instance, it would follow that our own position is correct.
Moreover—due to the destruction of the caste of Brāhmaṇa-hood and so forth by means of great sins (mahāpātaka) and the like—[one might object]:

"But surely, according to the technical rule (paribhāṣā) 'the prescription of a suffix depends on the semantic capacity of the word' (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), since taddhita suffixes are prescribed only from a semantically capable word, the suffix *ḍhak* [in the form *āgneya*] would be contradicted if Agni were not accompanied by others, because his status as a deity [would not be established]. Therefore, in that case, it must refer to Agni alone."
It has been stated that even when the renunciation of the substance (*dravya*) has been performed, the *agnīṣomīya* [offering] itself has not yet been performed.

In that context, since both Agni and Soma are intended to constitute a single deity residing in both through mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), there would otherwise arise the contingency of forming a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix—such as in "from *dyāvāpṛthivī*, *śunāsīra*, *marutvat*, *agnīṣoma*, *vāstoṣpati*, and *gṛhamedha*"—if this were not the case; therefore, he says: "just like the status of being a deity" (*devatātvavat*).
Having explained the statement regarding the nectar (*sudhāvākya*) according to the first position, he himself refutes the second position with the words: "pratyeka... (each individually).

At the conclusion of the commentary on the passage beginning with "likewise [the distinction] between the two specific castes," he declares the eternity of caste through both scripture and the reasoning stated in the *Tattvaviveka-ṭīkā*: "There is both difference and non-difference between Brāhmaṇahood and the physical body; [otherwise], the caste would perish due to a mortal sin (mahāpātaka)," and so forth. Furthermore, he states: "Moreover, by means of a mortal sin and the like..."
“The Brahmin who sells milk becomes a Śūdra within a month”—
by such scriptural authorities (āgama), the production of castes such as Śūdra-hood is established.
As for the production of the caste of Brāhmaṇa-hood in Viśvāmitra:
From Gādhi was born one of great splendor, like a kindled fire;
having abandoned the *kṣatriya* nature through asceticism, he attained the luster of a *brahman*.

The production of castes such as *śūdra* and so forth for Viśvāmitra, Śaṅkha, and others—resulting from the destruction of their previous caste, such as *kṣatriya*, through boons or curses and the subsequent production of castes such as *brāhmaṇa*—is established by scripture (*āgama*).

Furthermore, the production of a caste such as "gold-ness" (*kāñcanatva*) upon the destruction of "iron-ness" (*ayas-tva*) through contact with fire and the like is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). How, then, can there be a rule of the eternality of caste?
Furthermore:

"All objects of experience are indeed distinct and possess distinct attributes"— thus, the distinction of attributes for each individual entity is established by such scriptural testimony (*śruti*) as this,
and is also established by traditional authority (*āgama*).
The birth of the kṣatriya named Triśaṅku into the caste of a caṇḍāla:
"His son was Satyavrata, renowned as Triśaṅku;
he attained the state of a caṇḍāla due to the curse of his guru. . . .
Thus, the birth of Kalmāṣapāda as a Brahma-rākṣasa of a particular species is established by the scripture in the seventh chapter of the ninth book [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*]:
"They call him Mitrāsaha, who was once known as Kalmaṣāṅghri (the 'Stained-footed')."
Due to Vasiṣṭha’s curse, he became a Rākṣasa. . . .
The meaning is that [the power] is established by such examples.
"Sparśavedhin" is the name of a specific medicinal herb.
He cites the scriptural authority as explained in the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the Vaiśeṣika system: "And they are distinct," etc.

Nor should it be suspected that the phrase "possessing distinct attributes" means "possessing attributes distinct from their own selves," for such an interpretation would contradict the specific scriptural statement: "And they are non-distinct through their respective attributes. This is the intended meaning.

One might object: "Could it not be that the scriptural passage beginning with 'By [selling] meat for a month he becomes a Śūdra' is intended merely to censure the sale of milk, or perhaps to demonstrate the loss of the duties of the three higher castes? To this, he says: "And not... (na ca).
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). [The verse continues:
"From *ata* and *jati*, the suffix *bāka*."

And in the absence of a subverting factor, it is not logical for a scripture to have a figurative meaning, nor is it appropriate to regard the recognition "a lump of iron has become gold" as a cognitive error. (Jativada, p. 301)

Furthermore, since the non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) has been established elsewhere, how could there be a continuous persistence (*anugati*) of the universal (*jāti*) which is non-different from the individual (*vyakti*)? Therefore, if [the passage] were intended for the purpose of censuring the ritual action (*karmanindā*), then—just as the prohibition against threatening a Brāhmaṇa in the statement “one should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa” is subordinate to that prohibition—the statements regarding the hundredfold torments, such as “he who threatens him shall be punished with a hundred [strokes],” would also be intended for the censure of the action. Consequently, they would lack the status of having a [specific] fruit (*phala*). Thus, [the objection regarding] the *śaṃyo*...
Furthermore, there would arise a contradiction with the *avagoraṇādhikaraṇa* in the fourth pāda of the third adhyāya [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], which states "and all [acts] such as causing distress.

Moreover, if the purpose were to establish the loss of the ear for the three castes, then in passages such as "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should install the sacred fires," it could be argued that the word "Brāhmaṇa" refers to one who is devoid of the duties of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; consequently, since the Śūdra would also be capable of possessing the sacred fires and Vedic knowledge...

It should also be noted that [the opponent's view] would entail the consequence of falling under the scope of Vedic rituals, which would contradict the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning those who are not Śūdras) located in the first quarter of the sixth book [of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā Sūtra].
As for the argument that even the scripture stating "Viśvāmitra was born from Gādhi" and so forth refers only to Viśvāmitra’s fitness for the duties of a Brāhmaṇa—
that too is not correct;
for in the absence of a subverting factor (bādhaka), it is improper to abandon the primary meaning.
The meaning is that the permanence of the genus (*jāti*) remains unestablished even now.

Now, as for what was said regarding "piercing by touch" and so forth, that is not so; for such a perception is unestablished. Or, even if it were established, let it be considered an error. To this, he says: "the iron ball."
And the phrase "provided there is no subverting proof" (*bādhaka*) should be supplied [to the previous argument].
The sense is that the process of the ripening of *pīlu* fruits is both unauthoritative and contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
By this, one should understand that the previously mentioned statement, "only when a substance exists," and so forth, is also established.
"In another place" means:
The intended meaning is that [this is established] in the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the Vaiśeṣika system, as well as in works such as the *Tattvaviveka*.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Second Chapter, p. 302) (Note: Variants noted in the manuscript: 1. *pakāra* – Naṃ. U. E.; 2. *ddhadoṣam* – Naṃ. U. E.)
By this, the claim that "jāti" (the universal) is one and the same due to parsimony is refuted;
and it has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*:
"In the same way, even 'humanity' and so forth are understood as being distinct properties according to their respective instances."

Thus, like color and other qualities, a "universal" (*jāti*) is not a single entity; rather, "generality" (*sāmānya*) is simply similarity, based on the etymological derivation that "generality" is the state (*bhāva*) of those things that are similar.
And this, according to the method already stated, is what is "concomitant.
Therefore, from the destruction of an individual qualified by a universal, there arises through perception such cognitions as "the jar is destroyed."

By means of arguments such as the destruction of the genus (*jāti*) occurring through the destruction of its inherent substratum (*samavāyin*) or through its complete exhaustion in each individual instance, [it is shown that] the destruction of properties like "copper-ness" occurs only while the individual object exists; this is established by perception. Furthermore, the destruction of the genus "Brahmin-ness" and so forth is established by scripture. Thus, there is a distinction of properties for each individual.
Having thus refuted the eternality and the pervasive nature (*anugatatva*) of the genus, he refutes its unity as well with the words "by this" (*etena*).
The meaning is: "by means of the refutation of [the notions of] permanence and pervasiveness.
And it has been said: //
The meaning is that the non-inclusion of the universal (jāti) has been stated in the section concerning the Vaiśeṣikas; "is cognized" (īyate) means "is perceived" (pratīyate).
Now, one might ask: "In that case, what is the status of conventional usage regarding universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and so forth? To this, he says: "But the universal... and so on.
"Of those who are equal" means "of those who are similar";
[this is] according to the manner stated above.
The meaning is: "in accordance with the method stated in the Śaktivyaptyādigrahasamarthana-vāda";
[this refers to] by means of perception such as "the jar has perished."
The meaning is: "by means of a perception whose object is a specific destruction.

Furthermore, because [the two statements]—one expressed by the words "only when the substance exists" and so forth, and the other expressed by the words "pierced by touch" and so forth—have the same referent and thus constitute a single simultaneous synthesis, this is a restatement of the earlier inclusion even though it was mentioned later as being established by scripture (āgama).
Furthermore, they say that this is merely a re-elucidation by means of another example of what was already stated in the passage beginning with "only when the substance exists," etc.;

moreover, this is for the purpose of demonstrating that [the cognition] is non-erroneous by showing it to be a perception in the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and for the purpose of refuting the theory of the baking of atoms (*pīlupākavāda*). Therefore, there is no fault of redundancy.
Since it is established by the aforementioned scripture that the meaning [of words] is the individual (vyakti), there is no following of the genus (jāti). (Vidhivāda, p. 303)
Thus, even in the absence of a universal (jāti), it is logical to grasp the expressive power (śakti) as residing in that which is associated [with the word].

Thus, even the verbal suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are capable of denoting an injunction in the form of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) when conjoined [with other words]; therefore, the cognition of being a means to a desired end alone is the motivator of action.
[This is] the refutation regarding the [view that the universal] is inherent in the individuals.
// 31 // Now, he summarizes the meaning of the three arguments stated previously—beginning with "In your view, [the universal] which subsumes all individual cows"—with the words:
"Therefore, in this way... (tadevam).
He says "evam" (thus) at the beginning of the introduction to the respondent's argument.

Based on the Master’s statement, "One acts only after knowing that [the action] is a means to what is desired," he says: the cognition that something is a means to what is desired is itself the motivator.

Now, an objection is raised: "The cognition of an injunction (*vidhi*) is the motivator, and the injunction consists in the optative suffix (*liṅ*), according to the traditional rule of Pāṇini: 'The optative (*liṅ*) and the imperative (*loṭ*) are used in the senses of injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), permission (*āmantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*saṃpraśna*), and prayer (*prārthana*),' and so forth.
How can this be so? To this it is replied: "In the sense of an injunction consisting in being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*)."
It is stated as "anvita" (connected) in order to make known its distinction from the Nyāya view.
The meaning is: "connected with that which is either fit for sacrifice and so forth, or its opposite."
An objection regarding [the view that] the genus is inherent [in the individual].
// 31 // Now, an objection regarding the view that the intention of the speaker constitutes the meaning of the indicative mark (liṅga) and so forth. // 32 //
But surely, being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is not the injunction (*vidhi*).
For if that were the case, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) would be [identical] with the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*liṅ-artha*).
Now, [the author states] the refutation of the view that the intention of a trustworthy person (*āptābhiprāya*) is the meaning of the injunctive suffix and other such markers: // 32 //
He raises an objection to what was stated previously: "Now, indeed... (nanv ati).

The meaning is that the "injunction" (*vidhi*) mentioned in Pāṇini’s sūtra beginning with *vidhinimantraṇa* as having the sense of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, does not consist in being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (Second Chapter, page 304).

If it is argued that because the instrumental case is already expressed by the verbal suffix (*liṅga*), the third case ending prescribed under the rule governing "unexpressed" [factors] (*anabhihitādhikāra*)—as in "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid* (*udbhidā yajeta*)"—would be untenable, we say no;
for even though the general capacity as a means (*sādhanatva*) is expressed, its specific aspect, namely instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), remains unexpressed.
This is because another indicator (*liṅga*)—namely, the proximity to its own base (*svaprakṛti*)—[establishes it].
The sense is that by this [means], that knowledge becomes the initiator [of action].
"By way of the meaning of an injunction" (*vidhyarthena*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the meaning is "by being expressed," that is, "by being stated."

The section concerning the unexpressed (*anabhihitādhikāra*). In the third word of the second [section], the governing rule (*adhikārasūtra*) is “when not expressed” (*anabhihite*). This means that when [the agent or object] is not already expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), a primary derivative (*kṛt*), a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), or a compound (*samāsa*). Within the section on the continuity of the term “when not expressed” (*anabhihita-anuvṛtti-prakaraṇa*), by the rule “the third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument” (*kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā*), [the third case is prescribed].
Since it is prescribed that the third case ending occurs for the agent and the instrument when they are not already expressed by verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), the third case would not apply here;

for in the sentence "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the fact that the sacrifice is the means for achieving the desired result in the form of cattle resides in the sacrifice itself, and thus, being connected to the sacrifice, it is already expressed by the verbal suffix in "yajeta."

And because, according to the logic of the *udbhid* section in the fourth pāda of the first adhyāya, the word *udbhid*—as a qualifying adjunct (*upapada*)—denotes a sacrifice, the meaning of the third case ending in the word *udbhid* is precisely the instrumentality residing in the sacrifice; therefore, [the term refers to] that specific [sacrifice].

The meaning is as follows: according to Pāṇini’s rule, "the most effective means is the *karaṇa* (instrument)," the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) consists in a specific kind of instrumentality characterized by being the most effective means.

Since it is precisely this [status] that is the meaning of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), and since we accept that the injunction (*vidhi*) consists solely in being a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), rather than accepting that the injunction consists in being the instrument for what is desired (*iṣṭakaraṇatva*), the sense conveyed by both the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and the third case-ending is that the sacrifice called *udbhid* is both a means to what is desired and an instrumental factor (*karaṇakāraka*).

Now, one might object: "Even if the sacrifice such as *udbhid* is not denoted by the verbal suffix (*liṅ*) as the cause (*kāraṇatva*), since it is nonetheless denoted as the means (*sādhanatva*), why is there not an instrumental case ending? To this he replies with the words "not... by the suffix" (*na... liṅga*), stating that the specific [term] such as *udbhid* is not denoted even as the means.

Alternatively, he says "liṅga" [in the verse], meaning that even though the word *liṅga* expresses causality (*kāraṇatva*), there is no expression of the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) obtainable from the third case ending.

Because the connection with the meaning of the nominal stem (*liṅga*) occurs prior to the connection with the meaning of the suffix (*upapada*), it is the more "internal" (*antaraṅga*) factor; this is the reason [for its priority]. [This applies] even before the introduction of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth.
[This is stated] because the meaning of the suffix is dependent upon the meaning of the stem.
Vidhivāda, p. 305:

Even though the fact that [the sacrifice] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is expressed as residing in the mere meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), since that [means-to-an-end-ness] residing in the meaning of the nominal stem *udbhid*—which constitutes the specific form of the sacrifice—is not expressed, the third case ending following the nominal stem *udbhid* is possible.
In that regard, the reason is: "one's own nature."

Even in the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related), the meaning of a word is understood as being related to others only in a general sense; the specific relation to other [words] is brought about by the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other words—this is the intended meaning. By this, the objection that "in the case of *udbhidā*, the instrumental suffix is redundant because the means is already known through the indicative mark (*liṅga*), or it serves merely for the grammatical correctness of the word" is refuted. This is because the instrumental suffix can be meaningful either by signifying the instrumentality not expressed by the indicative mark, or by signifying the instrumentality residing in the meaning of the nominal stem *udbhid*.

As for what Rucidatta and others have stated— that because the specific sacrifice in the form of the *udbhid* is denoted by way of the general property of being a means (*sādhanatva-sāmānya*) or by way of the general property of being a means to the sacrifice (*yāga-sādhanatva-sāmānya*),

the third case (*tṛtīyā*) prescribed by the rule on "the unexpressed" (*anabhihitādhikāra*) is not appropriate— that is incorrect. For if the third case were inapplicable due to some manner of being "denoted," then in cases such as "one should make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kuryāt*), where the optative suffix (*liṅ*) signifies that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), the second case would become untenable, since the mat would also be "denoted" by virtue of its being the object of desire.
For in the present case as well, it is the same: that very reality which was stated in that form serves as the refuter of the second [alternative] and the others.

As for the claim that the meaning of Pāṇini’s sūtra is: "When the number residing in the agent or the instrument is not expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) and so forth, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) occurs;

but when it is expressed, it does not," and that according to this principle, the third case occurs here because the number residing in the instrument is expressed—this is the view of Pakṣadhara and others.
That is not so;

for in the treatise establishing that the agent and the object are the meanings of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), it will be refuted that [the suffix] expresses merely the number residing in the agent and so forth.
However,
some say that even the status of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) pertaining to the sacrifice is obtained solely through the force of syntactic relation (*saṃsargamaryādā*),
and is not directly denoted (*abhidhīyate*).
But even so—[it might be argued that] the injunction is not the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*).

Why? Because when the question "Whence does this [status of] being an agent arise? is asked, *iṣṭasādhanatva* is made the reason for the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatva*), as in the statement "because it is a means to a desired end."

"Even though the fact that [the sacrifice] is a means to a desired end is understood through the explanatory passage (arthavāda), ‘He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes death and overcomes the murder of a Brahmin,’ there is still an inference of the injunctive suffix (vidhipratyaya) because of it.

Regarding the point made in the *Maṇi* at the end of the section on injunctions (*vidhivāda*), prior to the words "But the moderns (*navyāḥ*) say," where a resolution is offered—namely, that the status of the sacrifice as a means to a desired end is actually obtained through the theory of expressed connection (*abhihitānvaya*), since the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is merely the state of being a means to a desired end—the author states: "Some, however... (*kecit tu*).

And here, since the sacrifice is obtainable from the verbal root (dhātu), and since the relation of the sacrifice being a means to a desired end and the relation of locus and located can be established through the scope of syntactic connection (saṃsarga-maryādā) by the force of the co-utterance (samabhivyāhāra) of the base and the suffix, the meaning is that the denotation of the optative suffix (liṅ) applies only to "being a means to a desired end" alone, because the function of denoting [the sacrifice] would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava).

The seed of dissatisfaction here, however, is as follows: since it has been established that if the denotation of the related (anvitābhidhāna) were possible through relation alone, it would result in the fault of the meaning not being verbal (*aśābdatva*), the function of denotation (*abhidhā*) itself must be admitted there; thus, even in your view, since the relation—which constitutes the sentence-meaning—is not something capable of being denoted, its communication by means of an indicator (*liṅga*) and so forth certainly exists. This is what should be kept in mind. The author of the *Maṇi* (Gaṅgeśa), at the end of the section on injunction (*vidhi*), restated the view of Udayana—that the meaning of an indicator and so forth is simply the speaker’s intention—and the author now raises an objection against this with the words "But surely... (*nanu*).

He explains the five reasons found in the verse to be cited beginning with "Because of being a cause" (*hetutvāt*) by stating their extracted meaning according to the method set forth in the *Kusumāñjali* and *Vardhamāna*, starting with the words "From where does this [arise]? (*kuta idam*).

If the status of something as a means to a desired end is understood through the optative suffix (*liṅ*), the imperative (*loṭ*), the gerundive (*tavya*), and so forth, then the statement of a reason would be redundant.

Since the intention of a trustworthy person (*āpta*) is the meaning of the optative suffix and other such markers, the phrase "this should be done" would mean: "the speaker has a desire conducive to my performing this."
Regarding the view that the suffix *-liṅ* expresses the meaning of *āpta* (trustworthiness)—
[this is] the theory of injunction (*vidhivāda*), page 307.

Following the cognition that [an action] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), at the time of performing the ritual, the second-person and first-person suffixes (*madhyama* and *uttama puruṣa*) employed in the forms *kuryāḥ* and *kuryām* express nothing other than the intentions regarding the actions performed by the person being addressed and the agent himself, respectively.
And because it is so understood;
for it is established that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others, which have meanings such as addressing (*āmantraṇa*) consisting of a particular form of desire, denote desire itself.

Furthermore, in that context, when there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to "why [is this so]?", the reason "because it is a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatvāt*) becomes meaningful—this is the intended sense.
Regarding the phrase "being a means to what is desired":

In the case of the *aśvadāyāga* (horse-giving sacrifice), although its status as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is understood from the *brahma* [mantra] during the crossing, it is nonetheless established here through the inference of an injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth by means of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because the inseparable connection between the injunction and the explanatory passage has been proven in the *Arthavāda-adhikaraṇa*; or else, because being a means to a desired end is pervaded by the injunction, the injunction is inferred by means of that [status].

Alternatively, [the meaning is as follows]: if the capacity to convey that something is a means to a desired end were established through [independent] indicators such as the *liṅga* suffix, then the inference of a Vedic injunction—such as "one who desires to cross over the sin of killing a Brahmin should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha"—would be redundant.

However, if it is the intention of a trustworthy person (*āpta*), there is no fault; for the distinction between the two types of inference is this: in the case of the Aśvamedha and so forth, one infers, "Because this is a means to what I desire, the trustworthy person has a desire conducive to my purpose. This is the underlying point.
He clarifies the third reason, beginning with "madhyama" (middle), by stating "iṣṭa" (desired).

For it is observed that even when there is the desire "May my result be accomplished through fate or even by the action of another," despite the knowledge of the specific capacity to produce a desired object as described by you, [action does not follow].
And even when there is the cognition that [an action] is achievable through effort, there is an absence of activity due to the absence of the desire "I shall accomplish this result through effort."
If it is argued: "In that case, you too must admit that the cognition of an action as being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatvajñāna*) is a motivator"; [the reply is: True.
[This is what is meant by] "desire for the aforementioned result."

The phrase "I shall accomplish the fruit of the action" means a desire characterized by the mode [of cognition] that it is to be accomplished by an effort (kṛti) as previously stated; [this refers to] "of a conscious being."
It should be understood that this is for the sake of clarifying the meaning or for establishing the connection with the phrase "when the two cognitions exist.

This is a specification by way of explaining the phrase "the cognition of being a task to be accomplished" (*kāryatvajñāna*)—namely, "and the cognition of being achievable through volitional effort."
"By the absence of desire."

The meaning is that it is accepted that a desire for a fruit characterized by the mode of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is the cause of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
[This is stated] "as that which instigates" (*pravartakatvena*).
The meaning is that the cognition of a result as being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is accepted as the cause for the desire for a result of the aforementioned nature.

Thus, since that cognition is produced by the injunctive suffixes (*liṅgādi*) and so forth, it follows that "being achievable through effort" is also the meaning of the injunctive suffixes; this is the core point. Keeping in mind the statement from the *Karmanirṇaya*, "But the meaning of the injunctive suffixes and so forth is simply 'being a means to what is desired' (*iṣṭasādhanatva*)," he offers a rebuttal with the words beginning "True... (*satyam*).

If so, by what means then is there the cognition that [an action] is to be accomplished through effort, and why is it not produced from an inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth? To this he says: "Of the action... (kriyāyā iti).
The meaning is: "consisting of sacrifice and so forth. It is not, however, produced by words that possess those [sacrificial acts] as their indicative mark (*liṅga*).

Since the fact that an action is to be accomplished through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is understood through positive and negative concomitance with effort, the *liṅ* suffix is not postulated as having its expressive power (*śakti*) in that respect.
For the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) does not state that the sacrifice is possible for one who desires heaven;
rather, it states only that it is a means to what is desired (*iṣṭasādhana*).
In that regard, one who is capable engages [in action], whereas one who is incapable does not.
Furthermore, the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is not "being a means to a desired end" while being achievable through effort.

Even though there is no contradiction between the states of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*) and being a means (*sādhanatva*) due to the difference in their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) and the difference in time—[the author] says "Not so" (*na hi*) in response to the following objection: "Now, just as it is said that although the mere state of being a means (*sādhanatvamātra*) can be the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*), yet by the force of [actual] cognition, the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) is the meaning of the optative suffix and so on; in the very same way, let it be said that by the force of cognition, the state of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is also the meaning of the optative suffix and so on. He says "Not so": *na hi*.
"It is possible."
The meaning is that he says, "it is to be accomplished by human effort," and specifically,
"it is the means to achieve what is desired."
The term "sacrifice" (yāga) is to be supplied [to the verse].
If that is so, why do not all people engage in it, or why do not all people refrain from it? To this he says: "In that regard, one who is capable."
The meaning is that he is capable of accomplishing the rite through a *kṛtyā*.
He says "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*) in response to one who is mistaken regarding the absence of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

With the words "To this it is said," and so forth, he restates their lack of contradiction according to the direction set forth in the *Maṇigrantha* of the Vidhivāda school—beginning with "sādhyatva" (the state of being a goal), and so on.
The counter-correlative.
Although it is contradictory for the same thing, such as cooking, to be both the goal (sādhya) with respect to one [agent] and the means (sādhana) with respect to that same [agent],
there is no contradiction in its being the goal with respect to its own causes, such as firewood, and the means with respect to its effects, such as boiled rice.
Because of the difference in the defining perspective (*nirūpaka*).

Likewise, at the very time when there is the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatva*), there is simultaneously the state of being the probans (*sādhanatva*). Otherwise, even in the section concerning the *vājapeya*, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) based on the impossibility [of simultaneous application] would not be established, since— according to the method of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)— it would be possible for both [the sacrifice and the substance] to be presented simultaneously by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).
This is because the two factors that cause [that application], namely the two impossibilities, are mutually contradictory when occurring one after the other in a single instance.
However, there is no contradiction with respect to time;

for at the time when [a property] is unestablished (*asiddha*), it is the "probandum" (*sādhya*), while in the state of being established (*siddha*), it is possible for it to be the "probans" (*sādhana*).
The meaning is "nevertheless."
"Because of the impossibility of their presence"— here,
the words "of the states of being the probandum and the probans" are to be supplied.
"Otherwise" (anyathā) means even without repetition, when [the two] appear simultaneously.

This refers to the fifth section (*adhikaraṇa*) within the fourth quarter (*pāda*) of the first book (*adhyāya*), concerning the phrase "If it be argued that because a quality is heard in a name, there must be an injunction":
"One who desires self-sovereignty [should sacrifice] with the Vājapeya"—is this an injunction regarding a quality consisting of a liquid substance, or is it the name of a ritual action?

In the case of doubt, since the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) contains, by virtue of the verbal suffix, a *bhāvanā*— which is synonymous with effort— and since the sacrifice (*yāga*) is understood through the force of the co-occurrence of the root and the suffix to have a general relationship that is common to both being an object (*karman*) and being a cause (*kāraṇa*), it follows that upon adopting the aspect of being an object, the connection— "one should perform the sacrifice with the substance *vāja* (food/grain) which is to be drunk, as denoted by the term *vājapeya*"— is possible simultaneously; thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that this [injunction] is intended to enjoin a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Since the mere relation [of the sacrifice] would be understood through its status as an object (*karmatva*) or its status as a cause (*kāraṇatva*), and because it would follow that either the accessory (*guṇa*) or the fruit (*phala*) would connect with the sacrifice [independently], it is impossible—without repetition—to bring about the specific presentation of both its status as an object and its status as a cause; therefore, one must accept that the sacrifice is understood solely by way of its being a cause, and it is only its connection with the fruit that needs to be stated. Thus, it was established in the Siddhānta that the word *vājapeya* is a name (*nāmadheya*).

And this achievability through one's own effort is not conveyed by the word [of the Veda].
Is this sacrifice to be accomplished by my own effort because it does not exist without my effort? If so,

Nor should it be argued that [the cognition] is verbal (śābda) because the *liṅ* suffix, which generates the impelling knowledge, is presented by the word [“liṅ”].

For this sacrifice must be performed by me who desires heaven, because its verbal root-meaning is headed by a *liṅ* suffix situated within a valid sentence co-occurring with the word “desiring heaven” (*svargakāma*). Thus, since everything would be established by inference alone, it would follow that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*)—just like other verbal suffixes—is merely the *kṛti* (effort), and not also the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). He says "Moreover" (api ca) because it is impossible for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth to denote a qualified [object] consisting of both being achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) and being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), since those two are established by other means; thus, the optative suffix and the like do not have that as their primary meaning.
Thus, [it is established] by means of inference alone.

The sense is that it is exactly so, as stated by you in your theory of injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, because one must necessarily strive with effort, thinking "I shall accomplish the result," the over-extension [of the definition] is prevented by the desire for the result alone;

In such injunctions as "One desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the Vājapeya," there arises a conflict regarding the sacrifice (*yāga*): on one hand, it possesses a triad of properties consisting of being the object of reference (*uddeśyatva*), being the subject of restatement (*anuvādyatva*), and being primary (*prādhānya*);

on the other hand, it possesses a triad of properties—being the thing to be adopted (*upādeyatva*), being the thing to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*), and being subordinate (*guṇatva*)—which reside in the same substratum as the means (*sādhana*).

These two triads of properties are mutually contradictory, because the triad beginning with "object of reference" stands in opposition, respectively, to the triad beginning with "thing to be adopted. Thus, these two contradictory sets of three properties would seemingly converge upon the single sacrifice.

The meaning is that this was stated in the *Sudhā* commentary, during the explanation of the concluding sentence—"Thus, the means [of proof] is accepted"—in the section refuting the "being-an-effect" (kāryatā) theory of others, which begins with "And there would be no such thing as being an effect," within the *Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa*.

For [the authors of] the *Sudhā* and the *Nirṇaya-ṭīkā*, having accepted that the cognition of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*)—which arises from another means of knowledge—is indeed the cause of inclination (*pravṛtti*), they merely negate that the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is the state of being achievable through effort.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Karmanirṇaya*: "The meaning of the optative suffix and so forth is simply the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*)," and "The purpose of the optative suffix and so forth is fulfilled precisely by its having the state of being a means to a desired end as its meaning."
In the commentary (*ṭīkā*) on that [verse] as well, regarding "the state of being achievable through action" (*kṛtisādhyatā*):

This is according to the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*:

The meaning is that the import of the sentence concerning the determination of truth is this: one engages in action only after knowing that the verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) express the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*).

it is not itself the motivator.

And thus, while the *Nirṇaya-ṭīkā* denies the direct utility of the knowledge that an action is to be accomplished by effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), it is instead concerned with its indirect utility; therefore, there is no contradiction.

The absence of an obstacle is required for all causal operations. Thus, the doctrine of injunction (vidhivāda) serves as the negation of any other possible basis for the cognition that [an action] is to be accomplished by volitional effort (kṛtisādhyatvajñāna).

However, the desire for the fruit (*phalecchā*), like the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥsaṃyoga*) and so forth, is a cause of activity in its own right as an existing entity, specifically by being the object of an effort (*kṛti*) directed toward that which is a means to the desired end.

Furthermore, you yourself must admit that this [desire], although separated from the effort directed toward the means by some intermediate steps, is nonetheless a cause of activity provided it is not interrupted by an operation contrary to itself.

350) @----------------------- ---------- -- But when [the object] is known, attachment and aversion—which exist by their very nature—are the causes; however, for the initial activity of an infant, the cognition that something is a means to a desired end arises from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous birth through the power of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living. Thus, everything is well-established.
The refutation of the claim that "being a means to a desired end" qualified by "being achievable through human effort" and so forth constitutes the nature of an injunction. // 35 //

The meaning is that there is no fault in stating that what is known as the immediate cause for activity and so forth is precisely the form of being a means to achieve a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and the like.
The refutation of the view that the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*) consists in being a means characterized by being achievable through human effort. // 35
